[Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, commentary on Surah 37, verse 5]

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ This sentence follows the emphasis on the Oneness of God with an argument that establishes that truth, because an oath, which is given for emphasis, does not convince the addressees, since they deny the one who conveyed the oath to them. The sentence is therefore a resumptive clause of explanation (*istinaf bayani*) that clarifies the One God, and it incorporates (*idmaj*) an argument for identifying Him by mentioning a attribute that is among His distinctive qualities, which necessitates that He alone is divine.

The phrase ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimated sense is: "He is the Lord of the heavens," meaning: your God, who is One, is He whom you know to be the Lord of the heavens and the earth, and so on to the end of the verse.

The phrase (﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and its omission follows the usual manner of omitting the subject of a statement that comes after a prior reference to it, as the author of *al-Miftah* (*Miftah al-'Ulum*) has noted.

The polytheists, despite their extremism in associating partners with God, did not dare to claim that their idols created or governed the upper worlds. How could they reach them, when they are mere lowly beings upon the face of the earth? Thus God's sole creatorship was the most decisive argument against them regarding the falsehood of the divinity of the idols.

The heavens, the earth, and what is between them include all the worlds visible to people, with their celestial bodies, their inhabitants, and the beings that exist within them.

The singling out of the easts (*al-mashariq*) for mention from among what lies between the heavens and the earth is because they are states that are witnessed every day.

The plural form *al-mashariq* is used in view of the variation in the rising point of the sun over the half-year of its cycle, which is the solar year, and which comprises one hundred and eighty risings (easts). This is considered in relation to the longest day of the solar year and its shortest, each recurring twice in the year, beginning from the winter solstice to the autumn equinox. These are close rising points, not identical ones. The word *al-mashriq* (singular, "the east") is the name for the place where the sun rises, that is, its appearance. If they regard the direction without distinguishing the seasons, they say *al-mashriq* in the singular. If the two seasons, winter and summer, are considered, it is said *rabb al-mashriqayn* ("Lord of the two easts"). The plural *al-mashariq* may also be understood in view of the variation of the rising points at the beginnings of the four seasons. The verse is suitable for both considerations, so that each group of people may take lessons from it according to the extent of their own reflection.

[p. 88]

**"Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars* and [made it] a guard against every rebellious devil"** (Q. 37:6–7). This sentence comes within the statement "the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them" (Q. 37:5) as evidence that He is the Lord of the heavens. He limited the statement to the lordship over the heavens because their existence necessitates the lordship over the earth by a fortiori reasoning (*bi-ṭarīq al-awlā*).

It also includes a favour upon people, in that He placed for them in the sky the adornment of the stars, which delights their gaze, for the beauty of sights is a pleasure to those who look. He, may He be exalted, said: **"And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home [at evening] and when you send them out [to pasture]"** (Q. 16:6). It is also a favour upon the Muslims, in that He placed in those stars a guard against the devils' eavesdropping on the Unseen decreed by God, in order to cut off the path by which the soothsayers (*kuhhān*) could gain knowledge of some of what would happen on earth, so that they would not mislead people in Islam as they had misled them in the Jahiliyya. This also honours the Prophet (ﷺ), in that soothsaying was cut off at the time of his mission. It further points to the great religious benefit in it, which is the removal of doubt about the revelation, just as it has a worldly benefit, namely adornment and guidance by them in the darkness of land and sea.

They are of several kinds: some are great, some lesser; among them are the wandering stars (planets), the fixed stars, and fragments that revolve around the sun. There are wisdoms in the stars; among them is that they are an adornment of the sky at night. The stars are therefore the things by which the sky was adorned. As for the annexation (*iḍāfa*, construct) of *zīna* (adornment) to *al-kawākib* (the stars): if you take *zīna* as a verbal noun on the pattern *fi'la*, like *niṣba* (a relation), then it is the annexation of the verbal noun to its agent, meaning the stars adorned the sky; or to its object, meaning God adorned the stars, i.e. made them an adornment. If you take *zīna* as a noun for that with which one is adorned, like our saying *līqa* (the paste) for that with which the inkwell is smeared, then the annexation is genuine, in the sense of the origin (*ibtidā'iyya*), i.e. an adornment that results from the stars. In any case, the insertion of the word *zīna* is for emphasis, and the *bā'* (with) is causal, meaning: We adorned the nearest heaven by means of the adornment of the stars. It is as if it were said: "We adorned the nearest heaven with the stars, an adornment," so that "with the adornment of the stars" has the force of "with the stars, an adornment." Thus "bi-zīnati" is a verbal noun emphasizing the verb "zayyannā" (We adorned) in meaning, but with a shift in the construction: making "zīna" the element attached to "zayyannā," so as to convey the sense of causation and the sense of annexation in one construction, in the manner of concision. For it is already known that the stars are an adornment from their being linked to the verb "zayyannā," without any need to repeat "zīna," were it not for the meaning of causation and emphasis intended.

*al-dunyā* (the nearest): originally a feminine adjectival form of *al-adnā*, meaning "the nearer," i.e. nearness. What is meant is its nearness to the earth, namely the first of the seven heavens.

It is described as "the nearest" either because it is nearer to the earth than the rest of the heavens. On this view, the nearest heaven is the sphere that surrounds the terrestrial atmospheric sphere and is of great dimensions. The meaning of its adornment with the stars and meteors on this view is that God made the stars and meteors float in the concave of that sphere at various distances, and beyond that sphere are the seven heavens, one encompassing another, in dimensions whose extent no one knows except God, may He be exalted. The system of the stars, called the solar system, on this view is among the conditions of the nearest heaven, and there is no objection to this, for these are terminologies, and the Qur'an is compatible with them, though it did not come to detail them, yet it does not contradict them. On this view, the nearest heaven is the one described in the hadith of the Night Journey as "the first."

Or it is described as such because what is meant by the nearest heaven is the atmospheric sphere surrounding the earth, in which there is none of the stars or meteors, and the stars and meteors are in their orbits, which are the six heavens and the Throne. On this view, the entire solar system is not among the conditions of the nearest heaven.[p. 89] The meaning of the adornment of the nearest heaven with the stars and meteors on this possibility is that God, may He be exalted, made the surface of the nearest heaven receptive to the penetration of the light of the stars in the half of the celestial sphere that is covered by darkness, owing to the distance of the sun's light from it; so the lights of the stars appear shining at night, and those lights become an adornment for the nearest heaven, which is beautified by them.

The verse is suitable for both possibilities, because it establishes only that the nearest heaven is beautified with the adornment of the stars, and that does not necessitate that the stars float in the nearest heaven. The adornment relates to people, and the things by which people are adorned are different from them and separate from them, like our saying: "The sea was beautified by the light of the moon."

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of readers) read *"bi-zīnati al-kawākib"* with the annexation of *zīna* to *al-kawākib*. Ḥamza read *"bi-zīnatin al-kawākib"* with tanwīn on *zīna* and the genitive on *al-kawākib*, taking *al-kawākib* as an apposition (*badal*) to *zīna*. Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, read *"bi-zīnatin al-kawākiba"* with tanwīn on *zīna* and accusative on *al-kawākib*, on the basis of specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), by supposing the verb "I mean" (*a'nī*).

The discussion of the adornment of the sky with the stars, and their being a guard against the devils, has already been mentioned at the words of His, may He be exalted: **"And We have set in the sky constellations and adorned them for the observers. And We have guarded them from every accursed devil"** (Q. 15:16–17), in Surat al-Ḥijr. And the mention of the stars has been made in His words "(he saw a star)" in Surat al-Anʿām.

*ḥifẓan* (as a guard) is put in the accusative by coordination (*ʿaṭf*) on *"bi-zīnati al-kawākib"*, as a coordination on the meaning (*ʿaṭf ʿalā al-maʿnā*), as al-Zamakhsharī holds in *al-Kashshāf*, and what we have just explained confirms it, namely that His words "(with the adornment of the stars)" have the force of saying "with the stars, an adornment," and its governing verb is *zayyannā*.

Guarding against the devils is one of the wisdoms in God's creation of the stars, in His knowledge, because the stars were created before the devils became deserving of being stoned. That did not occur except after Iblīs was expelled from the world of the angels. So the condition of the unity of the agent of the object of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*) with its governing verb at the same time was not fulfilled. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī does not regard this condition as required. Perhaps al-Zamakhsharī follows him in this, in that he makes it an object of purpose; and this is the truth, because on his view it may be a hidden cause, just as he permitted the state (*ḥāl*) to be a hidden one.

It is also permissible to make *ḥifẓan* accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) substituting for its verb, so that it is in the sense of "and We guarded," coordinated on *zayyannā*, i.e. "We guarded with the stars from every rebellious devil." This is the view of al-Mubarrad. The thing guarded is the sky, i.e. "and We guarded it with the stars from every devil."

The thing by which the guarding is done is not the whole of that by which the adorning is done. Rather, the cause is distributed: what is an adornment is seen by the eyes, and what is a guard is that explained by His words **"then a piercing flame pursued him"** (Q. 37:10).

The meaning of the stars being a guard against the devils is that among the stars are the meteors by which the devils are pelted when they attempt to steal hearing; so the devils flee for fear that they will be struck, for if they strike their like, they pierce them and they break apart; perhaps their forms disappear through that disintegration, so that their substance is annihilated, or they are scattered for a moment before they re-cohere, and they suffer from that tearing and rejoining. The meteors that appear to the observer as shining fragments like stars moving through the sky are in fact metallic bodies that revolve around the sun. When they come near the earth, the earth's gravity overpowers them and takes them away from the sun's gravity, so they plunge swiftly toward the earth's center. Because of the great speed of their plunge, heat sufficient to burn the small ones is generated in the atmospheric sphere, and the large ones are heated to a degree of heat that causes them to shine. They fall until they land on the earth, mostly in the sea, and sometimes on land. Some people may come upon them, finding them lying on the earth as metallic pieces of varying sizes, and sometimes they burn whatever they strike of trees or houses.

The fall of some of them has been dated to the year 616 BCE in the land of China, where they broke several vessels and killed men. The Arabs mentioned them in their poetry before Islam. Dawūs ibn Ḥajar, describing a wild bull, said:

*He pounced like a shooting star, followed by a rising dust cloud which you take for a tent-rope.*

Bishr ibn Khāzim, whom al-Jāḥiẓ quoted in *al-Ḥayawān*, said:

*The wild ass is pursued by the wild donkey and its foal, and the star-like pouncing follows the two of them like the pouncing of a shooting star.*

In the year 944 [CE], the passage of fiery spheres in the atmosphere was recorded, which burned several houses.[p. 91] They fell in the Tunisian region two or three times, among them a fragment that fell at the beginning of this century in the middle of the kingdom, which I believe was in the area of Tālah. I saw a splinter of it resembling iron, and the common people think it is lightning and call it "the lightning stone." Their falling occurs both at night and by day, but we do not see their passage by day, because the sun's ray hides them from view.

From what you have learned of the rolling of these meteors from the orbit of the sun to the orbit of the earth, the reason for their being from the nearest heaven becomes clear to you, and the reason for their connection with the satanic bodies rising from the earth, which seek connection with the heavens.

They have been called meteors (*shuhub*) by way of comparison with a brand of fire, that is an ember, and this was mentioned earlier at His words, may He be exalted: **"Or I will bring you a burning brand"** (Q. 27:7), in Surat al-Naml.

*al-mārid* (rebellious): one who has rebelled against obedience and does not stay in obedience even for an hour. He, may He be exalted, said: **"And among the people of Madīnah are those who have persisted in hypocrisy"** (Q. 9:101). In describing him as *mārid* there is an indication that what afflicts his fellows of harm by the meteors does not deter him from renewing the attempt at stealing, because of the satanic nature disposed in him to persist in those wicked traits, just as the moth does not desist from hurling itself around the lamp despite what touches the tips of its wings from the touch of the fire.

**Ibn ʿAshur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 37, verses 8–10:**

"﴿They cannot listen to the Exalted Assembly, and they are pelted from every side,﴾ ﴿driven away, and theirs is a constant punishment,﴾ ﴿except one who snatches a snatch, and is pursued by a piercing flame﴾." This is an interjection (*iʿtiraḍ*, a parenthetical insertion) placed between the sentence "Indeed We adorned the nearest heaven" and the sentence "So ask them: are they stronger in creation?" Its purpose is to describe the story of the expulsion of the devils.

If *wa-ḥifẓan* ("and as protection") is taken as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) standing in place of its verb, then the sentence "they cannot listen" may be considered an explanation (*bayān*) of the manner of the protection. In that case, the sentence occupies the position of an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf al-bayān*) to the phrase "and as protection," in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam, shall I direct you…"﴾ [Taha: 120]. The meaning is that by this protection, the devils' hearing of the Exalted Assembly was cut off.

[p. 92]

The preposition *ilā* ("to") indicates that the verb *yasmaʿūna* ("they hear") implies the meaning of *yantahūna* ("they reach"), so that the sense is: they cannot reach the Exalted Assembly and hear, since the shooting of meteors does not leave them arriving there as a seeker arrives at the place sought. Rather, they are repelled before they arrive, so they do not snatch from the knowledge of what happens in the Exalted Assembly anything but scattered fragments that are not clearly understood. This is further from their hearing, because they do not reach it, and so they do not hear. In *al-Kashshaf* it is stated that *samiʿtu* with a direct object conveys perception, while *samiʿtu* with *ilā* conveys listening together with perception.

The majority of readers recited ﴿*lā yassammaʿūna*﴾ with a sukūn on the *sīn* and a lightened *mīm*. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾi, Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim, and Khalaf recited ﴿*lā yasmaʿūna*﴾ [Fussilat: 4] with a doubled *sīn* and a doubled *mīm*, both vowelled with fatḥa, on the basis that the original form is *lā yatasammaʿūna*. The *tāʾ* was changed into *sīn* to facilitate assimilation (*idghām*). *Tasammuʿ* means seeking to hear and straining to do so. The intended meaning is direct eavesdropping, which becomes possible for them when they reach the place where the voices of the Exalted Assembly can be heard; that is, they are repelled before they reach the sought-after place. The two readings have the same meaning.

What is reported from Abu ʿUbayd concerning a distinction between the two in meaning and usage is not sound.

The essential meaning of the two readings is that the meteors prevent the devils from hearing anything from the Exalted Assembly. Before the Muhammadan mission, they would sometimes snatch a snatch and cast it to the soothsayers. When God sent Muhammad (ﷺ), He decreed an increase in the guarding of the heaven by sending meteors after one another, so that whoever snatched a snatch would not return safely, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾. Thus the meteors existed before, but they did not prevent the devils from catching fragmentary reports from the Exalted Assembly. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, the devils were deprived of this.

*Al-Malaʾ* means the group of people of standing and rank. Here it refers to the angels. Describing the *malaʾ* as *al-aʿlā* ("the Exalted") is to honour what is described.

*Al-qadhf* means stoning, *al-jānib* means the direction, and *al-duḥūr* means expulsion. It is in the accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) of *yuqdhafūna* ("they are pelted"). The verb *yuqdhafūna* is in the passive voice because the one who pelts is known, namely the angels appointed to the guarding mentioned in His saying: ﴿And we touched the heaven and found it filled with a strong guard and meteors﴾ [Jinn: 8].

[p. 93]

*Al-ʿadhāb al-wāṣib* means the lasting punishment. It is said: *waṣaba yaṣibu wuṣūban*, when it lasts. The meaning is that they are driven away in this world and are despised, and that for them there is a lasting punishment in the Hereafter, since the devils are for the Fire: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils, then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees﴾ [Maryam: 68], in Surah Maryam. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the punishment of being pelted, and that it is *wāṣib*, meaning it does not leave them, whenever they attempt to eavesdrop, because they are created with a disposition to keep attempting it.

The clause ﴿and theirs is a constant punishment﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the clause containing the excepted element, which is ﴿they cannot listen to the Exalted Assembly﴾, and the exception.

The phrase ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾ is an exception from the pronoun in *lā yasmaʿūna*, so it is in the nominative position as a substitute (*badal*) for it.

*Al-khaṭf* means quickly seizing something, and *al-khaṭfa* is a single instance of it. It is an absolute object of *khaṭifa* to specify the number of times the verbal noun occurred, that is, one snatch. Here it is used metaphorically for the swift hearing of whatever fragment of speech they are able to hear, as in His saying: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], in Surah al-Baqarah.

*Atbaʿahu* means the same as *tabiʿahu* ("followed him"), so its *hamza* does not make it transitive. It is like the *hamza* of *abāna* in the sense of *bāna* ("was clear").

*Al-shihāb* is the flame and the ember of fire. Here it refers to what is called the meteorite in the terminology of the science of astronomy, and this was mentioned in His saying: ﴿then a clear flame pursued him﴾ [al-Hijr: 18], in Surah al-Hijr.

*Al-thāqib* means piercing, that is, what pierces a hole in the body it strikes; meaning, it pierces him. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the meteor does not kill the devil it strikes, but it burns him and disables him, meaning it corrupts his constitution so that his properties vanish. If he does not perish, he becomes unable to attempt to steal hearing a second time. The meaning is that whoever manages to approach a place where he hears words from the words of the Exalted Assembly is pursued by a flame that pierces him, so he does not return to where he came from. This is one of the distinguishing features of the period after the Muhammadan mission.

The discussion of eavesdropping has already been presented at His saying: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down﴾ [al-Shuʿaraʾ: 210], ﴿nor is it befitting for them﴾ [al-Shuʿaraʾ: 211], in Surah al-Shuʿaraʾ."

**Ibn ʿAshur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 37, verses 8–10:**

"﴿They cannot listen to the Exalted Assembly, and they are pelted from every side,﴾ ﴿driven away, and theirs is a constant punishment,﴾ ﴿except one who snatches a snatch, and is pursued by a piercing flame﴾." This is an interjection (*iʿtiraḍ*, a parenthetical insertion) placed between the sentence "Indeed We adorned the nearest heaven" and the sentence "So ask them: are they stronger in creation?" Its purpose is to describe the story of the expulsion of the devils.

If *wa-ḥifẓan* ("and as protection") is taken as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) standing in place of its verb, then the sentence "they cannot listen" may be considered an explanation (*bayān*) of the manner of the protection. In that case, the sentence occupies the position of an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf al-bayān*) to the phrase "and as protection," in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam, shall I direct you…"﴾ [Taha: 120]. The meaning is that by this protection, the devils' hearing of the Exalted Assembly was cut off.

[p. 92]

The preposition *ilā* ("to") indicates that the verb *yasmaʿūna* ("they hear") implies the meaning of *yantahūna* ("they reach"), so that the sense is: they cannot reach the Exalted Assembly and hear, since the shooting of meteors does not leave them arriving there as a seeker arrives at the place sought. Rather, they are repelled before they arrive, so they do not snatch from the knowledge of what happens in the Exalted Assembly anything but scattered fragments that are not clearly understood. This is further from their hearing, because they do not reach it, and so they do not hear. In *al-Kashshaf* it is stated that *samiʿtu* with a direct object conveys perception, while *samiʿtu* with *ilā* conveys listening together with perception.

The majority of readers recited ﴿*lā yassammaʿūna*﴾ with a sukūn on the *sīn* and a lightened *mīm*. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾi, Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim, and Khalaf recited ﴿*lā yasmaʿūna*﴾ [Fussilat: 4] with a doubled *sīn* and a doubled *mīm*, both vowelled with fatḥa, on the basis that the original form is *lā yatasammaʿūna*. The *tāʾ* was changed into *sīn* to facilitate assimilation (*idghām*). *Tasammuʿ* means seeking to hear and straining to do so. The intended meaning is direct eavesdropping, which becomes possible for them when they reach the place where the voices of the Exalted Assembly can be heard; that is, they are repelled before they reach the sought-after place. The two readings have the same meaning.

What is reported from Abu ʿUbayd concerning a distinction between the two in meaning and usage is not sound.

**Page 94**

﴿So ask them: are they harder to create, or those (other things) that We have created? Indeed, We created them from clinging clay.﴾ The fa' (فَ) here marks a consequence (tafri'): it follows His saying ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of the stars﴾ [al-Saffat: 6], in view of what that implies of great power over bringing things into being. That is: ask them about their denial of resurrection and their deeming it impossible that their creation be restored after they have become bones and crumbled dust. Is their creation then harder for Us, or the creation of those great created beings? The pronoun of absence in His saying "fa-istaftihim" (so ask them) refers to something not mentioned, since it is known from the context; they are those who deemed the re-creation after death impossible. The same applies to the pronouns of absence that come after it, while the pronoun of address in it is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "so ask them." It is a question of argument and refutation.

Al-istiftā' (الاِسْتِفْتاء) means seeking a fatwa (fatwā), with the fa' vowelled with a fatha and with waw; it is also said al-futyā with a damma on the fa' and with ya'. It is an informing about a matter that is hidden from anyone other than the specialists, concerning some purpose. It is either an informing about knowledge specific to the one informing, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿Yusuf, O man of truth, give us your verdict concerning seven fat cows﴾ [Yusuf: 46], the verse in full, and He said ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning al-kalalah﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], and it has preceded in His saying (﴿by which you two sought a ruling﴾ [Yusuf: 41]) in Surat Yusuf.

Or it is an informing about an opinion sought from a person of trusted judgment, and from it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿She said: O chiefs, give me your opinion in my affair﴾ [al-Naml: 32] in Surat al-Naml.

The meaning: ask them for their opinion. Since what is asked about is a matter requiring the exercise of reflection, the verb istiftā' was applied to asking about it.

The hamza of (﴿a-hum ashaddu khalqan﴾) is the interrogative used for confirmation (taqrir), regarding the weakness of human creation in comparison with the heavenly created beings, because the interrogation results in affirmation, since it compels the questioner to affirm the intended matter from both sides of the question. Thus istiftā' has the meaning of interrogation, and so it is used in everything in which interrogation is used.

Ashadd means: more difficult and more arduous.

**Page 95**

"Khalqan" is a specification (tamyiz): that is, is their creation harder, or the creation of the one We created, whose description you have heard?

By (﴿man khalaqna﴾) is meant what Allah created of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, including the angels, the devils, and the stars mentioned just before, by the indication of the fa' of sequence (ta'qib) being placed after the mention of that. This is like His saying ﴿Are you harder to create, or the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27] and its like.

The relative "man" (مَن), which is used for rational beings, is employed here by way of prevailing (taghlib) for rational creatures among the created things.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We created them from clinging clay﴾ is in the position of a cause for what arises from the meaning of the interrogation in His saying ﴿Are they harder to create, or those We have created?﴾, namely the affirmation that they are weaker in creation than the creation of the heavens and their worlds. It is an argument against them: that the bringing about of their creation after annihilation is easier than the bringing about of the great created beings mentioned just before, which had not been created previously. They were created from clay, because their origin, Adam, was created from clay, as is established among all people. So how can they deem resurrection impossible with their sayings, among which is their saying (﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 82])?

Al-tin (الطِّين) is dust mixed with water.

Al-lazib (اللّازِب) is that which clings to other things, and from it the term is applied to a matter that is obligatory; "lazib" appears in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And they do not reckon evil a binding blow."

It has been said that the ba' of lazib is a substitution for the mim of lazim, and the meaning is: it is ancient clay that has become black mud.

The pronoun in (﴿Indeed, We created them﴾) refers to the polytheists, and it is by omission of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning: We created their origin, which is Adam, for he is the one who was created from clinging clay. So if their origin was produced from dust, how can they deny the possibility of re-creating every human from dust?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 12–14:

﴿Nay, but you wonder, while they mock.﴾ ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock it.﴾ "Bal" (بَلْ) is for a transitional turning away (al-idrab al-intiqali) from the reproachful affirmation to the statement that their condition is a matter of wonder.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read ﴿بَلْ عَجِبْتَ﴾ with a fatha on the ta', as an address (lil-khitab). The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), the one addressed in His words ﴿So ask them for a fatwa﴾ [al-Saffat: 11]. The past-tense verb is used in the sense of a command, which is the use of a report to express a demand for emphasis, just as a report is used to effect forms of contracts, such as "I have sold" (bi'tu). The meaning is: "Wonder at them."

It is also possible that wonder arose in the Prophet (ﷺ) when he saw their aversion and their lack of fairness, in which case the report is used in its literal sense.

It is also possible that the speech is on the presumption of an interrogative hamza, i.e., "Nay, do you wonder?"

The meaning in all cases is that their condition deserves to be wondered at, like His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿And if you wonder, then wondrous is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5] in Surat al-Ra'd.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿بَلْ عَجِبْتُ﴾ with a damma on the ta' for the speaker. It is possible that what is intended is that God attributed wonder to Himself. It is known that the intended meaning is not the literal wonder, which entails astonishment and surprise at a matter not anticipated; rather, the intended meaning is causing wonder, or a metonymy for its consequence, which is magnifying the matter wondered at. There is no parallel to this usage in the Qur'an, but it has been repeated in the prophetic speech. Among it is his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed God wonders at two men, one of whom kills the other, and both enter Paradise: one fights in the way of God and is killed, then God accepts the repentance of the killer, and he is martyred." Narrated by al-Nasa'i with this wording. That is, the killer, who had been an unbeliever, then embraces Islam and fights and is martyred in the way of God.

And his saying in the hadith of the Ansari and his wife, when they hosted a man and gave him their supper while leaving their children hungry: "God wondered at your deed."

And there was revealed concerning them ﴿and they prefer others over themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]. And his saying: "God wonders at a people who enter Paradise in chains." He turned away from the explicit, which is magnifying, because metonymy is more eloquent than explicit statement. The thing that diverts the meaning from the explicit sense in His saying "I wonder" is what is known of His being unlike created things.

It is also possible that "you wonder" (عَجِبْتَ) is used in the sense of requital for their wonder, because His saying ﴿So ask them: are they stronger in creation?﴾ [al-Saffat: 11] indicates that they wondered at the re-creation, so God threatened them with punishment for their wonder. He applied the verb "wonder" to that punishment, just as He applied "plotting" to the requital of their plotting in His saying ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54].

The waw in (وَيَسْخَرُونَ) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in (عَجِبْتَ), meaning: their affair was a wonder while they were mocking you in their asking for a fatwa.

The present tense is used in (يَسْخَرُونَ) to convey the renewal of mockery and that they do not desist from it.

Al-sukhriyya is ridicule (al-istihza'), and it was mentioned in His saying ﴿So those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to mock﴾ [al-An'am: 10] in Surat al-An'am.

The reminder is that they should recall what they are heedless of regarding God's power over them, and the comparison of their situation with that of the nations whom God uprooted; yet they do not take heed of this out of obstinacy. So (لا يَذْكُرُونَ) is used in the sense of the effect of the act, meaning: the effect of remembering what they are reminded of does not occur in them, even though they have remembered it.

It is also possible that what is meant by (لا يَذْكُرُونَ) is what they were reminded of, meaning: due to the intensity of their aversion from reflecting upon what they were reminded of, since what they were reminded of is firmly fixed in their minds, they do not recall what they are heedless of, in the manner of His saying ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like cattle﴾ [al-Furqan: 44].

(﴿And when they see a sign﴾) meaning a breach of custom which the Messenger (ﷺ) displayed, indicating his truthfulness, because God does not alter the order of His creation in the world except when He wills to confirm the Messenger, since the breaking of custom from the Creator of customs and the Arranger of the laws of the cosmos stands in place of His saying: "This Messenger has spoken truly concerning what he has reported from Me." They saw the splitting of the moon and said: "This is magic." God said ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1] ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: "Continuous magic."﴾ [al-Qamar: 2].

(يَسْتَسْخِرُونَ) is an intensification of mockery, so the sin and ta' are for emphasis, as in His saying ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195] and His saying ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 43].

The mockery mentioned in His saying "and they mock" is mockery of the Prophet's (ﷺ) argumentation against them with proofs. The mockery mentioned here is mockery of the appearance of the miraculous signs; that is, they increase their mockery of whoever among them thought that the appearance of the miracles would turn them from their disbelief. Do you not see that they said ﴿It nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not persevered in them﴾ [al-Furqan: 42]?

The present tense is used in (يَسْخَرُونَ) to convey the renewal of mockery and that they do not desist from it.

**[Page 98]**

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿So ask them, are they the harder to create?﴾ [al-Saffat 37:11] and what follows it. The reference in ﴿They said, "This is nothing but manifest magic"﴾ is to the content of ﴿So ask them, are they the harder to create?﴾ [al-Saffat 37:11], which is the re-creation at the Resurrection. The statement ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised up again?"﴾ clarifies it. The meaning is: they said, in rejecting the argument contained in ﴿Are they the harder to create, or those We have created?﴾ [al-Saffat 37:11], that the claim that life is restored after decay is manifest magic, that is, speech that cannot be understood, intended to bewitch the listener. This is the way of explaining this verse that fits its composition, unlike the explanation that the exegetes have customarily adopted.

Nafi' alone recited ﴿"Shall we indeed be raised up again?"﴾ with a single hamza, the hamza of inna (ʾinna), on the basis that it is the answer (jawab) to "idha" (when), which falls within the scope of interrogation (istifham), and therefore belongs to the domain of the interrogative.

The others recited ʾaʾinna with two hamzas. The first is the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham), reinforcing the hamza that enters upon "idha" (when).

As for the statement ﴿"Or our forefathers of old?"﴾, Qalun, on the authority of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far recited the waw of (aw, "or") with sukun, on the basis that the hamza together with the waw is a single particle, (aw), the coordinating particle, which here expresses division (taqsim).

**[Page 99]**

The purpose of coordinating with "aw" is that they made the forefathers of old a separate category. Its coordination is thus an ascent (irtiqa') in demonstrating the impossibility of re-creating this category, because the time elapsed since their annihilation was long, so restoring their lives was further in impossibility.

The rest recited the waw with fatha, on the basis that the waw is the waw of coordination (waw al-ʿatf) and the hamza is the interrogative hamza, so they are two particles. The interrogative hamza was placed before the coordinating particle according to the common usage. The implied sense is: "And our forefathers of old, [shall they be raised up] like us?"

On both readings, its (ʾābāʾunā, "our forefathers") being in the nominative is by coordination with the grammatical position (mahall) of the subject of inna (ism inna), which was a subject before inna entered. The prevailing practice in coordinating on the subject of inna is to put the coordinated noun in the nominative, taking account of the position, as in the Almighty's statement ﴿That Allah is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:3]. Alternatively, it is made coordinated on the pronoun concealed in the predicate of inna, which here is in the nominative by substitution for the agent. The separation between the coordinated item, which is an attached pronoun, and the coordinating particle does no harm. Nor does the separation between the item coordinated upon and the coordinated item by the hamza, which leads to governing what precedes the hamza over what follows it, and that would conflict with the leading position of the interrogative (sadr al-istifham). This is because the leading position of the interrogative is with respect to the whole sentence, so the operation of a governor from a clause before it does not conflict with it. Governing is a consideration that the speaker takes into account and the listener understands, so it does not conflict with the verbal order.

The interrogative in ﴿"When we have died"﴾ is one of denial (inkari), as was previously mentioned. Therefore the Almighty's statement ﴿Say, "Yes"﴾ is the answer to their statement ﴿"When we have died"﴾, in the wise mode of address (al-uslub al-hakim), by turning their intention from the interrogative to its apparent form. They were treated as if they were asking: "Will they be raised up?" It was said to them: "Yes", affirming the resurrection that they asked about; that is, yes, you will be raised up. "Say" was used without a coordinating particle, because it follows the customary manner of relating dialogues, as was previously mentioned at the Almighty's statement ﴿They said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And you are humbled﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). "Dakhirun" means the abject and debased, that is, you will be raised up in a resurrection of humiliation, announcing the expectation of punishment, not a resurrection of honour.

Deduced from the affirmation of the resurrection that results from the word "Yes", is that their resurrection is imminent and requires neither effort nor time. It is nothing but a re-creation awaiting a single cry (zajra).

**[Page 100]**

The "zajra" is the shout. The Almighty's statement ﴿So by those who drive with a driving﴾ [al-Saffat 37:2] was mentioned just before.

"Wahida" (single) is an emphasis of what the pattern "fa'la" (the form of a single act) indicates of the meaning of a single occurrence, to avert the suspicion that the shout is meant as a kind rather than as a single occurrence, because the pattern "fa'la" comes for the meaning of the verbal noun, not the single occurrence.

The pronoun in ﴿"hiya"﴾ is the pronoun of the matter and the affair (damir al-qissa wa al-sha'n). It has no antecedent; it is explained only by the clause that follows it.

Following on from this is ﴿then, when they are, they look on﴾. The "fa" of sequence indicates the immediacy of the surprise, and the particle of surprise (harf al-mufaja'a) indicates the speed with which this happens. This was previously mentioned at the Almighty's statement ﴿It will be only one shout, and then they will all be brought before Us﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:53] in Surat Ya-Sin.

Using "yanzurun" (they look), the perfect life that is not mixed with bewilderment is alluded to, because looking happens only with the completeness of life.

"Naẓar" (looking) was chosen from among the rest of the senses for its greater suitability to the context, which is an allusion to the bewilderment that has seized them at the confusion of the gathering.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 20:

﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense."﴾

It is permissible that the waw (wa) be for the circumstantial state (hal), meaning: saying, "Woe to us!" That is, all of them say, "Woe to us!" each one saying it on behalf of himself and his companions.

It is also permissible that it be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause "yanẓurūn" (they look), and the meaning is: "and they looked and said."

Al-Waylu (woe): the evil of condition. The particle of address (ya) is for emphasis (lil-ihtimam). Its counterpart has already been mentioned in His saying, ﴿Oh, the regret over the servants!﴾ [Yasin: 30] in Surat Yasin.

The indication is to the day that is witnessed. Al-Din (the Recompense): the requital, and it has been mentioned in Surat al-Fatiha.

This is the day of Decision (al-Fasl) which you used to deny.

It is permissible that this is words addressed to them from the side of God, the Exalted, as a response to their saying, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense" (Qur'an 37:20). The statement is used to convey a warning by way of allusion. It is also permissible that it is part of their own speech, meaning some of them say to others, "This is the Day of Decision."

Al-Fasl (decision): the distinguishing of truth from falsehood. What is meant by it is judgment and sentencing, meaning: this is a day on which you will be sentenced to the punishment you have deserved.

[Page 101]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 22–26:

﴿Gather those who did wrong, along with their spouses and what they used to worship﴾ ﴿besides God, and guide them to the path of the Blazing Fire﴾ ﴿and stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ ﴿"What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?"﴾ ﴿Rather, today they are submitting.﴾ This is a transition from the warning of the occurrence of the Resurrection to an announcement of what will befall them afterward if they persist in their polytheism and their denial of the Resurrection and recompense.

"Gather" (ihshurū) is an imperative, and an imperative requires one who issues it, namely one who speaks it. Therefore this is the object of an implied speech (qawl maḥdhūf), because it is evident that it cannot be connected to anything preceding it. The omission of the speech is from the style of "the sea" (ḥadīth al-baḥr). It is clear that this is a command from God Most High to the angels charged with human beings on the Day of Reckoning.

"Al-ḥashr" (gathering) means bringing together those who are dispersed into one place.

"Those who did wrong" (alladhīna ẓalamū) are the polytheists: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].

As for "al-azwāj" (the spouses), its apparent meaning is that it refers to their wives. This is the explanation of Mujahid and al-Hasan. It is also reported from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who narrates it from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Its interpretation (ta'wil) is that they are the wives who agreed with them in associating partners with God, whereas those who believed among them are safe from the consequences of their husbands. This is like the mention of the spouses of the believers in His words ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56], for what is meant is their believing spouses, and it was stated in absolute form by analogy with the qualified form in His words ﴿and whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23].

The mention of the spouses is an intensification of the threat and warning, lest they assume that polytheistic women bear no consequence.

This is like their being singled out for mention in His words ﴿the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 102]

It has also been said: "al-azwāj" means the kinds (al-aṣnāf), that is, their partisans in polytheism and its branches. This was said by Qatadah, and it is a narration from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn 'Abbas.

From al-Dahhak: "al-azwāj" are those who were paired with them from the devils.

The pronoun in "ya'budūn" (they worship) refers back to "those who did wrong and their spouses." The referent of "mā" (what) is non-rational beings. As for rational beings, ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164].

The object pronoun in "fahdūhum" (guide them) refers back to "those who did wrong and their spouses and what they used to worship, besides God," that is, the idols.

The conjunction of "fahdūhum" with the particle fa' of sequence indicates the swiftness of the command to take them to the Fire immediately after that gathering. Thus the command is primary in the Qur'an.

"Al-hidāyah" and "al-hudā" mean indicating the way to one who does not know it, so it is guidance toward something desired. The term has come to be dominant in this sense, because the guided person's desire to know the way is a necessary consequence of the act of guidance. Accordingly it is contrasted with "al-ḍalālah," which is bewilderment about the way. Hence the mention of "guide them" (uhdūhum) here is sarcastic toward the polytheists, like the words of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We hosted you, and we hastened your hospitality
before the dawn, with the grinding stones that crush."

"Al-ṣirāṭ" means the path, that is, the path of Hell.

The meaning of "wqifūhum" (stop them) is a command to halt them at the beginning of their journey, due to the immediacy implied by the imperative, as indicated by the particle fa' of sequence that conjoins it. That is, detain them briefly from moving on, so that they may be questioned with a question of despair, belittlement and severity. Then it will be said to them: ﴿"What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?"﴾, that is, why does none of you help the other to ward off the wretchedness in which he is? Where is the mutual help you used to give one another in the world, and your rallying against the Messenger and the believers?

Thus the interrogative in ﴿"What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?"﴾ is used to express incapacity (ta'jīz), together with an alert to the error in which they were during the worldly life.

The clause ﴿"What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?"﴾ explains the ambiguity of "mas'ūlūn" (they are to be questioned). The interrogative in it is used to express wonder, to remind them of what grieves them. It is evident, therefore, that the questioning is not literal,

[Page 103]

but what is meant by it is its necessary implication, which is wonder. The meaning is: what thing has befallen you? Thus "mā" (what) is the interrogative pronoun serving as the subject (mubtada'), and "lakum" (for you) is its predicate.

The clause "lā tanāṣarūn" (you do not help one another) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in "lakum," and it is the basis of the interrogation. That is, this state necessitates wonder at your failure to help one another.

Al-Jumhur read "lā tanāṣarūn" with the second tā' lightened, considering it to be the omission of one of the two tā's. Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, and Abu Ja'far read it with the letter doubled, considering it an assimilation (idghām) of one of the two tā's into the other.

The redirection (iḍrāb) indicated by "bal" (rather) is a redirection to negate the possibility of mutual help among them. This is not something the hearing might suppose, so the redirection serves as an emphasis of what the interrogation indicated of incapacity.

"Al-istisлām" means strong Islam, that is, the submission of the self and the abandonment of resistance. It is thus an intensive form of aslama (to submit).

The mention of "al-yawm" (today) serves to show their humiliation, that is, what they had of mutual help and of domination over the Muslims before today, that is, in the world, has been removed from them. For they used to say: ﴿We are a united body that will prevail﴾ [al-Qamar: 44], and Abu Jahl said it on the day of Badr, meaning: we are a group that cannot be defeated. Thus the mention of the day carries a striking effect in this context.

[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur on Qur'an 37:27–32]

*"And they will turn to one another, questioning each other."* (Qur'an 37:27) "They will say: 'Indeed, you used to come to us from the right.'" (37:28) "They will say: 'Rather, you were not believers.'" (37:29) "'We had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people.'" (37:30) "'So the word of our Lord has come true against us; indeed we are to taste [the punishment].'" (37:31) "'So we led you astray; indeed we were astray.'" (37:32)

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon *"mustaslimūn"* (submitting), meaning: they submitted, and some of them turned upon others with blame. The ones questioning each other (*al-mutasā'iltūn*) are those exchanging accusations, namely the leaders of polytheism and their common followers, as the recounting of their dialogue shows, in His saying *"We had no authority over you"* and His saying *"So we led you astray"*, and so on.

[p. 104]

He expressed their turning toward one another in the past tense, though it is something that will happen on the Day of Resurrection, to affirm that it will certainly occur; for this has greater effect in warning their leaders against deceiving them, and in warning their common followers against taking pride in being deceived. Yet the indication of the future is evident from the context, in His saying *"Then they will look"* (37:19), and so on.

*Al-iqbāl* (turning toward) means coming from the direction facing a thing, i.e., from its front. It is the coming of one who confronts openly, not of one who sneaks and fears. It is used here metaphorically for directing speech and attention toward something, as if one came to it from another place.

The overall meaning is a recounting of reproach and blame that the followers direct at their leaders and chiefs. The structure indicates that *al-atyān* (coming) is used for propaganda and rhetoric directed at them, since *al-atyān* implies intention without necessarily implying physical arrival, as in the saying of al-Nābighah:

*"A man has come to you, harboring resentment toward me,*
*and his coming has been [an approach] of intention."*

The usage of this word and its synonym *al-majī'* (coming) has already occurred together in His saying, exalted is He: *"They said: 'Rather, we have brought you that about which they were disputing'"* (15:63) and *"And We have brought you the truth"* (15:64), in Surat al-Hijr.

Alternatively, *al-yamīn* (the right) may mean the direction of good, because the Arabs attribute good to the direction of the right. The word is derived from *al-yumn* (blessing), and it indicates attaining what is sought in their view. On this basis their beliefs concerning the flight of birds and wild animals were formed: auspiciousness with the *sānih* (a bird or animal passing from the right of the traveler), and inauspiciousness (*al-tashā'um*), that is, awaiting the arrival of evil from the left.

The verb *"ta'tūnanā"* (you come to us) should have been followed by the direction of the right with the preposition *min* (from). Since it was followed by the preposition *'an* (from/away from), which expresses passing beyond, it became necessary to take *ta'tūnanā* as implying the meaning of *taṣuddūnanā* (you turn us away), to fit the sense of passing beyond. That is, "you come to us diverting us away from the right," i.e., away from good. This is the interpretation adopted by Ibn 'Aṭiyyah and al-Zamakhsharī, and many have been confused in interpreting it. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said, in summary: "The commentators have differed on the meaning of their saying *'from the right'*. Ibn Zayd and others expressed it as 'the path to Paradise', and similar expressions which are interpretation by meaning and are not specific to the wording itself. Some also inclined to an interpretation specific to the wording, and from this several meanings result: that by *al-yamīn* is meant strength and force (I say: this is from Ibn 'Abbās and al-Farrā'), so it is as if they said: 'You used to entice us with strength from yourselves.' Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: 'You come to us from the direction in which your deception and misguidance appear good, and in which you show that it is the direction of right guidance' (this is from al-Zajjāj and al-Jubā'ī). Another meaning the verse may bear is: 'You used to come to us' i.e., you cut us off from news of good and blessing, and so they expressed it by the right. Among the meanings is also that they mean: 'You come from the direction of desires and of not looking [at the truth], because the direction of a person's right side has his liver in it, and the direction of his left has his heart in it, and a person's looking is from his heart.' It was also said: 'You swear to us.'" End of quote.

The response of the leaders, in their saying *"Rather, you were not believers"*, is a *iḍrāb* of nullification (*iḍrāb ibṭāl*, a rhetorical shift that negates a prior claim) against the followers' claim that the leaders were those who diverted them from the path of good. That is: rather, you yourselves were not among those who accept faith. Because the negation is applied to the verb of existence (*kāna*), rather than saying "you did not believe", it indicates that faith was not part of their nature: rather, you yourselves were those who refused to accept faith.

*"We had no authority over you"*, i.e., no compulsion or dominance by which we might force you to reject faith. Therefore they emphasized this meaning with their saying: *"Rather, you were a transgressing people"*, i.e., transgression, which is arrogance in refusing to accept the call of a man from among yourselves, was your condition and your disposition. For this reason they inserted the word *"qawman"* (a people) between *kāna* (was) and its predicate, because bringing them to mind under the title of peoplehood in transgression indicates that transgression is one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as we previously noted at His saying, exalted is He: *"Surely there are signs for a people who reason"* (2:164), in Surat al-Baqarah.

They built upon their statement the acknowledgment that they all deserved the punishment. So their saying *"So the word of our Lord has come true against us; indeed we are to taste [it]"* is a consequential statement of the admission (*tafrī' al-i'tirāḍ*, a consequential sequence of an objection), i.e., the command of our Lord to make us taste the punishment of Hell was true. The verb *ḥaqqa* means *thabata* (was established).

The sentence *"indeed we are to taste"* explains *"the word of our Lord."*

The speech is reported in the sense of the words, following the method of *iltifāt* (a shift in grammatical person). Were it not for the *iltifāt*, they would have said: "Indeed you are to taste," or "Indeed they are to taste."

The point of the *iltifāt* is to increase the explicit specification of those who are meant by tasting the punishment.

The object of *dhā'iqūn* (tasting) is omitted, because the context indicates it, namely the command in His saying, exalted is He: *"Then guide them to the path of Hellfire"* (37:23).

[p. 106]

They also built upon the content of their reply to them, from their saying *"Rather, you were not believers"* up to *"a transgressing people"*, their saying *"So we led you astray."* That is: we did not compel you to associate partners with God, but we found you holding fast to it and desirous of it, so *"we led you astray"*, i.e., we strengthened you in your error, *"indeed we were astray"*, so we beautified for you what we had chosen for ourselves. Thus the clause *"indeed we were astray"* holds the position of a causal explanation.

The particle *inna* (indeed) takes the place of the causal *lām* (the particle of causation, "because") and the consequential *fā'* (so/then), as we have mentioned more than once.

The addition of *kunnā* (we were) serves to indicate the establishment of error within their souls, and it has become clear to them that what they were upon was error, so they acknowledged it. We had previously noted, at His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Mu'minūn: *"And when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they question one another"* (23:101), that their negated questioning there is the seeking by some of them from others of aid and support, whereas their questioning here is questioning about the causes of their predicament. So there is no contradiction between the two verses.

So their saying *"So the word of our Lord has come true against us; indeed we are to taste [it]"* is a consequential statement of the admission (*tafrī' al-i'tirāḍ*, a consequential sequence of an objection), i.e., the command of our Lord to make us taste the punishment of Hell was true. The verb *ḥaqqa* means *thabata* (was established).

The sentence *"indeed we are to taste"* explains *"the word of our Lord."*

The speech is reported in the sense of the words, following the method of *iltifāt* (a shift in grammatical person). Were it not for the *iltifāt*, they would have said: "Indeed you are to taste," or "Indeed they are to taste."

The point of the *iltifāt* is to increase the explicit specification of those who are meant by tasting the punishment.

The object of *dhā'iqūn* (tasting) is omitted, because the context indicates it, namely the command in His saying, exalted is He: *"Then guide them to the path of Hellfire"* (37:23).

They also built upon the content of their reply to them, from their saying *"Rather, you were not believers"* up to *"a transgressing people"*, their saying *"So we led you astray."* That is: we did not compel you to associate partners with God, but we found you holding fast to it and desirous of it, so *"we led you astray"*, i.e., we strengthened you in your error, *"indeed we were astray"*, so we beautified for you what we had chosen for ourselves. Thus the clause *"indeed we were astray"* holds the position of a causal explanation.

The particle *inna* (indeed) takes the place of the causal *lām* (the particle of causation, "because") and the consequential *fā'* (so/then), as we have mentioned more than once.

The addition of *kunnā* (we were) serves to indicate the establishment of error within their souls, and it has become clear to them that what they were upon was error, so they acknowledged it. We had previously noted, at His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Mu'minūn: *"And when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they question one another"* (23:101), that their negated questioning there is the seeking by some of them from others of aid and support, whereas their questioning here is questioning about the causes of their predicament. So there is no contradiction between the two verses.

[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur on Qur'an 37:27–32]

*"And they will turn to one another, questioning each other."* (Qur'an 37:27) "They will say: 'Indeed, you used to come to us from the right.'" (37:28) "They will say: 'Rather, you were not believers.'" (37:29) "'We had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people.'" (37:30) "'So the word of our Lord has come true against us; indeed we are to taste [the punishment].'" (37:31) "'So we led you astray; indeed we were astray.'" (37:32)

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon *"mustaslimūn"* (submitting), meaning: they submitted, and some of them turned upon others with blame. The ones questioning each other (*al-mutasā'iltūn*) are those exchanging accusations, namely the leaders of polytheism and their common followers, as the recounting of their dialogue shows, in His saying *"We had no authority over you"* and His saying *"So we led you astray"*, and so on.

[p. 104]

He expressed their turning toward one another in the past tense, though it is something that will happen on the Day of Resurrection, to affirm that it will certainly occur; for this has greater effect in warning their leaders against deceiving them, and in warning their common followers against taking pride in being deceived. Yet the indication of the future is evident from the context, in His saying *"Then they will look"* (37:19), and so on.

*Al-iqbāl* (turning toward) means coming from the direction facing a thing, i.e., from its front. It is the coming of one who confronts openly, not of one who sneaks and fears. It is used here metaphorically for directing speech and attention toward something, as if one came to it from another place.

The overall meaning is a recounting of reproach and blame that the followers direct at their leaders and chiefs. The structure indicates that *al-atyān* (coming) is used for propaganda and rhetoric directed at them, since *al-atyān* implies intention without necessarily implying physical arrival, as in the saying of al-Nābighah:

*"A man has come to you, harboring resentment toward me,*
*and his coming has been [an approach] of intention."*

The usage of this word and its synonym *al-majī'* (coming) has already occurred together in His saying, exalted is He: *"They said: 'Rather, we have brought you that about which they were disputing'"* (15:63) and *"And We have brought you the truth"* (15:64), in Surat al-Hijr.

Alternatively, *al-yamīn* (the right) may mean the direction of good, because the Arabs attribute good to the direction of the right. The word is derived from *al-yumn* (blessing), and it indicates attaining what is sought in their view. On this basis their beliefs concerning the flight of birds and wild animals were formed: auspiciousness with the *sānih* (a bird or animal passing from the right of the traveler), and inauspiciousness (*al-tashā'um*), that is, awaiting the arrival of evil from the left.

The verb *"ta'tūnanā"* (you come to us) should have been followed by the direction of the right with the preposition *min* (from). Since it was followed by the preposition *'an* (from/away from), which expresses passing beyond, it became necessary to take *ta'tūnanā* as implying the meaning of *taṣuddūnanā* (you turn us away), to fit the sense of passing beyond. That is, "you come to us diverting us away from the right," i.e., away from good. This is the interpretation adopted by Ibn 'Aṭiyyah and al-Zamakhsharī, and many have been confused in interpreting it. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said, in summary: "The commentators have differed on the meaning of their saying *'from the right'*. Ibn Zayd and others expressed it as 'the path to Paradise', and similar expressions which are interpretation by meaning and are not specific to the wording itself. Some also inclined to an interpretation specific to the wording, and from this several meanings result: that by *al-yamīn* is meant strength and force (I say: this is from Ibn 'Abbās and al-Farrā'), so it is as if they said: 'You used to entice us with strength from yourselves.' Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: 'You come to us from the direction in which your deception and misguidance appear good, and in which you show that it is the direction of right guidance' (this is from al-Zajjāj and al-Jubā'ī). Another meaning the verse may bear is: 'You used to come to us' i.e., you cut us off from news of good and blessing, and so they expressed it by the right. Among the meanings is also that they mean: 'You come from the direction of desires and of not looking [at the truth], because the direction of a person's right side has his liver in it, and the direction of his left has his heart in it, and a person's looking is from his heart.' It was also said: 'You swear to us.'" End of quote.

The response of the leaders, in their saying *"Rather, you were not believers"*, is a *iḍrāb* of nullification (*iḍrāb ibṭāl*, a rhetorical shift that negates a prior claim) against the followers' claim that the leaders were those who diverted them from the path of good. That is: rather, you yourselves were not among those who accept faith. Because the negation is applied to the verb of existence (*kāna*), rather than saying "you did not believe", it indicates that faith was not part of their nature: rather, you yourselves were those who refused to accept faith.

*"We had no authority over you"*, i.e., no compulsion or dominance by which we might force you to reject faith. Therefore they emphasized this meaning with their saying: *"Rather, you were a transgressing people"*, i.e., transgression, which is arrogance in refusing to accept the call of a man from among yourselves, was your condition and your disposition. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 33–34:

﴿So they, that Day, will be sharers in the punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals.﴾ This statement from God, exalted is He, is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. It seems to be a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) between the account of God's dialogue with the people of polytheism on the Day of Resurrection and God's rebuke of them in His words: ﴿Indeed, you are going to taste the painful punishment﴾ [al-Saffat: 38].

The فاء (fa') here is the fa' of explanation (al-fa' al-fasihah), because it comes after the description of certain states, and what follows the fa' is a consequence of those states. So the fa' makes explicit an implied condition, meaning: if their condition is as you have heard, then they, on the Day of Resurrection, will be sharers in the punishment, because of their sharing in polytheism and their collusion. That is, there is no excuse for either group: not for the leaders, through their enticing, nor for the masses, through their support of them. The punishment of the misleading callers may be harsher than the punishment of the others, but this does not contradict their sharing in the same general kind of punishment, as other texts indicate. This is because the purpose here is to show that the excuse of neither group, nor their disclaiming, will avail them.

This sentence is parenthetical between the sentences describing their situation during the reckoning.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals﴾ gives the reason for what the sentence ﴿So they, that Day, will be sharers in the punishment﴾ entails. That is, the recompense of the criminals will be like that recompense in the holding to account of the follower and the one followed.

By "the criminals" is meant the polytheists, that is, criminals of the same kind as their crime. The sentence ﴿Indeed, they, when it was said to them, "There is no god but Allah," were arrogant﴾ [al-Saffat: 35] has made this clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 35–36:

﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no god but Allah," they would be arrogant﴾ ﴿and say, "Shall we really abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ This is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani) which conveys the reason for their recompense and explains their wrongdoing, by mentioning what they were upon of arrogance against acknowledging the Oneness of Allah, and of describing the Messenger (ﷺ) with what is far removed from him, a description by which they aimed to deny what he brought. Here the particle (inna) is not for emphasis, because their being so is something beyond dispute; rather it is for drawing attention to the report, and therefore it conveys causation and connection, and it serves the role of the particle of consequence (fa').

The verb of being (kana) is mentioned to indicate that what the report contains is a firmly established attribute of theirs, so it is not discontinued, nor do they deviate from it.

The meaning of ﴿it was said to them, "There is no god but Allah"﴾ is that it is said to them by way of invitation (da'wah) and instruction (ta'lim).

The agent of the verb "it was said," which is in the passive form, is the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is omitted because it is known.

Al-istikbar (arrogance) is an intensified form of pride; the sin and the ta' are for emphasis, meaning they magnify themselves so as not to accept this from a man like themselves. You may also take the sin and the ta' to denote seeking, meaning displaying pride, i.e., pride and aversion appear upon them at this statement.

Their arrogance is accompanied by one of them saying to another: "We will not abandon our gods for a mad poet." They used the negation in the form of a denying interrogative, to show that what the Messenger (ﷺ) calls them to is an abhorrent matter, one that they do not expect to be accepted, as a warning to whoever hears their speech lest any reflection on the Messenger's (ﷺ) saying "There is no god but Allah" should cross his mind. They strengthened this warning by making the particle of denial govern a sentence emphasized by the particle of emphasis, to indicate that if they were to do what they deny, they would already have been certain to abandon their gods, treating some of those addressed as one who doubts that belief in the Oneness of God leads to abandoning their gods, in order to block for the addressees every avenue of hesitation through which it might enter their minds.

The lam in "li-sha'irin" is the lam of cause and purpose, meaning "for the sake of a poet," i.e., for the sake of his call.

Their saying "a mad poet" is a distributed statement (qawl muwazza'), meaning some of them say: "He is a poet," and some say: "He is mad," or they say at one time: "A poet," and at another time: "Mad," as in the other verse: ﴿Thus did no messenger come to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52].

Translation:

﴿Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers.﴾ This is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraḍ) at the end of another parenthetical statement, its purpose being to hasten to declare the Prophet (ﷺ) free of what they said.

"Bal" (nay, rather) here is a particle of retraction (idrab ibṭāl), negating their saying "﴿a mad poet﴾ [al-Saffat: 36]," and affirming his attribute of truth in order to explain the reality of what he brought. In describing what he brought as the truth, there is sufficient refutation of his being a poet or a madman, for the polytheists did not intend by describing him as a poet or a madman anything but to deter people from following him. They likened him to a poet of a tribe who satirizes the enemies of his tribe, or to a madman who says what the sane people of his folk do not say. Thus the words of the Exalted, ﴿Nay, he has brought the truth﴾, affirm that the Messenger is other than what they described him as, an affirmation based on clear evidence.

He followed this by reminding them that he brought nothing but the like of what the messengers before him had brought, so fairness required that they place him in the group that resembles them, not in the group of poets or madmen.

The confirmation of the messengers (taṣdīq al-mursalīn) encompasses what the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, both in general and in detail, because what he brought is no more than either a confirmation of what the earlier law-codes (sharā'i') brought, and so it is a confirmation of them and an attestation to them, or an abrogation (naskh) of some of what the earlier law-codes brought. The announcement of its abrogation and the ending of acting upon it is itself a confirmation of the messengers who brought it at the time of their coming. All of this is included in the meaning of confirmation. The first of this is the affirmation of the oneness of God (tawḥīd) through His lordship (rubūbiyyah) to God the Exalted. The meaning is: that what he called you to of monotheism (tawḥīd) was already called to by the messengers before him, and this is an argument from transmitted testimony (naql) following an argument from rational reflection (naẓar).

[Page 109]

﴿Indeed, you are going to taste the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ This is a statement of God, spoken on the Day of Resurrection and addressed to the polytheists right after their questioning and dialogue. Between this and their dialogue, which ends with their saying, ﴿Indeed, we were astray﴾ [al-Saffat 37:32], it is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ). That is, when they finished their exchange, they were addressed with words that cut off their hope of being accepted when each of the two groups disclaims the consequences borne by the other group. This is so that they would be more certain of the punishment they already knew about from their own words, ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us. Indeed, we are going to taste [it]﴾ [al-Saffat 37:31]. This is what the meaning of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) in His words, "those who are going to taste the punishment," requires, because the active participle is literally about the present state, that is, the state of being engaged in the action. When they were told this, they were on the verge of falling into the punishment, and in Arabic usage that is the time of a present state.

When He described their punishment as painful, He followed it with news that this amount is not unjust to them, because it corresponds to their deeds that they used to do in the world, which stem from shirk (association of partners with God). The greatest share of this recompense is the share of shirk, but shirk is referred to by its actions, whereas shirk itself is a matter of belief.

In this there is evidence that the disbelievers are recompensed for their evil deeds, both words and actions, such as glorifying their gods and calling upon them, denying the Messenger ﷺ and harming him and the believers, saying about their idols that they are intercessors with God, and saying about the angels that they are the daughters of God, and from the killing of souls, raiding for wealth, burying daughters alive, and fornication. All of this increases their punishment, and it supports the view of those who held that the disbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Sharia (furu' al-shari'ah, the detailed legal rulings) and that this is indeed the case.

﴿Except for the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿For them is a known provision,﴾ ﴿fruits; and they will be honoured,﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Delight,﴾ ﴿on couches, facing one another.﴾ ﴿A cup will be passed around to them from a flowing spring,﴾ ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers,﴾ ﴿neither harmful to them nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their glances, with beautiful eyes,﴾ ﴿as if they were eggs well-guarded.﴾

This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception where the excluded item is not part of what precedes) with the meaning of an adversative correction (istidrak, a statement that corrects or qualifies what came before by contradicting it). This correction follows His saying ﴿Indeed, they, that Day, will be sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Saffat: 33], for the state of the sincere servants of Allah is the complete opposite of the state of those who did wrong. It is not necessary that the adversative correction be the removal of an assumed misunderstanding; that is only the usual case. So the statement of some scholars defining it as "a statement that corrects by removing what is assumed to be affirmed or negated" is a definition of the dominant case, or else what is intended is the slightest of assumptions, because the disjunctive exception is more general than that. It may be an exclusion from a ruling and not from the subject of the ruling. They explicitly stated that the exception particle in the disjunctive exception stands in place of *lakin* (but). For this reason they limit themselves to mentioning the exception particle and the excepted item; rather, they follow it with a clause that clarifies the place of the correction, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾ [al-A'raf: 11], and His saying ﴿except Iblis, who refused﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34]. Likewise is His saying here: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah; those will have a known provision﴾. Had the meaning been that of an exception, He would not have followed the excepted item with a predicate about it, because in that case it would affirm for it the opposite of the ruling of the excluded item merely by the exception, and that is what *illa* (except) implies. A parallel to this with *lakin* (but) is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then can you save those who are in the Fire?﴾ [al-Zumar: 19] ﴿But those who feared their Lord will have upper chambers﴾ [al-Zumar: 20], the verse in Surat al-Zumar.

Mentioning the believers with the attribute of servanthood ('ubudiyyah) attributed to Allah, exalted is He, is an honouring of them and a bringing near. This is a common usage in the Qur'an for the terms 'abd (servant) and 'ibad (servants) when attached to His pronoun, exalted is He, as in His saying ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength﴾ [Sad: 17] ... ﴿And remember Our servants Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾ [Sad: 45] ... ﴿O My servants, no fear will there be upon you today, nor will you grieve﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 68]. [Page 112]

because kindness may come without being accompanied by praise and esteem nor by harm, and this is the usual case, and it may come accompanied by harm, and that spoils its purity. [Page 113]

Malik narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam: "Its colour is bright and fine, so it is not like the wine of this world with its ugly appearance of redness or blackness."

The clause ﴿neither harmful to them﴾ is a fourth attribute of *ka's* in view of its application to wine.

So *al-tarf* here means the eyes, meaning women restraining their eyes. It was previously discussed at His saying ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 43] in Surat Ibrahim, and His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ [al-Naml: 40] in Surat al-Naml.
