*'In* is the plural of *'ayna'*, a woman with wide, large eyes and beautiful, long lashes.

*Al-bayd al-maknun* (the guarded eggs) is the eggs of the ostrich. The ostrich hides its eggs in holes in the sand and lines them with fine feathers. These holes are called *al-udahiyy*, and the singular is *udhhiyyah* on the pattern of *uthfiyyah*. The egg is then very lustrous in colour, white with a yellowish tinge

[Page 115]

﴿Except for the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿For them is a known provision,﴾ ﴿fruits; and they will be honoured,﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Delight,﴾ ﴿on couches, facing one another.﴾ ﴿A cup will be passed around to them from a flowing spring,﴾ ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers,﴾ ﴿neither harmful to them nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their glances, with beautiful eyes,﴾ ﴿as if they were eggs well-guarded.﴾

Had the meaning been that of an exception, He would not have followed the excepted item with a predicate about it, because in that case it would affirm for it the opposite of the ruling of the excluded item merely by the exception, and that is what *illa* (except) implies. ﴿Except for the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿For them is a known provision,﴾ ﴿fruits; and they will be honoured,﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Delight,﴾ ﴿on couches, facing one another.﴾ ﴿A cup will be passed around to them from a flowing spring,﴾ ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers,﴾ ﴿neither harmful to them nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their glances, with beautiful eyes,﴾ ﴿as if they were eggs well-guarded.﴾

[Page 111]

with the context of rebuke in His saying ﴿Did you lead these, My servants, astray?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], because the attribute of leading astray is an indicator that the attribution is not for bringing near. It is with a fatha on the lam when what is intended is those whom Allah has purified for His guardianship, and with a kasra on it, meaning those who purified their religion for Allah. Its purpose is to draw attention to the fact that they deserved what follows the demonstrative, because of the attribute of sincerity affirmed for them, as this is one of the implications of defining the subject by a demonstrative, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], after His saying ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-rizq* (provision) is food; He, exalted is He, said ﴿There she found provision﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], and He said ﴿No food will come to you both that you are provided with﴾ [Yusuf: 37]. *Al-ma'lum* (known) is that which does not fail its appointed time and which its people do not await.

"*Fawakih*" (fruits) is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to "*rizq*." The meaning is that all their food is of the kinds of food by which one enjoys oneself, not what is eaten for the sake of satiety. *Al-fawakih* are fruits and delicious vegetables.

He mentioned, in the midst of describing what is prepared for them of physical bounty, that for them is the bounty of honour, which is more important, because by it the soul is revived, along with what this involves of the purity of the favour from one who would spoil it

[Page 112]

because kindness may come without being accompanied by praise and esteem nor by harm, and this is the usual case, and it may come accompanied by harm, and that spoils its purity. He, exalted is He, said ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and harm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. So when kindness is with expressions of honour and a good welcome, that is the reward.

*Sururun* (couches) is the plural of *sarir*, which is like a wide chair on which one can recline. Sitting on a couch was a mark of kings and their likes, and it is the sitting of the people of bliss, because one seated on a couch does not feel boredom, for he changes his posture however he wishes.

"*Mutaqabilin*" (facing one another): each one is opposite the other. This is more complete for intimacy, because in it is the intimacy of gathering and the intimacy of looking at one another, for seeing a beloved and a companion delights the soul.

The apparent meaning of their being *mutaqabilin* is facing one another as individuals, each group with its companions, and that they are groups according to their ranks in the levels of Paradise, and that the people of each level are divided into groups according to their kinship in Paradise, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56]. The multitude of each group does not contradict their facing one another on couches and on canopied thrones, and their conversing, because the affairs of that world do not proceed in the manner familiar in this world.

The meaning of "*yutaf*" (is passed around) is that it is circulated among them while they are in their gatherings. *Al-ka's* (with a hamza after the kaf) is the vessel of wine, and it is feminine; it is a vessel with no handle and no spout, wide-mouthed, meaning the place from which it is poured. They cited the words of al-A'sha:

"And a cup I drank with pleasure, and another by which I treated myself."

[Page 113]

"*Ma'in*" with a fatha on the mim. It was said that its origin is *ma'yun*. Some said its mim is original, and it is derived from *ma'n*, as one says *ma' ma'n* (flowing water). Then *ma'in* is on the pattern *fa'il*, an intensive form from *al-ma'n*, which is going far in an action; he likened its flow to going far in walking. This is more apparent in derivation. Others said its mim is extra, and it is derived from *'anahu*, meaning to see him, because it appears on the face of the earth as it flows. Its pattern is then *maf'ul*, and its origin is *ma'yun*. It is derived from a solid noun, namely the noun for eye ('ayn), and the verb *'ana* is not in use; they dispensed with it by the verb *'ayana*.

"*Bayda'*" (white) is an attribute of "*ka's*." Since the cup is intended to mean the wine within it, the attribute "white" is for the wine. The feminine form of the attribute came in agreement with the expression of wine by the word *ka's*, although the word for wine is masculine and feminine, and the feminine is more common. Malik narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam: "Its colour is bright and fine, so it is not like the wine of this world with its ugly appearance of redness or blackness."

*Al-ladhdhah* (delight) is a noun whose meaning is a perception agreeable to the soul of the perceiver. One says *ladhdhahu* and *ladha bihi*; the verbal noun is *al-ladhdhah* and *al-ladhadhah*. The clause ﴿neither harmful to them﴾ is a fourth attribute of *ka's* in view of its application to wine.

He placed the subject before the predicate, and the predicate is a verb, in order that the fronting should express restricting the subject to the verbal predicate, meaning, unlike the drinkers of wine among the people of this world.

"*Yunzafun*" is in the passive voice in the recitation of the majority; one says *nuzifa al-sharib* in the passive when it is intransitive, so he is *manzuf* and *nazif*. Its origin is from *nazafa al-rajul ma' al-bi'r* in the transitive form, when he drained the well and nothing remained of it.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited *yunzifun* with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the za', from *unzifa al-sharib*, when his intellect has gone, meaning he became one having intoxication; so the hamza is for becoming, not for transitivity.

*Qasirat al-tarf* means restraining their glances out of modesty and coquetry. *Al-taraf* is the eye, and it is singular with no plural from its own form, because the origin of *al-taraf* is the verbal noun of *taraf bi-'aynihi* on the pattern *daraba*, when he moved his eyelids; then the eye was called *taraf*. So *al-tarf* here means the eyes, meaning women restraining their eyes. It was previously discussed at His saying ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 43] in Surat Ibrahim, and His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ [al-Naml: 40] in Surat al-Naml.

"*'Inda*" (with) is mentioned to express that they are in company with them in their gatherings in which the cup of Paradise is circulated among them. The presence of maidens at drinking gatherings was among the things that completed delight and merriment among the chiefs of the Arabs. Tarafah said:

"My companions are fair like stars, and a singing girl who circulates among us between the cold and the mixed (wine)."

*'In* is the plural of *'ayna'*, a woman with wide, large eyes and beautiful, long lashes.

*Al-bayd al-maknun* (the guarded eggs) is the eggs of the ostrich. The ostrich hides its eggs in holes in the sand and lines them with fine feathers. These holes are called *al-udahiyy*, and the singular is *udhhiyyah* on the pattern of *uthfiyyah*. The egg is then very lustrous in colour, white with a yellowish tinge

[Page 115]

and that colour is the most beautiful of women's complexions. In former times people likened beautiful women to ostrich eggs. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And a sheltered maiden whose tent is not approached, who enjoyed the pleasures with her without haste."

﴿Except for the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿For them is a known provision,﴾ ﴿fruits; and they will be honoured,﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Delight,﴾ ﴿on couches, facing one another.﴾ ﴿A cup will be passed around to them from a flowing spring,﴾ ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers,﴾ ﴿neither harmful to them nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their glances, with beautiful eyes,﴾ ﴿as if they were eggs well-guarded.﴾

[Page 111]

with the context of rebuke in His saying ﴿Did you lead these, My servants, astray?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], because the attribute of leading astray is an indicator that the attribution is not for bringing near. Here the indicator of predominance (taghlib, the inclusion of a broader group under a term) is the basis for the exception of the deviators from His saying "My servants." "What increased me in honour and pride, and nearly made me walk on the Pleiades with my toes, is my entry under Your saying, 'O My servants' [al-'Ankabut: 56], and that You sent Ahmad as a prophet for me."

"*Al-mukhlasin*" is an attribute of "servants of Allah." It is with a fatha on the lam when what is intended is those whom Allah has purified for His guardianship, and with a kasra on it, meaning those who purified their religion for Allah. Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf recited it with a fatha on the lam. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited it with a kasra on the lam.

"*Ula'ika*" (those) is a demonstrative referring to "servants of Allah." Its purpose is to draw attention to the fact that they deserved what follows the demonstrative, because of the attribute of sincerity affirmed for them, as this is one of the implications of defining the subject by a demonstrative, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], after His saying ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-rizq* (provision) is food; He, exalted is He, said ﴿There she found provision﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], and He said ﴿No food will come to you both that you are provided with﴾ [Yusuf: 37]. *Al-ma'lum* (known) is that which does not fail its appointed time and which its people do not await.

"*Fawakih*" (fruits) is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to "*rizq*." The meaning is that all their food is of the kinds of food by which one enjoys oneself, not what is eaten for the sake of satiety. *Al-fawakih* are fruits and delicious vegetables.

"*Hum mukramun*" (and they will be honoured) is conjoined to ﴿For them is a known provision﴾, meaning they are treated with warmth and joy. He mentioned, in the midst of describing what is prepared for them of physical bounty, that for them is the bounty of honour, which is more important, because by it the soul is revived, along with what this involves of the purity of the favour from one who would spoil it

[Page 112]

because kindness may come without being accompanied by praise and esteem nor by harm, and this is the usual case, and it may come accompanied by harm, and that spoils its purity. *Sururun* (couches) is the plural of *sarir*, which is like a wide chair on which one can recline. Sitting on a couch was a mark of kings and their likes, and it is the sitting of the people of bliss, because one seated on a couch does not feel boredom, for he changes his posture however he wishes.

The apparent meaning of their being *mutaqabilin* is facing one another as individuals, each group with its companions, and that they are groups according to their ranks in the levels of Paradise, and that the people of each level are divided into groups according to their kinship in Paradise, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56]. The multitude of each group does not contradict their facing one another on couches and on canopied thrones, and their conversing, because the affairs of that world do not proceed in the manner familiar in this world.

The meaning of "*yutaf*" (is passed around) is that it is circulated among them while they are in their gatherings. *Al-ka's* (with a hamza after the kaf) is the vessel of wine, and it is feminine; it is a vessel with no handle and no spout, wide-mouthed, meaning the place from which it is poured. It may be of silver, of gold, of clay, or of glass, and it is called *qadah* (cup), which is masculine. The plural of *ka's* is *kasat*, *ku'us* and *akwas*. *Ka's* was used exclusively for pouring wine, to the point that *ka's* became one of the names of wine by naming the container after its contents. They cited the words of al-A'sha:

"And a cup I drank with pleasure, and another by which I treated myself."

[Page 113]

"*Ma'in*" with a fatha on the mim. It was said that its origin is *ma'yun*. Some said its mim is original, and it is derived from *ma'n*, as one says *ma' ma'n* (flowing water). Then *ma'in* is on the pattern *fa'il*, an intensive form from *al-ma'n*, which is going far in an action; he likened its flow to going far in walking. This is more apparent in derivation. "*Bayda'*" (white) is an attribute of "*ka's*." Since the cup is intended to mean the wine within it, the attribute "white" is for the wine. The feminine form of the attribute came in agreement with the expression of wine by the word *ka's*, although the word for wine is masculine and feminine, and the feminine is more common. Malik narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam: "Its colour is bright and fine, so it is not like the wine of this world with its ugly appearance of redness or blackness."

The clause ﴿nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿neither harmful to them﴾.

He placed the subject before the predicate, and the predicate is a verb, in order that the fronting should express restricting the subject to the verbal predicate, meaning, unlike the drinkers of wine among the people of this world.

They likened the drinker's intellect to blood; one says *nuzifa dam al-jarih*, meaning it was drained. Its origin is from *nazafa al-rajul ma' al-bi'r* in the transitive form, when he drained the well and nothing remained of it.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited *yunzifun* with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the za', from *unzifa al-sharib*, when his intellect has gone, meaning he became one having intoxication; so the hamza is for becoming, not for transitivity.

*Qasirat al-tarf* means restraining their glances out of modesty and coquetry. *Al-taraf* is the eye, and it is singular with no plural from its own form, because the origin of *al-taraf* is the verbal noun of *taraf bi-'aynihi* on the pattern *daraba*, when he moved his eyelids; then the eye was called *taraf*. So *al-tarf* here means the eyes, meaning women restraining their eyes. It was previously discussed at His saying ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 43] in Surat Ibrahim, and His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ [al-Naml: 40] in Surat al-Naml.

﴿Except for the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿For them is a known provision,﴾ ﴿fruits; and they will be honoured,﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Delight,﴾ ﴿on couches, facing one another.﴾ ﴿A cup will be passed around to them from a flowing spring,﴾ ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers,﴾ ﴿neither harmful to them nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their glances, with beautiful eyes,﴾ ﴿as if they were eggs well-guarded.﴾

Sometimes 'abd is used unattached, also meaning bringing near, as in His saying ﴿And We gave to Dawud Sulayman; an excellent servant﴾ [Sad: 30], that is, a servant of Allah. Do you not see that when the intent is to mention a group of Allah's servants among the polytheists, the word 'ibad is not brought attached, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾ [al-Isra': 5], except

[Page 111]

with the context of rebuke in His saying ﴿Did you lead these, My servants, astray?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], because the attribute of leading astray is an indicator that the attribution is not for bringing near. Also His saying ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the deviators﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. Here the indicator of predominance (taghlib, the inclusion of a broader group under a term) is the basis for the exception of the deviators from His saying "My servants." It is attributed to al-Shafi'i:

"What increased me in honour and pride, and nearly made me walk on the Pleiades with my toes, is my entry under Your saying, 'O My servants' [al-'Ankabut: 56], and that You sent Ahmad as a prophet for me."

Those intended here are those who believed in the Prophet ﷺ, for they are the ones who come to mind when the states of the polytheists who disbelieved in him are mentioned, and who said about him what is far from him, the coming to mind of the opposite by mention of its opposite.

"*Al-mukhlasin*" is an attribute of "servants of Allah." It is with a fatha on the lam when what is intended is those whom Allah has purified for His guardianship, and with a kasra on it, meaning those who purified their religion for Allah. Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf recited it with a fatha on the lam. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited it with a kasra on the lam.

"*Ula'ika*" (those) is a demonstrative referring to "servants of Allah." Its purpose is to draw attention to the fact that they deserved what follows the demonstrative, because of the attribute of sincerity affirmed for them, as this is one of the implications of defining the subject by a demonstrative, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], after His saying ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-rizq* (provision) is food; He, exalted is He, said ﴿There she found provision﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], and He said ﴿No food will come to you both that you are provided with﴾ [Yusuf: 37]. *Al-ma'lum* (known) is that which does not fail its appointed time and which its people do not await.

"*Fawakih*" (fruits) is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to "*rizq*." The meaning is that all their food is of the kinds of food by which one enjoys oneself, not what is eaten for the sake of satiety. *Al-fawakih* are fruits and delicious vegetables.

"*Hum mukramun*" (and they will be honoured) is conjoined to ﴿For them is a known provision﴾, meaning they are treated with warmth and joy. He mentioned, in the midst of describing what is prepared for them of physical bounty, that for them is the bounty of honour, which is more important, because by it the soul is revived, along with what this involves of the purity of the favour from one who would spoil it

[Page 112]

He, exalted is He, said ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and harm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. So when kindness is with expressions of honour and a good welcome, that is the reward.

*Sururun* (couches) is the plural of *sarir*, which is like a wide chair on which one can recline. Sitting on a couch was a mark of kings and their likes, and it is the sitting of the people of bliss, because one seated on a couch does not feel boredom, for he changes his posture however he wishes.

The apparent meaning of their being *mutaqabilin* is facing one another as individuals, each group with its companions, and that they are groups according to their ranks in the levels of Paradise, and that the people of each level are divided into groups according to their kinship in Paradise, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56]. The multitude of each group does not contradict their facing one another on couches and on canopied thrones, and their conversing, because the affairs of that world do not proceed in the manner familiar in this world.

The clause ﴿neither harmful to them﴾ is a fourth attribute of *ka's* in view of its application to wine.

The placement of "*ghawl*" [Page 114] which is indefinite after the negating *la*, expresses the negation of this kind from its root, and its being nominative was required because the separation between it and the negative particle was by the predicate.

The clause ﴿nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿neither harmful to them﴾.

He placed the subject before the predicate, and the predicate is a verb, in order that the fronting should express restricting the subject to the verbal predicate, meaning, unlike the drinkers of wine among the people of this world.

*Al-ghawl*, with a fatha on the ghayn, is what afflicts the drinker of wine of headache and pain; it is derived from *al-ghawl*, the verbal noun of *ghala*, meaning to destroy him. This has the same meaning as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They will not be affected by it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19].

Fronting the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) before the predicate for the subject serves to restrict, meaning that it is negated of the wine of Paradise only, not of the wine known in this world; this is a *qasr qalb* (restriction that corrects a false belief). The placement of "*ghawl*" [Page 114] which is indefinite after the negating *la*, expresses the negation of this kind from its root, and its being nominative was required because the separation between it and the negative particle was by the predicate.

The clause ﴿nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿neither harmful to them﴾.

He placed the subject before the predicate, and the predicate is a verb, in order that the fronting should express restricting the subject to the verbal predicate, meaning, unlike the drinkers of wine among the people of this world.

"*Yunzafun*" is in the passive voice in the recitation of the majority; one says *nuzifa al-sharib* in the passive when it is intransitive, so he is *manzuf* and *nazif*. They likened the drinker's intellect to blood; one says *nuzifa dam al-jarih*, meaning it was drained. Its origin is from *nazafa al-rajul ma' al-bi'r* in the transitive form, when he drained the well and nothing remained of it.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited *yunzifun* with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the za', from *unzifa al-sharib*, when his intellect has gone, meaning he became one having intoxication; so the hamza is for becoming, not for transitivity.

*Qasirat al-tarf* means restraining their glances out of modesty and coquetry. *Al-taraf* is the eye, and it is singular with no plural from its own form, because the origin of *al-taraf* is the verbal noun of *taraf bi-'aynihi* on the pattern *daraba*, when he moved his eyelids; then the eye was called *taraf*. So *al-tarf* here means the eyes, meaning women restraining their eyes. It was previously discussed at His saying ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 43] in Surat Ibrahim, and His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ [al-Naml: 40] in Surat al-Naml.

"*'Inda*" (with) is mentioned to express that they are in company with them in their gatherings in which the cup of Paradise is circulated among them. The presence of maidens at drinking gatherings was among the things that completed delight and merriment among the chiefs of the Arabs. Tarafah said:

"My companions are fair like stars, and a singing girl who circulates among us between the cold and the mixed (wine)."

*'In* is the plural of *'ayna'*, a woman with wide, large eyes and beautiful, long lashes.

*Al-bayd al-maknun* (the guarded eggs) is the eggs of the ostrich. The ostrich hides its eggs in holes in the sand and lines them with fine feathers. These holes are called *al-udahiyy*, and the singular is *udhhiyyah* on the pattern of *uthfiyyah*. The egg is then very lustrous in colour, white with a yellowish tinge

[Page 115]

and that colour is the most beautiful of women's complexions. In former times people likened beautiful women to ostrich eggs. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And a sheltered maiden whose tent is not approached, who enjoyed the pleasures with her without haste."

[p. 116]

﴿So they turn to one another, questioning each other.﴾ ﴿A speaker among them says, "I had a companion﴾ ﴿who would say, 'Are you truly among those who affirm?﴾ ﴿'When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?'"﴾ ﴿He says, "Would you like to look?"﴾ ﴿So he looks and sees him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿He says, "By God, you nearly brought me to ruin.﴾ ﴿And had it not been for the favor of my Lord, I would surely have been among those brought forth [to punishment]."﴾

The *fa'* here is *fa' al-tafri'* (the "therefore" particle of consequence), because the custom of companions sitting together in pleasure is that they begin to converse, for there is delight in conversation with friends and boon-companions, as Muhammad ibn Fayyad said:

*"Of pleasures there remain only the talk of the noble over wine."*

When they perceive that what they have come to of bliss is a reward for their faith and sincerity before, one of them recalls the one who used to argue with him about the reality of resurrection and recompense, and he praises God for guiding him not to lend an ear to that obstructer. So he tells his companions about it and shows them him in the Fire. For this reason the mutual questioning of some of them is related with the *fa'* of sequence (*fa' al-ta'qib*). This indicates that in the Hereafter people's recollections return to them, which in this world were clear of evil thoughts and psychic turbidity, perceiving realities as they truly are.

In narrating this state the past-tense forms are used, although it is future, to affirm that it certainly occurs, as if it had already occurred, in the manner of His saying ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. The indicator is the consequence drawn from the reports concerning the conditions of the Hereafter.

*Al-tasa'ul* (mutual questioning) means that some ask others. The object of the questioning is omitted because what follows indicates it. Something similar is made explicit in His saying ﴿In Gardens, they ask one another﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 40] ﴿about the criminals﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 41] ﴿"What led you into Saqar?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42].

The clause ﴿A speaker among them says﴾ is a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive apposition, "a substitute containing the meaning of the preceding") for the clause "they question one another", meaning: one of them spoke in answer to the questioning of some of them. The meaning of questioning includes the meaning of answering, so we have treated it as *badal al-ishtimal*, not *badal al-ba'd* (partial apposition) nor *'atf al-bayan* (explicative apposition).

The *qarin* (companion) is meant generically, for this statement is one that many of the associates of polytheists would make before they accepted Islam. The *qarin* is the constant, adhering companion; the strong adherence is likened to tying two things together so that they cannot be separated. That is, when his companion became Muslim and his companion remained in unbelief, he argues with him about Islam and tries to create doubt about its soundness, hoping he will return him to unbelief. Sa'id ibn Zayd said: "I saw myself, and 'Umar was binding me [in chains] for Islam," meaning: making me bound because I had embraced Islam. Sa'id was the brother-in-law of 'Umar, married to his sister.

The interrogative in ﴿Are you truly among those who affirm?﴾ is used for denunciation: it was not right for you to believe this. The interrogative was attached to the emphatic particle to indicate that the news of his companion's Islam had reached him as firmly established, so he came to reject what had been confirmed to him. That is, his denial of his Islam was after the news had been verified; had he not verified it, he would not have supposed this of him.

*Al-musaddiq* (the affirmer) is the one who is certain of the report.

The clause ﴿"When we have died"﴾ [al-Saffat: 16] explains the clause ﴿Are you truly among those who affirm?﴾; it clarifies the vague denial with a detailed denial, namely denying that people will be resurrected after their parts have scattered and turned to dust after death and then be recompensed.

The clause "Indeed we are surely to be recompensed" is the answer of *idha* (when). It is joined with the emphatic particle for the reason you have learned in His saying ﴿Are you truly among those who affirm?﴾.

*Al-madin* means the one who is requited. It is said: *dana-hu yadinu-hu*, when he requited him. Its most common usage is for requital in kind, and *al-din* means recompense, as in the Surah al-Fatihah. Here it is said "we are surely to be recompensed" and at the beginning of the surah "we are surely to be resurrected", because of the difference among the speakers.

All read ﴿Are you truly﴾ with two hamzas (*'a'innaka*). All except Ibn 'Amir read ﴿When we have died﴾ with two hamzas, while Ibn 'Amir reads it with one hamza, which is *idha*, relying on the hamza of "Indeed we are surely to be recompensed" in his reading. Nafi' reads "Indeed we are surely to be recompensed" with one hamza, relying on the interrogative that enters on its condition. The rest read with two hamzas.

The clause ﴿He says, "Would you like to look?"﴾ is a *badal al-ishtimal* for the clause ﴿A speaker among them says﴾, because his saying ﴿Would you like to look?﴾, reported by it, is among what the first statement contained, since it is a completion of the first statement.

The interrogative in ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ is used for offering: he offered his companions to look toward seeing his companion and what he had come to. This is either because he knew that his companion had died in unbelief, having preceded him in death, or because it was cast into his heart that his companion had gone to the Fire; and he is certain that the keeper of the Fire will show them this companion, since the people of Paradise know that they will have whatever they ask for. God, the Exalted, said ﴿and they will have whatever they ask for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57].

The object of *muttali'un* (looking) is omitted, because the end of the speech indicates it by His saying ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾. The estimate is: "Would you like to look upon the people of the Fire, so that we may see him among them?"

In His saying "So he looks" there is sufficiency, meaning: so he looked and saw him, and they saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire. He only offered them the looking so they would know the reality of what he had told them about his companion. He mentioned only his own looking, not the looking of his companions, because he began by looking in order to distinguish his companion and show him to his companions.

*Sawa' al-Jahim* means its middle. Bal'a' ibn Qays said:

*"A sharp sword struck the middle of the head and split it."*

The clause ﴿He says, "By God, you nearly brought me to ruin"﴾ is resumed as a *isti'naf bayani* (explanatory resumption), because the description of this state arouses in the hearer's mind the question: "What happened when he looked?" It is answered: when he saw his companion, he began to rebuke him for what he had been trying on him, to the point that he nearly threw him into the Fire as well. This rebuke includes reproach for his attempt to turn him back from Islam.

The oath with the particle *ta'* (*ta-llahi*) is typically used when the answer to the oath is unusual, as previously mentioned in His saying ﴿They said, "By God, you certainly know"﴾ [Yusuf: 73] in the Surah Yusuf, and His saying ﴿"By God, I will surely plot against your idols"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 57] in the Surah al-Anbiya'. The place of strangeness is his escape from the snare of his companion, and the difference in the outcome of the two of them despite their former close adherence and companionship, and the grace of guidance that surrounded him, and how his companion had become entangled in the depths of error.

*In* (إن) is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the verb that abrogates (the nominal sentence) is attached to it, as is most common with it when it is deprived of its operation.

The *lam* that enters on the predicate of *kada* is the one that distinguishes the lightened *in* from the negative *in*. *Turdini* means "brings me to *al-radaa*", which is perdition. The root of *al-radaa* is death, then its metaphorical use for bad condition became widespread, likened to death because it was commonly considered the greatest calamity to befall a person.

The meaning is: you came close to leading me to the state of perdition by your insistence in turning me away from faith in resurrection, out of excessive companionship. And had it not been for the blessing of God's guidance and His steadying of me, I would have been among those brought forth with you to punishment.

The reading of the majority is ﴿لَتُرْدِينِ﴾ with a kasra-ended *nun* without the *ya'* of the first person, for lightening. This deletion is common in eloquent usage and is the dialect of the people of Najd. It is written in the codices without the *ya'*. Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', read it with the *ya'* affirmed, and this does not contradict the orthography of the codex, because many *ya's* were not written in the codex. The reciters read it with the *ya'* affirmed, since the scribes of the codex omitted many long vowels of *alif* and *ya'*.

By *al-muhdarun* (those brought forth) is meant those brought forth into the Fire, that is: I would have been among those brought forth with you for punishment. The application of *al-muhdar* and similar forms to one who is brought forth for punishment is very common.

Some exegetes have interpreted the *qarin* here as the devil who constantly accompanies a person to lead him astray and mislead him. But the manner of narrating the speaker from the people of Paradise taking the initiative to inform the people of his assembly of his state refutes this interpretation, for if the intended meaning were the devil, informing them of it would be of no benefit, since none of them lacks a companion from the devils, and none of them lacks knowledge that the destiny of the devils is the Fire.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning two partners, the two referred to in His saying ﴿Present to them the parable of two men: for one of them We had made two gardens of grapevines﴾ [al-Kahf: 32] in the Surah al-Kahf.

It is related from 'Ata' al-Khurasani that it was revealed concerning two brothers, one a believer and the other an unbeliever, who were both wealthy: the believer spent his wealth on charities, while the unbeliever spent his wealth on pleasures.

In this verse there is a lesson about beware of evil companions, and the obligation to guard oneself against what they call to and beautify of ruinous paths.

﴿So they turn to one another, questioning each other.﴾ ﴿A speaker among them says, "I had a companion﴾ ﴿who would say, 'Are you truly among those who affirm?﴾ ﴿'When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?'"﴾ ﴿He says, "Would you like to look?"﴾ ﴿So he looks and sees him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿He says, "By God, you nearly brought me to ruin.﴾ ﴿And had it not been for the favor of my Lord, I would surely have been among those brought forth [to punishment]."﴾

When they perceive that what they have come to of bliss is a reward for their faith and sincerity before, one of them recalls the one who used to argue with him about the reality of resurrection and recompense, and he praises God for guiding him not to lend an ear to that obstructer. This indicates that in the Hereafter people's recollections return to them, which in this world were clear of evil thoughts and psychic turbidity, perceiving realities as they truly are.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 58–60:

﴿Are we not to die﴾ ﴿except our first death? And we will not be punished﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾. The interrogative fa' (fa’ al-istifham) is conjoined to the clause ﴿He said: Would you like to look down?﴾ [al-Saffat: 54], so the interrogation is directed by this speaker to some of those who were questioning one another.

It is used in the sense of taqrir (affirmation in the form of a question), intended to remind of the blessing of eternal life. After he had informed them of the fate of his evil companion, he turned to his companions to complete his speech, speaking of the blessing, rejoicing and delighting in it, and mentioning it, for mentioning beloved things carries a pleasure. So consider the mention of a blessing in which they were immersed and whose eternity they were certain of. Perhaps the arrangement of this reminder in the form of an affirmative interrogation is intended so that he hears the repetition of this matter when his companions answer him by saying: Yes, we are not to die.

The exception in His words ﴿except our first death﴾ is munqati' (disjunctive), because the death that is negated is death in the present or future, as is the case with the active participle. It is therefore determined that the excepted item is not included in the negated item, so it is disjunctive, meaning: but the first death. This corrective exception is an emphasis of the negation, and its accusative case is due to the disjunction, not to the negation.

He conjoined ﴿and we will not be punished﴾ so that the interrogation would be purely for speaking of the blessing, because the polytheists too are not dying, but they are punished, and their condition is worse than death. It was said to one of the wise men: What is worse than death? He said: That in which death is wished for.

The apparent view is that the clause ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾ is a quotation of the rest of the speech of the speaker to his companions, so it stands as a concluding and summarizing statement (tadhyil and fadhlaka) for their state, some of which is witnessed and some of which is described by his words ﴿Are we not to die﴾.

This is a tail-piece (tadhyil) to the narration of the state of God's sincere servants. It is a statement from God Most High, serving to honour what the sincere servants of God possess, and to encourage acting in the same manner as they acted, through which God granted them sincerity (ikhlas) toward Him. The reference in His words "﴿For the like of this﴾" is to what is contained in His words "﴿Those will have a known provision﴾" [al-Saffat: 41] and what follows, that is, for the like of their bliss, their intimacy, their joy, their pleasures, their delight, and the everlasting nature of all of that.

The "like of it" means its counterpart of bliss given to other sincere servants. By "those who work" (al-'amilin) is meant those who do good and walk according to what the law of Islam (shari'at al-Islam) has laid down for them. The object of (ya'mal) is omitted for brevity, since it is evident from the context.

The lam in "li-mithl" is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil). The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb serves to convey restriction (qasr), meaning: not for the work of anyone else. This is an inversion (qalb) in response to the polytheists who imagine that they are doing righteous deeds and boast of them, a matter of vanity. God Most High said: "﴿Say: Shall we inform you of those who are greatest in loss as to their deeds?﴾" [al-Kahf: 103] "﴿Those whose effort is lost in the worldly life while they think that they are doing well in work﴾" [al-Kahf: 104].

The meaning is: for attaining the like of this; the mudaf (the governed noun) has been omitted, since the lam indicates its meaning.

The fa' is for the consequence drawn from the content of the narrative mentioned before it, from His words "﴿except the sincere servants of God﴾" [al-Saffat: 40] and what follows.

The imperative in "fa-l-ya'mal" is an earnest directive (irshad sadiq) toward obligatory and recommended acts.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 62–68 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is that better as a hospitable provision, or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ ﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of the Hellfire.﴾ ﴿Its fruit-stalks are like the heads of devils.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it.﴾ ﴿Then indeed for them thereafter is a mixture of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire.﴾

This is a resumption after the completion of the story of the believer and his companions, intended to draw attention to the gulf between the condition of the believer and that of the disbeliever. It follows the Qur'an's usual practice of appending to narratives and parables a reminder of their lessons and admonitions.

The main point of the statement is His saying ﴿Indeed, We made it﴾, meaning the tree of zaqqum is a trial for the wrongdoers, to the end of the verses. The discourse was framed in this manner in order to arouse eagerness for what follows.

The interrogative is used figuratively to draw attention to the superiority of the believer's condition and his success, and to the loss of the disbeliever. It is addressed to every listener.

The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ refers to what preceded concerning the condition of the believers in bliss and eternity. The demonstrative is used in the singular with regard to the thing mentioned, and it is marked with distance to magnify what is indicated, meaning the distance of rank and its loftiness, for a precious and noble thing is imagined as elevated, and elevation is accompanied by distance from the usual place, which is the low. How far the Pleiades are from the dust!

Nuzul (نُزُل), with two vowels, and it is also said nuzl with a single vowel and sukun, is in its original linguistic sense the place where the one who alights (nazil) stays, as stated by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Manzur (author of Lisan al-'Arab) and al-Fayruzabadi (author of al-Qamus) followed this. It was widely and commonly applied to food prepared for a guest, because it was prepared for him for his alighting, a designation by the name of its place, like the usage of suknā (سُكْنَى) with a sukun on the kaf for food prepared for the resident of a house, since the dwelling (maskan) is also called sakn.

Most of the exegetes adopted this meaning, and al-Raghib did not mention anything other than it.

It is possible that the intended meaning of nuzul here is the food of hospitality in Paradise.

It is possible also that it is meant as a place of alighting, with an elided noun in His saying ﴿or the tree of zaqqum﴾, the sense being: or the place of the tree of zaqqum.

On both interpretations, the accusative of ﴿nuzulan﴾ is as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the demonstrative, and the referent of the demonstrative ﴿that﴾ is what suits both interpretations from His saying ﴿provision known﴾ [al-Saffat: 41], ﴿fruits, and they will be honored﴾ [al-Saffat: 42], ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾ [al-Saffat: 43].

On both interpretations, the sense of the counterpart of the interrogative (mu'adil al-istifham) also applies. It may be that you estimate: or the dwelling of the tree of zaqqum, on the pattern of His, exalted is He, ﴿Which of the two parties is better in position and finer in assembly?﴾ [Maryam: 73], where two places were mentioned. Or you may estimate: or the descent of the tree of zaqqum; and on this second interpretation the counterpart is a mock-parallel (mushakalah), used in derision, since the food of the tree of zaqqum does not deserve to be called a nuzul.

The tree of zaqqum is mentioned here as something already known from before, because it appears defined by the genitive construction, being situated in a context of contrast between two conditions, good and evil. It is therefore fitting that the reference be to two well-known examples. As for the first: it is a name the Qur'an gave to a tree in Hell, and its mention had preceded in His saying ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers, will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 51–52] in Surat al-Waqi'ah, whose revelation was before Surat al-Saffat. What clarifies this is what al-Kalbi related: when that verse of Surat al-Waqi'ah was revealed, Ibn al-Za'bara said: "God has increased zaqqum in your houses, for the people of Yemen call dates and butter zaqqum." Then Abu Jahl said to his slave-girl: "Bring us zaqqum," and she brought him butter and dates, and he said: "Eat zaqqum!"

And from Ibn Sidah: "It has reached us that when there was revealed ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44], that is, in Surat al-Dukhan, Quraysh did not recognize it. Abu Jahl said: 'O slave-girl, bring us dates and butter, let us eat zaqqum (nazdaqimuhu),' and they began to eat and say: 'Is it with this that Muhammad threatens us regarding the Hereafter?'" End of quotation. The more fitting view is that this statement of theirs was made when they heard the verse of Surat al-Dukhan, where it came in indefinite form.

As for the second: it is the name of a known tree that is disliked. It was said: it is one of the most evil of trees, found in Tihamah and in the barren lands bordering the desert, foul-smelling, with small leaves, poisonous, with a milky sap; if it touches human skin, the skin swells and the person generally dies from it. This was stated by Qutrub and Abu Hanifah.

The Qur'an's detailed description of it here requires that it was not known to them, so it mentioned it in summary in Surat al-Waqi'ah. When they said what they said, it detailed its attributes here in this verse, and in Surat al-Dukhan with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44] ﴿like molten brass it boils in the bellies﴾ [al-Dukhan: 45] ﴿like the boiling of scalding water﴾ [al-Dukhan: 46].

The Qur'an named it with this idafa as though it were derived from zuqmah, with a damma on the zay and sukun on the qaf, which is the name of the plague. Ibn Durayd said: zaqqum is not derived from tazaqqum, which is excessive eating to the point of disgust. He intends to refute those who said it is derived from tazaqqum, meaning swallowing with difficulty because of aversion to the thing.

Then it continued describing it by saying that God made it a trial for the wrongdoers, that is, a punishment, like the sense in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], that is, they punished them with the trench of fire.

Fitnah has also been explained as: the report of the tree of zaqqum was a trial for the polytheists, since it incited them to denial and mockery. Thus the sense of "We made it" is: We made its mention and its report (a trial), that is, when the verse of Surat al-Waqi'ah was revealed, we made its mention a stimulus to their trial through denial and mockery without understanding. This is like His saying ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels, and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. When His saying about Hell was revealed, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30], Abu Jahl said to Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! Ibn Abi Kabshah tells you that the guardians of the Fire are nineteen, and you are the multitude! Can not each ten of you overpower one man of them?" (that is, of the guardians of the Fire). Then Abu al-Ashadd al-Jumahi said: "I will suffice you for seventeen, so suffice me with two of you." So God revealed ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31] (meaning none of them is like one of mankind) ﴿and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

He resumed with a second resumption describing it, in which He used the word ﴿indeed﴾ (innaha) with emphasis for awe. The sense of ﴿sprouts forth﴾ (takhruju) is "grows," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. Among the wondrous power of God, the Exalted, is that He made a tree from fire, while it is necessarily of fire. God formed in the fire a tree of fire, and an approximation of this is what is pictured in fiery firework displays, with shapes and colours like palm trees and the like.

He made for it a ṭal' (طَلْع), that is, fruit, and the name ṭal' was applied to it figuratively, likening it to the spathe of the palm, because the name ṭal' is specific to palms. Ibn 'Atiyyah said, from al-Suddi and Mujahid: the disbelievers said: "How does Muhammad report that fire makes trees grow, when it consumes them and destroys them?" So their saying this and similar things is a trial for them, because it increases them in disbelief and denial.

The phrase ﴿heads of devils﴾ may mean the heads of devils of the jinn, the plural of shaytan in its well-known sense. The heads of these devils are unknown to them, so the comparison refers them to what their imagination pictures. The fruit of the tree of zaqqum was unknown, so it was described to people as hideous and repulsive, and its repulsiveness was likened to the repulsiveness of the heads of devils. This comparison is of the intelligible to the intelligible, like the comparison of faith to life in His saying ﴿that he may warn whoever is alive﴾ [Ya-Sin: 70]. The purpose here is to bring the condition of the thing compared closer, so there is no barrier to the compared thing (the tree) or the comparing thing (devils' heads) being unknown.

A parallel to this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*And sharpened, blue, like the fangs of ghouls*

It was also said: what is meant by the heads of devils is the fruit of the astan (الأستن), with an open hamzah, a sukun on the sin, and an open ta'. The astan is a tree in the Yemeni desert that resembles the figures of people, and its fruit is called the heads of devils. They called it so because of its ugly appearance, and then it became well known, so it was compared to it in the verse. It was also said that shayatin is the plural of shaytan, which among snakes is one that has crests on its head. The rajiz said, comparing his wife to a snake of this kind:

*Ungarded, she swears when I swear, like the shaytan of the hammat, the one with crests.*

Al-hammat is the plural of hammatah, with an open ha: a tree in which snakes abound. Al-'anjard, with a kasrah on the ra': the bad-tempered woman.

These attributes by which the tree of zaqqum is described reach a great degree of blame, and this blame is what was expressed by the word "accursed" in His saying ﴿and the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾ [al-Isra': 60] in Surat al-Isra', and likewise in the verses ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum is the food of the sinful, like molten brass it boils in the bellies, like the boiling of scalding water﴾ in Surat al-Dukhan.

They have been warned that they will indeed eat from it, a strongly emphasized warning, meaning they will eat from its fruit, which is that ṭal'. The pronoun in "from it" refers to the tree, following the common usage of people: "I ate from the palm tree," meaning from its fruit.

The meaning is: they will eat from it unwillingly, and that is part of the punishment. When the food is disgusting, its foul appearance increases the aversion, just as when the desired food is pleasant to look at, approaching it is with eagerness, because of the evident difference between eating a yellow apple and eating a rosy-coloured apple. Likewise are the adornments of drink. Do you not see how Ka'b ibn Zuhayr extended in describing the adornments of the water mixed with the wine in his saying:

*Mixed with water of Dhi Shabam from a cistern, pure, in Abtah, which has become mixed*
*The winds clear its impurities, and the clouds' rain from the white heavy showers pours it abundantly upon it*

Filling the bellies is a metaphor for the great quantity they eat from it despite its disgust.

The attribution of eating and filling the bellies to them is a literal attribution, even though they are compelled to that eating and filling.

The fa' in His saying ﴿fa-mali'un﴾ is the fa' of consequence, and it carries the sense of immediate sequence, meaning their bellies will be filled without delay, due to the speed of gulping. This is a depiction of its repulsiveness, for a disgusting food, like medicine, when its consumer takes it, he swallows it quickly and takes large mouthfuls so that its taste does not settle on the organ of taste.

The thumma (then) in His saying ﴿Then indeed for them thereafter is a mixture of scalding water﴾ is for graded (rutbi) delay, because it conjoins a sentence, and there is no meaning of delay in the reporting except to convey that what follows the particle of delay is more important or more wondrous than what precedes it, such that the hearer was not awaiting it. It is higher in rank in the sense that it is an increase in punishment over what preceded it, so its effect is more severe. The word "over it" (alayha) has indicated this, meaning after it, that is, after their eating from it.

The shawb (شَوْب) is originally a verbal noun: shaba al-shay' bi-al-shay' when he mixed it with it, and it is applied to the thing mixed with, using the verbal noun for the object, like khalq for makhluq. Both meanings are possible here.

The pronoun in "over it" refers to the tree of zaqqum by way of its fruit.

The 'ala (على) is in the sense of ma'a (with), and it is valid that it is for elevation, because they drink the scalding water after eating, so it descends upon it into the intestines.

The ḥamim is the liquid pus flowing from a boil. It has been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am.

The discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire﴾ is the same as the discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed for them thereafter is a mixture of scalding water﴾.

Al-marji' (the place of return) means the place to which one who has departed from it returns after leaving it. It may also be used metaphorically for moving from a temporary state to an original state, by analogy with leaving a place and then coming back to it. An example is the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in his speech with Hunay, the client (of the protected pasture, al-hima), "If their livestock perishes, the two of them will return to palm trees and crops," meaning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. He only meant that they would move from benefiting from livestock to benefiting from palm trees and crops. In the same way, the word "return" (al-ruju') in the verse should be interpreted, because when the polytheists eat from the tree of al-Zaqqum and drink boiling water (al-hamim), they have not departed from the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim). Thus the intent is to draw attention to the fact that the punishment of eating from al-Zaqqum and drinking boiling water is an addition to the punishment of the Blazing Fire. Do you not see His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of the Blazing Fire﴾? So there is no departure from the Blazing Fire such that the return would be literal. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) upon his return from one of his military campaigns: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad," meaning the striving against the self (mujahadat al-nafs). He did not mean that when they were occupied with jihad they had abandoned the striving against their selves; rather, he meant that they were in an additional jihad and then moved on to the earlier jihad.

Then Abu Jahl said to his slave-girl: "Bring us zaqqum," and she brought him butter and dates, and he said: "Eat zaqqum!"

And from Ibn Sidah: "It has reached us that when there was revealed ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44], that is, in Surat al-Dukhan, Quraysh did not recognize it. End of quotation. The more fitting view is that this statement of theirs was made when they heard the verse of Surat al-Dukhan, where it came in indefinite form.

As for the second: it is the name of a known tree that is disliked. It was said: it is one of the most evil of trees, found in Tihamah and in the barren lands bordering the desert, foul-smelling, with small leaves, poisonous, with a milky sap; if it touches human skin, the skin swells and the person generally dies from it. He intends to refute those who said it is derived from tazaqqum, meaning swallowing with difficulty because of aversion to the thing.

When His saying about Hell was revealed, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30], Abu Jahl said to Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! Then Abu al-Ashadd al-Jumahi said: "I will suffice you for seventeen, so suffice me with two of you." He resumed with a second resumption describing it, in which He used the word ﴿indeed﴾ (innaha) with emphasis for awe. The sense of ﴿sprouts forth﴾ (takhruju) is "grows," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. God formed in the fire a tree of fire, and an approximation of this is what is pictured in fiery firework displays, with shapes and colours like palm trees and the like.

He made for it a ṭal' (طَلْع), that is, fruit, and the name ṭal' was applied to it figuratively, likening it to the spathe of the palm, because the name ṭal' is specific to palms. *And sharpened, blue, like the fangs of ghouls*

*Ungarded, she swears when I swear, like the shaytan of the hammat, the one with crests.*

When the food is disgusting, its foul appearance increases the aversion, just as when the desired food is pleasant to look at, approaching it is with eagerness, because of the evident difference between eating a yellow apple and eating a rosy-coloured apple. Likewise are the adornments of drink. Do you not see how Ka'b ibn Zuhayr extended in describing the adornments of the water mixed with the wine in his saying:

*Mixed with water of Dhi Shabam from a cistern, pure, in Abtah, which has become mixed*
*The winds clear its impurities, and the clouds' rain from the white heavy showers pours it abundantly upon it*

Filling the bellies is a metaphor for the great quantity they eat from it despite its disgust.

The attribution of eating and filling the bellies to them is a literal attribution, even though they are compelled to that eating and filling.

The fa' in His saying ﴿fa-mali'un﴾ is the fa' of consequence, and it carries the sense of immediate sequence, meaning their bellies will be filled without delay, due to the speed of gulping. This is a depiction of its repulsiveness, for a disgusting food, like medicine, when its consumer takes it, he swallows it quickly and takes large mouthfuls so that its taste does not settle on the organ of taste.

The thumma (then) in His saying ﴿Then indeed for them thereafter is a mixture of scalding water﴾ is for graded (rutbi) delay, because it conjoins a sentence, and there is no meaning of delay in the reporting except to convey that what follows the particle of delay is more important or more wondrous than what precedes it, such that the hearer was not awaiting it. It is higher in rank in the sense that it is an increase in punishment over what preceded it, so its effect is more severe. The word "over it" (alayha) has indicated this, meaning after it, that is, after their eating from it.

The pronoun in "over it" refers to the tree of zaqqum by way of its fruit.

The 'ala (على) is in the sense of ma'a (with), and it is valid that it is for elevation, because they drink the scalding water after eating, so it descends upon it into the intestines.

The ḥamim is the liquid pus flowing from a boil. It has been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am.

The discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire﴾ is the same as the discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed for them thereafter is a mixture of scalding water﴾.

Al-marji' (the place of return) means the place to which one who has departed from it returns after leaving it. It may also be used metaphorically for moving from a temporary state to an original state, by analogy with leaving a place and then coming back to it. The tree of zaqqum is mentioned here as something already known from before, because it appears defined by the genitive construction, being situated in a context of contrast between two conditions, good and evil. It is therefore fitting that the reference be to two well-known examples. What clarifies this is what al-Kalbi related: when that verse of Surat al-Waqi'ah was revealed, Ibn al-Za'bara said: "God has increased zaqqum in your houses, for the people of Yemen call dates and butter zaqqum." Then Abu Jahl said to his slave-girl: "Bring us zaqqum," and she brought him butter and dates, and he said: "Eat zaqqum!"

And from Ibn Sidah: "It has reached us that when there was revealed ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44], that is, in Surat al-Dukhan, Quraysh did not recognize it. Abu Jahl said: 'O slave-girl, bring us dates and butter, let us eat zaqqum (nazdaqimuhu),' and they began to eat and say: 'Is it with this that Muhammad threatens us regarding the Hereafter?'" End of quotation. The more fitting view is that this statement of theirs was made when they heard the verse of Surat al-Dukhan, where it came in indefinite form.

As for the second: it is the name of a known tree that is disliked. It was said: it is one of the most evil of trees, found in Tihamah and in the barren lands bordering the desert, foul-smelling, with small leaves, poisonous, with a milky sap; if it touches human skin, the skin swells and the person generally dies from it. This was stated by Qutrub and Abu Hanifah.

The Qur'an's detailed description of it here requires that it was not known to them, so it mentioned it in summary in Surat al-Waqi'ah. The Qur'an named it with this idafa as though it were derived from zuqmah, with a damma on the zay and sukun on the qaf, which is the name of the plague. Ibn Durayd said: zaqqum is not derived from tazaqqum, which is excessive eating to the point of disgust. He intends to refute those who said it is derived from tazaqqum, meaning swallowing with difficulty because of aversion to the thing.

Then it continued describing it by saying that God made it a trial for the wrongdoers, that is, a punishment, like the sense in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], that is, they punished them with the trench of fire.

Thus the sense of "We made it" is: We made its mention and its report (a trial), that is, when the verse of Surat al-Waqi'ah was revealed, we made its mention a stimulus to their trial through denial and mockery without understanding. This is like His saying ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels, and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. When His saying about Hell was revealed, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30], Abu Jahl said to Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! Ibn Abi Kabshah tells you that the guardians of the Fire are nineteen, and you are the multitude! Can not each ten of you overpower one man of them?" (that is, of the guardians of the Fire). Then Abu al-Ashadd al-Jumahi said: "I will suffice you for seventeen, so suffice me with two of you." So God revealed ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31] (meaning none of them is like one of mankind) ﴿and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

He resumed with a second resumption describing it, in which He used the word ﴿indeed﴾ (innaha) with emphasis for awe. The sense of ﴿sprouts forth﴾ (takhruju) is "grows," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. Among the wondrous power of God, the Exalted, is that He made a tree from fire, while it is necessarily of fire. God formed in the fire a tree of fire, and an approximation of this is what is pictured in fiery firework displays, with shapes and colours like palm trees and the like.

He made for it a ṭal' (طَلْع), that is, fruit, and the name ṭal' was applied to it figuratively, likening it to the spathe of the palm, because the name ṭal' is specific to palms. *And sharpened, blue, like the fangs of ghouls*

*Ungarded, she swears when I swear, like the shaytan of the hammat, the one with crests.*

*Mixed with water of Dhi Shabam from a cistern, pure, in Abtah, which has become mixed*
*The winds clear its impurities, and the clouds' rain from the white heavy showers pours it abundantly upon it*

The word "over it" (alayha) has indicated this, meaning after it, that is, after their eating from it.

The ḥamim is the liquid pus flowing from a boil. It has been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am.

The discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire﴾ is the same as the discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed for them thereafter is a mixture of scalding water﴾.

Al-marji' (the place of return) means the place to which one who has departed from it returns after leaving it. It may also be used metaphorically for moving from a temporary state to an original state, by analogy with leaving a place and then coming back to it. An example is the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in his speech with Hunay, the client (of the protected pasture, al-hima), "If their livestock perishes, the two of them will return to palm trees and crops," meaning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. He only meant that they would move from benefiting from livestock to benefiting from palm trees and crops. In the same way, the word "return" (al-ruju') in the verse should be interpreted, because when the polytheists eat from the tree of al-Zaqqum and drink boiling water (al-hamim), they have not departed from the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim). Thus the intent is to draw attention to the fact that the punishment of eating from al-Zaqqum and drinking boiling water is an addition to the punishment of the Blazing Fire. Do you not see His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of the Blazing Fire﴾? So there is no departure from the Blazing Fire such that the return would be literal. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) upon his return from one of his military campaigns: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad," meaning the striving against the self (mujahadat al-nafs). He did not mean that when they were occupied with jihad they had abandoned the striving against their selves; rather, he meant that they were in an additional jihad and then moved on to the earlier jihad.

He only meant that they would move from benefiting from livestock to benefiting from palm trees and crops. In the same way, the word "return" (al-ruju') in the verse should be interpreted, because when the polytheists eat from the tree of al-Zaqqum and drink boiling water (al-hamim), they have not departed from the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim). The demonstrative is used in the singular with regard to the thing mentioned, and it is marked with distance to magnify what is indicated, meaning the distance of rank and its loftiness, for a precious and noble thing is imagined as elevated, and elevation is accompanied by distance from the usual place, which is the low. On both interpretations, the sense of the counterpart of the interrogative (mu'adil al-istifham) also applies. The tree of zaqqum is mentioned here as something already known from before, because it appears defined by the genitive construction, being situated in a context of contrast between two conditions, good and evil. It is therefore fitting that the reference be to two well-known examples. What clarifies this is what al-Kalbi related: when that verse of Surat al-Waqi'ah was revealed, Ibn al-Za'bara said: "God has increased zaqqum in your houses, for the people of Yemen call dates and butter zaqqum." Then Abu Jahl said to his slave-girl: "Bring us zaqqum," and she brought him butter and dates, and he said: "Eat zaqqum!"

And from Ibn Sidah: "It has reached us that when there was revealed ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44], that is, in Surat al-Dukhan, Quraysh did not recognize it. Abu Jahl said: 'O slave-girl, bring us dates and butter, let us eat zaqqum (nazdaqimuhu),' and they began to eat and say: 'Is it with this that Muhammad threatens us regarding the Hereafter?'" End of quotation. The more fitting view is that this statement of theirs was made when they heard the verse of Surat al-Dukhan, where it came in indefinite form.

As for the second: it is the name of a known tree that is disliked. It was said: it is one of the most evil of trees, found in Tihamah and in the barren lands bordering the desert, foul-smelling, with small leaves, poisonous, with a milky sap; if it touches human skin, the skin swells and the person generally dies from it. This was stated by Qutrub and Abu Hanifah.

The Qur'an named it with this idafa as though it were derived from zuqmah, with a damma on the zay and sukun on the qaf, which is the name of the plague. Ibn Durayd said: zaqqum is not derived from tazaqqum, which is excessive eating to the point of disgust. He intends to refute those who said it is derived from tazaqqum, meaning swallowing with difficulty because of aversion to the thing.

Then it continued describing it by saying that God made it a trial for the wrongdoers, that is, a punishment, like the sense in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], that is, they punished them with the trench of fire.

Thus the sense of "We made it" is: We made its mention and its report (a trial), that is, when the verse of Surat al-Waqi'ah was revealed, we made its mention a stimulus to their trial through denial and mockery without understanding. This is like His saying ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels, and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. When His saying about Hell was revealed, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30], Abu Jahl said to Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! Then Abu al-Ashadd al-Jumahi said: "I will suffice you for seventeen, so suffice me with two of you." So God revealed ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31] (meaning none of them is like one of mankind) ﴿and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

He resumed with a second resumption describing it, in which He used the word ﴿indeed﴾ (innaha) with emphasis for awe. The heads of these devils are unknown to them, so the comparison refers them to what their imagination pictures. *And sharpened, blue, like the fangs of ghouls*

*Mixed with water of Dhi Shabam from a cistern, pure, in Abtah, which has become mixed*
*The winds clear its impurities, and the clouds' rain from the white heavy showers pours it abundantly upon it*

Filling the bellies is a metaphor for the great quantity they eat from it despite its disgust.

The attribution of eating and filling the bellies to them is a literal attribution, even though they are compelled to that eating and filling.

The fa' in His saying ﴿fa-mali'un﴾ is the fa' of consequence, and it carries the sense of immediate sequence, meaning their bellies will be filled without delay, due to the speed of gulping. This is a depiction of its repulsiveness, for a disgusting food, like medicine, when its consumer takes it, he swallows it quickly and takes large mouthfuls so that its taste does not settle on the organ of taste.

It is higher in rank in the sense that it is an increase in punishment over what preceded it, so its effect is more severe. The word "over it" (alayha) has indicated this, meaning after it, that is, after their eating from it.

The pronoun in "over it" refers to the tree of zaqqum by way of its fruit.

The 'ala (على) is in the sense of ma'a (with), and it is valid that it is for elevation, because they drink the scalding water after eating, so it descends upon it into the intestines.

The ḥamim is the liquid pus flowing from a boil. It has been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am.

The discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire﴾ is the same as the discussion of the conjunction in ﴿Then indeed for them thereafter is a mixture of scalding water﴾.
