The particle "inna" conveys the causal explanation for God's recompensing Noah with the favors He enumerated, because he was a doer of good, meaning one who is characterized by goodness, which is pure faith, as explained in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Goodness (ihsan) is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." And what clearer proof of his goodness is there than his perseverance in calling to monotheism and piety, and the harm he endured from his people throughout the long period of his calling.

The meaning is: We indeed recompense those who do good in the same way. In this there is a commendation of Noah (peace be upon him): his reward was the model and the exemplar for the reward of the doers of good, according to the levels of their goodness and the varying degrees of their closeness to Noah's goodness and his strength in conveying the call. He was the first to be harmed for God's sake, so he established the pattern of reward for whoever is harmed for God's sake, and his own reward was of this same form. Thus it may be that he has a share (kifl) in every reward that anyone receives for patience when harmed for God's sake. Accordingly, the attribute of goodness (ihsan) is affirmed for Noah, and this is the seventh blessing. And it is affirmed for him that he is an exemplar for the doers of good in their reward for their goodness, and this is the eighth blessing.

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our servants, the believers﴾ is a causal justification for his deserving the recompense described by the words ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾. Therefore the effect of this cause differs from the effect of the preceding cause.

The description ﴿Indeed he is among Our servants﴾ conveys that he is among those who merited this description. You have learned more than once that the word "servant" ('abd), when it is attributed to the pronoun of Majesty, implies nearness and elevation of rank. He restricted the description of the servants to "the believers" to honour the matter of faith, so that those who believe may increase in faith and the polytheists may abandon polytheism. This is the ninth blessing.

Along with it, "among Our servants" is inserted to honour him through that attribution, in the same manner as what has preceded a little earlier in His words, ﴿except the sincere servants of God; for those there is a known provision﴾ [al-Saffat: 40]. This is the tenth blessing, and in it is an alert to the great worth of faith.

In this story there is a lesson for the polytheists through what befell the people of Noah, a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), and making Noah a model for him. It also contains an intimation that God will support him as He supported Noah against his people and will save him from their harm, and a commendation of the believers.

The "then" (thumma) in His words ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ indicates sequence and a delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because some of what was mentioned before it in the discourse actually occurred after the content of its clause in reality, as is evident. The meaning of the delay in rank here is that the drowning of those who denied him, along with his salvation and the salvation of his family, is greater in rank in supporting him, in showing his high standing with God the Exalted, and in showing the great power and gentleness of God the Exalted.

The meaning of "the others" (al-akharin) is those other than him and his family, that is, the rest of his people. In referring to them as "the others" there is a kind of contempt. And among what is in the hadith is that a man came to him and said, "Indeed the other (al-akhar) has committed fornication," meaning himself, according to the narration of al-akhar with the hamza extended, which is one of two narrations in the hadith.

The mention of Noah and his story has preceded at His words ﴿Indeed God chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 33] in Al 'Imran, and in al-A'raf, and in Surat Hud, and the mention of his ark in the beginning of Surat al-'Ankabut.

* * *

"﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾ ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ ﴿when he said to his father and his people, 'What is it that you worship?'﴾ ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾ ﴿Then what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾" This transitions to narrating the stance of Abraham (peace be upon him) toward his people in calling them to monotheism, what he encountered from them, and how God supported him and saved him from them. This transition came to it by describing him as among the partisans of Noah, so that with this single expression it conveys the confirmation of praise for Noah and the beginning of praise for Abraham, and the perpetuation of a distinction for Noah in that Abraham, the great messenger, was among his partisans, and that is enough praise.

Likewise, he gathered the virtues of Abraham into the phrase of his being among the partisans of Noah, which implies his sharing with him in his attributes, as will come. This is like His words ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ [al-Isra': 3].

The word "shi'ah" is a name for one who supports a man and his followers and is partisan toward him, so the word shi'ah applies to the singular and the plural. It may be pluralized as shi' and ashya' when groups are intended, each group being a shi'ah of someone. This has been mentioned previously at His words ﴿And We had certainly sent before you among the sects of the former peoples﴾ [al-Hijr: 10] in Surat al-Hijr, and at His words ﴿and He made its people into sects﴾ [al-Qasas: 4] in Surat al-Qasas.

Abraham was of the descendants of Noah, and his religion agreed with the religion of Noah in its foundation, which is the rejection of polytheism.

Abraham was made among the partisans of Noah because messengers came upon the religion of Noah before Abraham, among them Hud and Salih, for they were before Abraham, since the Qur'an mentioned them more than once directly after mentioning Noah and before mentioning Lot, the contemporary of Abraham. And [this is shown] by Hud's saying to his people, "﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69]," and by Salih's saying to his people, "﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]," and by Shu'ayb's saying to his people, "﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to earn [a punishment] like what struck the people of Noah or the people of Hud or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [Hud: 89]." Thus he made the people of Lot nearer in time to his people than the people of Hud and the people of Salih. Lot was a contemporary of Abraham, so all of these were partisans of Noah, and Abraham was among that partisanship. This is the eleventh blessing.

The emphasis of the statement with "indeed" (inna) and the lam of initiation is a response to the polytheists, because they claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham. This is like His words ﴿And he was not among the polytheists﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135].

"Idh" (when) is an adverb of past time, and it is connected to the implied predicate of the prepositional phrase that occurs as the predicate of "inna" in His words ﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾, or it is connected to the word shi'ah because of what it contains of the meaning of supporting and following, meaning: he was among his partisans at the time he came to his Lord with a sound heart, just as Noah came. Therefore the time of his being among his partisans is that time, that is, because Noah came to his Lord with a sound heart. In "idh" there is the meaning of causation for his being among his partisans, for the meaning of causation frequently arises with "idh," as in His words ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 39]. This is a blessing upon Noah, and it is the twelfth.

The "bi" in "﴿with a sound heart﴾" is for accompaniment, meaning that a heart whose attribute is soundness came with him, so it is interpreted to mean: when he came to his Lord with soundness of heart. The heart was mentioned first and then described as "sound" because in mentioning the heart there is the bringing to mind of the reality of that pure heart, and for this reason the indefinite "a heart" was preferred over definiteness.

"Salim" (sound) is a derived attribute (sifah mushabbahah) from soundness (salamah), which is freedom from defects and diseases. Since the heart was mentioned, it became clear that its soundness is its freedom from what hearts are afflicted with of their maladies, so it is not permissible that it means bodily diseases, because they did not mean by "heart" anything other than the seat of perception and character. Therefore it is determined that the intended meaning is the possessor of the heart in relation to himself, with such things as the following of desire, self-admiration and conceit, and in relation to people, with such things as arrogance, malice, envy, showing off, and contempt.

He used the word "coming" for his dealing with it in himself by what pleases his Lord, in the manner of a figurative image of one who comes to someone bringing to him what he requested, such as weapons, gifts, or kindnesses. God had commanded him to purify his soul and he complied, so his condition resembled that of one who was called and then came. This is like His words ﴿Respond to the caller of God﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31].

His words ﴿with a sound heart﴾ comprise comprehensive elements of the perfection of the soul, and these are the source of praiseworthy deeds. In the hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."

It has been related about Abraham that he said, ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. So the pillar of the religion of Abraham was that which branches from His words ﴿with a sound heart﴾, and that is the sum of noble character. For this reason He described Abraham with His words, ﴿Indeed Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, and penitent﴾ [Hud: 75], so he was free from every blameworthy trait and every false belief.

[Page 138]

Then, noble character is capable of increase, so Abraham's share of it was a complete share, perhaps more complete than Noah's share, based on the view that Abraham is the best of the messengers after Muhammad (ﷺ). God reserved the ultimate perfection of it for His messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason he said, "I was only sent to perfect noble character." For the same reason the religion of Abraham was described as al-hanifiyyah (the upright monotheistic faith), and Islam was described as that plus more, in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was sent with the easy upright faith (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah)."

The linking of his being among the partisans of Noah with this time, which is added to that state, is a kinayah (metonymy) for describing Noah with soundness of heart. Also, from His words ﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾ there results the affirmation of attributes similar to those of Noah for Abraham, and from His words ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ there results the affirmation of an attribute similar to Abraham's attribute for Noah, by way of kinayah in both affirmations. However, that was affirmed for Abraham explicitly, while it is affirmed for Noah by necessary implication, so it is weaker in him than in Abraham.

"﴿When he said to his father﴾" is a substitute for "﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾" as a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition), for his saying this arose from his heart being filled with monotheism and with zeal for God against the polytheists, so it was like something that his sound heart encompassed, and so it issued from him.

"﴿What is it that you worship?﴾" is a rhetorical interrogative of denial against their worshipping what they worship. For this reason he followed it with another rhetorical interrogative of denial, which is "﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾". What required the use of the demonstrative after "ma" (what), which is interrogative, is that it takes on the sense of the relative pronoun referred to, and so it required that what they worship be present before Abraham. Thus the interrogation was turned by this to a meaning other than its literal one, which is the meaning of denial. This differs from His words ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 70] in Surat al-Shu'ara', for that is an interrogation about their objects of worship. For this reason they answered it, ﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 71]. He intended by the interrogation there to prepare the way for debate, so he framed it in the form of an interrogation in order to hear their answer and then move on to refuting it, as is evident from the ordering of his argument there. So that is a narration of Abraham's words at the beginning of his call to his people, whereas what is here is a narration of some of his statements when repeating and reinforcing the call.

The sentence ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the sentence "What is it that you worship?" by which he clarified the target of the denial in his words "What is it that you worship?" and elucidated it, meaning: how is it that you desire gods that are a falsehood?

The desiring of a thing is seeking it and resolving to attain it, and the proper use of this verb is that it should be transitive to meanings. Ibn al-Dumayna said:

"You desire my killing, and you have indeed triumphed in that."

When it is transitive to essences, it is in the sense of something connected to those essences, like the saying of 'Amr ibn Shas al-Asadi:

"She desired 'Irar with humiliation, and whoever desires 'Irar with humiliation, by my life, has done wrong."

Therefore the transitivity of the verb "you desire" to "gods" is in the sense of: you desire them by worship or by deifying them, so the meaning of "gods" was a sign of the aspect of desiring them.

"Gods" is in the accusative as the object, and he placed the object before the verb for emphasis on it, and because in it there is an indication of the direction in which the meaning of the verb goes beyond to the object.

"Falsehood" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of "you desire," meaning: deceiving. "Falsehood" means lying. It is also permissible that it be a state from "gods," meaning: gods that are lied about, that is, the claim of their divinity is a lie.

Describing with the verbal noun is valid whether considering the meaning of the agent or the meaning of the patient.

The circumstantial state was placed before its referent for the sake of emphasis, to hasten the expression of their lying and their error.

His words "other than God" mean: in contrast to God and apart from Him. This is valid whether one considers his people as idol-worshippers who did not acknowledge any god other than their idols, or considers them polytheists alongside God who worshipped other gods, like the polytheists of the Arabs, because some remnants of the hanifiyyah remained among the Arabs, so they did not forget describing God with divinity. The people of Abraham, who were the Chaldeans, worshipped the stars, similar to what the Greeks and the Copts were upon.

The commentary continues the argument from the rhetorical question of denial, with another question: ﴿So what is your assumption about the Lord of the worlds?﴾ This is a question used to express denunciation and to make them stop and recognise their error, and by "assumption" (zann) is meant the mistaken belief.

It is called zann (assumption) because it does not correspond to reality, and it was not called 'ilm (knowledge) because 'ilm is applied only to belief that corresponds to reality. For this reason they defined it as: "a quality that produces a discrimination that does not admit the opposite," and the possibility of the opposite is not negated except when the belief agrees with reality.

The application of zann to mistaken judgement and compound ignorance is frequent, as in His saying ﴿They follow nothing but assumption, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116] in Surat al-An'am, and His saying ﴿Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28].

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech."

The meaning is: your belief concerning the Lord of the worlds is a reprehensible ignorance.

When the verb zann is followed by the preposition bi- (ba'), it generally conveys an assumption that is not truthful, as He said: ﴿And you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10], and He said: ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you﴾ [Fussilat: 23]. From this comes the use of zanin (suspected one) for the accused, for its origin is "zanin bihi" (suspected of it), so the bi- was dropped and the adjective was connected directly. That is because when it is followed by bi-, the object is most often omitted, and the bi- is for metaphorical attachment, i.e., he assumed an assumption attached to Allah, meaning he claimed its connection to Allah; and this is only suitable for what is not fitting for Allah.

The indication of this was already mentioned at His saying ﴿And you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10] in Surat al-Ahzab.

The meaning is: "What is your evil assumption about Allah?" Since zann is one of the actions of the heart, its transitivity to the name of the essence without following the name with a qualifier is specific to the estimation of a suitable qualifier. The complement has been omitted here for the purpose of broadening the scope of the omitted element, by estimating it in every suitable possibility, to multiply the meanings. So it is permissible to take as the omitted element the attributes of the essence of the Lord of the worlds. It is also permissible to take from it the quiddity and reality. The consideration of the attribute is in two ways:

The first: the meaning derived from the word "Rabb" (Lord), which is lordship (ruboobiyyah), which is bringing a thing to its perfection gradually and gently, for the created being needs sustenance and provision, and that requires that the one who provides be thanked, so one does not turn away from worshipping his Lord. The estimate then is: "What is your assumption that He has partners, when He alone deserves gratitude, expressed in worship, because it is He who sustained you with His bounty?"

The second: that the meaning of ownership (malikiyyah) be considered, which is one of the two meanings of Rabb, and it implies the meaning of dominion and power over the owned. The estimate then is: "What is your assumption of what He will do to you in punishment for your disbelief, He being your Owner and the Owner of the worlds?"

As for the permissibility of considering the reality and quiddity of the Lord of the worlds, the estimate in it is: "What is your assumption regarding the quiddity of lordship? For you are ignorant of the attributes it requires, and at the forefront of them is oneness (wahdaniyyah)."

[p. 130]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 37, verses 75–87 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Noah had certainly called Us, and We are the best to respond.﴾ ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great calamity.﴾ ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors.﴾ ﴿And We left for him a good mention among the later generations.﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds.﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others.﴾

He followed the reminder and the consolation from the side of considering the traces of what befell the nations to whom the messengers were sent, and what He reported of their end in the Hereafter, with a reminder and consolation from the side of the report about the messengers whom their peoples denied and harmed, and how God gave victory to them, so that His Messenger (ﷺ) would be further steadied and the polytheists would be silenced with a decisive refutation.

In this surah He mentioned the stories of the messengers with their peoples, because in each story there is a distinctive feature that resembles the situation of the Messenger (ﷺ) with his people and his most perfect condition in his call. Thus in all the stories there is a lesson, an example, and a warning, as will be detailed when each story comes. What unites them all is the opposition to polytheism (shirk) and the opposition to its adherents.

[p. 131]

These six messengers were chosen: Noah is the first model, and Abraham is the messenger of the upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyya), which is the seed of the good tree, the tree of Islam. Moses is chosen because his law resembles the Islamic law in its detail and in its combining of religion and authority. These three messengers are the roots. Then He mentioned three messengers who branched off from them, and three who followed the same religion as the messengers before them. As for Lot, he follows the religion of Abraham; as for Elijah (Ilyas) and Jonah (Yunus), they follow the religion of Moses.

He began with the story of Noah with his people, for he was the first messenger God sent to the people, and he is the first model and the most excellent exemplar.

The beginning of the story with the mention of Noah's calling upon his Lord is an admonition to the polytheists, so that they would beware of the Messenger's (ﷺ) supplication to his Lord for victory against them, just as Noah supplicated against his people. This calling is what is related in His saying ﴿He said: My Lord, help me, for they have denied me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 26] in the Surah of al-Mu'minun, and in His saying ﴿Noah said: My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him only in loss﴾ [Nuh: 21] and the verses of the Surah of Nuh.

The fa' (ف) in His saying ﴿so how excellent are the responders﴾ is a consequence of "nadana" (called), meaning: He called Us, so We responded to him. The consequent was omitted because the phrase ﴿فَلَنِعْمَ المُجِيبُونَ﴾ indicates it, since it implicitly contains the meaning "so We responded to him," as the response of one of whom it is said: "How excellent is the Responder" (ni'ma al-mujib).

The object of praise is omitted, meaning: ﴿فَلَنِعْمَ المُجِيبُونَ﴾ "we are indeed the excellent responders." The first-person plural pronoun of association is used for magnification, as is well known.

The emphasis of the statement and the emphasis of what is derived from it by the oath particle (lam al-qasam) serves to affirm both matters, as a warning to the polytheists, since they were treated as one who denies that Noah called upon God and was answered.

Al-tanjiya (rescue) is causing someone to be saved (najin). Al-najat (salvation) is deliverance from a harm that has befallen. It is used here for safety from that harm before it occurs, because when his safety was attained at the time the harm encompassed his people, his safety from it, even though he was near it, was treated as deliverance from it after falling into it, by considering the approach of an act's occurrence as its occurrence. This is a frequent application of the word najat, such that it is correct to say: salvation is deliverance from a harm that has befallen or is expected.

By "his family" is meant his household, except those among them against whom the word had been decreed, and likewise the believers among his people. God said: ﴿We said: Load into it two of every kind, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth, and those who believe — and none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud: 40]. So the restriction to "his family" here is because of the small number of those who believed in him from outside them; or "family" is meant as the family of his religion, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 68].

His saying ﴿And We saved him and his family﴾ implies that the answer to Noah's supplication was by destroying his people.

Al-karb is intense grief and distress. Describing it as ﴿al-'azim﴾ (the great) indicates that it is great in its kind, so it is distress upon distress. What is meant by it is the Flood, which is a great calamity for those who fell into it. So Noah's rescue from it is his safety from falling into it, as you know, because it is a terror in appearance and a fear in its outcome, and falling into it is certain destruction. The fear does not cease to be with him until the water overwhelms him, and then he continues to suffer pains from shortness of breath, the trembling of cold, fear, and the certainty of destruction, until he drowns in the water.

God's rescuing him is a favor upon him, the rescuing of his family is another favor, the destruction of his oppressors is a greater favor, and making the population of the earth come from his descendants is a lasting favor, because they supplicate for him and his good deeds are mentioned among them, and God shows mercy to him on that account. Other favors will come that reach twelve.

The separating pronoun in His saying ﴿they are the survivors﴾ serves restriction, meaning: no one among mankind remained except those whom God saved with Noah in the Ark from his descendants, and then whoever descended from them. Thus none of the sons of Adam remained except the descendants of Noah, so all the nations are descended from the sons of Noah's three sons.

The apparent meaning of this is that those who believed with Noah, other than his sons, had no offspring. Ibn 'Abbas said: When Noah came out of the Ark, all who were with him died, men and women, except his son and his wives. By this, the contradiction between this verse and His saying in Surah Hud ﴿We said: Load into it two of every kind, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth, and those who believe — and none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud: 40] is resolved. This applies on the basis that the Flood covered the whole earth and eradicated all mankind except those whom Noah carried in the Ark, and its story has been related in Surah Hud.

The generality of the Flood is what the apparent meanings of the Book and the Sunnah require. As for those who said that the Flood did not cover the whole earth, they only denied it because of the brevity of the period in which the books of the Israelites delimit it, and it is not necessary to rely on those books in determining the age of the earth and its events. That is not among the decisive matters, and the restriction would be relative, meaning: no one remained from his people to whom he was sent. It may also be said: We grant that the Flood did not cover the entire earth, but it covered mankind, because they were confined to the lands that the Flood struck. Even if the evidence for the generality of the Flood is not definitive, the arguments of those who denied it are not sound, so the apparent meanings of the reports are not abandoned on their account.

God added to the list of Noah's honors, peace be upon him, His saying ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾, and this is a fifth favor.

Al-tark (leaving) in its real sense is leaving something behind and abandoning it. Here it is intended to mean continuance, in the sense of figurative metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal) or metaphor (al-isti'ara), because the nature of blessings in this world is that they are a passing enjoyment, after which they cease, whether they last long or short. So their cessation is as if it were a reclaiming by the Giver, as is stated in the hadith: "To God belongs what He took, and to Him belongs what He gave." So God honored Noah by letting His blessings upon him remain among nations after him.

The apparent meaning of "al-akhirin" (the later ones) is that it remains among all nations until the end of the world. The indication of the metaphor is the connection of "'alayhi" (upon him) with "taraknā" (We left), because it suits continuance; one says: "abqā 'alā kadhā," meaning he preserved it so that it would remain and not vanish. On this reading, "taraknā" has an object. Some of them assumed for it an object indicated by the context, meaning: We left a praise upon him. So this continuance may be understood as making him live a thousand years, which is the greatest extension of life that can be given to a living being beyond what is customary.

It may also mean the continuance of the good remembrance of him among nations, as Abraham said ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84]. Noah was thus remembered with praiseworthy qualities, so that it was said: No nation of the nations of the earth is ignorant of Noah, his virtue, and his glorification, even if the names by which they call him differ according to the differences of their languages. In the Book of Genesis, chapter nine, it is said: "Noah was a righteous man, perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God."

His mention appeared before Islam in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"You found trust had not betrayed it; thus was Noah, who did not betray."

His mention to the Children of Israel in the context of emulating him is in His saying ﴿Offspring of those whom We carried with Noah; indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra': 3].

[p. 133]

Ibn Khaldun mentioned that some claim Noah is Afridun, king of the land of Persia, and others claim Noah is Ushahnak, king of the Persians who came after Kayumarth by two hundred years. This agrees with the claim that Noah came after Adam by two hundred years, Adam being Kayumarth, according to the books of the Israelites. However, it is said that Kayumarth is Adam, as already mentioned in Surah al-Baqara.

The complement of "'alayhi" in His saying ﴿And We left upon him﴾ — none of the commentators, as far as I have seen, has hovered around it. The correct view is that "'alayhi" is connected to the verb "taraknā" by implying in this verb the meaning of "an'amnā" (We bestowed favor). Thus the apparent construction would require this verb to be followed by "li" (for), but since it was implicitly given the meaning of "an'amnā," its root conveyed the meaning of preserving for him, that is, giving him some of the stored-up virtues, which is like leaving someone a precious possession for one whom he leaves it to and who succeeds him in it. By attaching the preposition "'alā" (upon) to it, it conveys that this leaving is of the kind of bestowal and favor. This is the nature of implicit meaning (al-tadmin): that the implied verb conveys the meaning of two words, and it is one of the most elegant forms of concision (al-ijaz).

Then, since the object of "taraknā" is omitted, and the verb "an'amnā," which was implied in "taraknā," requires a complement denoting the object, that also is omitted together with its governing element. The original was: "and We left for him a praise, and bestowed favor upon him." So in His saying "taraknā 'alayhi" five words are omitted, which is a wondrous concision.

For this reason, most of the earlier commentators supplied "taraknā" with "a good praise upon him."

The sentence ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ is a performative statement (insha') of God's praise of Noah and a greeting to him, and its implied meaning is the consequence of a greeting, which is approval and drawing near. This is a sixth favor. The tanwin of "salam" is for magnification, and for this reason the beginning with an indefinite noun is common, since it is like a described noun.

By "the worlds" is meant the nations and the generations. It is a metonymy (kinaya) for the perpetuity of peace upon him, like His saying ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 15] concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, and His saying ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], ﴿Peace be upon Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat: 109].

"Among the worlds" (fi al-'alamin) is a circumstantial phrase (hal), so it is a fixed adverbial of place (zarf mustaqirr), or it is a second predicate (khabar thani) of "salam."

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari held that His saying ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ is in the position of the object of "taraknā," meaning: We left upon him this statement, namely ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾, which is among the speech whose quotation is intended, as you say: "I read [the surah]: 'A surah We sent down and made obligatory' [al-Nur: 1]", meaning: We made people greet him throughout all the generations, so they mention him only by saying "peace be upon him." They said the same about its parallels in these consecutive verses.

The description of Noah's peace in this surah as being "among the worlds" is added, unlike the peace upon others in the story of Abraham, Moses, Aaron, and Elijah, to indicate that the praise of Noah extended through all the nations, because they all trace their lineage to him and mention him with honest remembrance, as we have stated just before.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes of God's honoring of Noah. The particle "inna" conveys the causal explanation for God's recompensing Noah with the favors He enumerated, because he was a doer of good, meaning one who is characterized by goodness, which is pure faith, as explained in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Goodness (ihsan) is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." And what clearer proof of his goodness is there than his perseverance in calling to monotheism and piety, and the harm he endured from his people throughout the long period of his calling.

The meaning is: We indeed recompense those who do good in the same way. In this there is a commendation of Noah (peace be upon him): his reward was the model and the exemplar for the reward of the doers of good, according to the levels of their goodness and the varying degrees of their closeness to Noah's goodness and his strength in conveying the call. He was the first to be harmed for God's sake, so he established the pattern of reward for whoever is harmed for God's sake, and his own reward was of this same form. Thus it may be that he has a share (kifl) in every reward that anyone receives for patience when harmed for God's sake. Accordingly, the attribute of goodness (ihsan) is affirmed for Noah, and this is the seventh blessing. And it is affirmed for him that he is an exemplar for the doers of good in their reward for their goodness, and this is the eighth blessing.

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our servants, the believers﴾ is a causal justification for his deserving the recompense described by the words ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾. Therefore the effect of this cause differs from the effect of the preceding cause.

The description ﴿Indeed he is among Our servants﴾ conveys that he is among those who merited this description. You have learned more than once that the word "servant" ('abd), when it is attributed to the pronoun of Majesty, implies nearness and elevation of rank. He restricted the description of the servants to "the believers" to honour the matter of faith, so that those who believe may increase in faith and the polytheists may abandon polytheism. This is the ninth blessing.

Along with it, "among Our servants" is inserted to honour him through that attribution, in the same manner as what has preceded a little earlier in His words, ﴿except the sincere servants of God; for those there is a known provision﴾ [al-Saffat: 40]. This is the tenth blessing, and in it is an alert to the great worth of faith.

In this story there is a lesson for the polytheists through what befell the people of Noah, a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), and making Noah a model for him. It also contains an intimation that God will support him as He supported Noah against his people and will save him from their harm, and a commendation of the believers.

The "then" (thumma) in His words ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ indicates sequence and a delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because some of what was mentioned before it in the discourse actually occurred after the content of its clause in reality, as is evident. The meaning of the delay in rank here is that the drowning of those who denied him, along with his salvation and the salvation of his family, is greater in rank in supporting him, in showing his high standing with God the Exalted, and in showing the great power and gentleness of God the Exalted.

The meaning of "the others" (al-akharin) is those other than him and his family, that is, the rest of his people. In referring to them as "the others" there is a kind of contempt. And among what is in the hadith is that a man came to him and said, "Indeed the other (al-akhar) has committed fornication," meaning himself, according to the narration of al-akhar with the hamza extended, which is one of two narrations in the hadith.

The mention of Noah and his story has preceded at His words ﴿Indeed God chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 33] in Al 'Imran, and in al-A'raf, and in Surat Hud, and the mention of his ark in the beginning of Surat al-'Ankabut.

* * *

"﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾ ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ ﴿when he said to his father and his people, 'What is it that you worship?'﴾ ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾ ﴿Then what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾" This transitions to narrating the stance of Abraham (peace be upon him) toward his people in calling them to monotheism, what he encountered from them, and how God supported him and saved him from them. This transition came to it by describing him as among the partisans of Noah, so that with this single expression it conveys the confirmation of praise for Noah and the beginning of praise for Abraham, and the perpetuation of a distinction for Noah in that Abraham, the great messenger, was among his partisans, and that is enough praise.

Likewise, he gathered the virtues of Abraham into the phrase of his being among the partisans of Noah, which implies his sharing with him in his attributes, as will come. This is like His words ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ [al-Isra': 3].

The word "shi'ah" is a name for one who supports a man and his followers and is partisan toward him, so the word shi'ah applies to the singular and the plural. It may be pluralized as shi' and ashya' when groups are intended, each group being a shi'ah of someone. This has been mentioned previously at His words ﴿And We had certainly sent before you among the sects of the former peoples﴾ [al-Hijr: 10] in Surat al-Hijr, and at His words ﴿and He made its people into sects﴾ [al-Qasas: 4] in Surat al-Qasas.

Abraham was of the descendants of Noah, and his religion agreed with the religion of Noah in its foundation, which is the rejection of polytheism.

Abraham was made among the partisans of Noah because messengers came upon the religion of Noah before Abraham, among them Hud and Salih, for they were before Abraham, since the Qur'an mentioned them more than once directly after mentioning Noah and before mentioning Lot, the contemporary of Abraham. And [this is shown] by Hud's saying to his people, "﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69]," and by Salih's saying to his people, "﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]," and by Shu'ayb's saying to his people, "﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to earn [a punishment] like what struck the people of Noah or the people of Hud or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [Hud: 89]." Thus he made the people of Lot nearer in time to his people than the people of Hud and the people of Salih. Lot was a contemporary of Abraham, so all of these were partisans of Noah, and Abraham was among that partisanship. This is the eleventh blessing.

The emphasis of the statement with "indeed" (inna) and the lam of initiation is a response to the polytheists, because they claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham. This is like His words ﴿And he was not among the polytheists﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135].

"Idh" (when) is an adverb of past time, and it is connected to the implied predicate of the prepositional phrase that occurs as the predicate of "inna" in His words ﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾, or it is connected to the word shi'ah because of what it contains of the meaning of supporting and following, meaning: he was among his partisans at the time he came to his Lord with a sound heart, just as Noah came. Therefore the time of his being among his partisans is that time, that is, because Noah came to his Lord with a sound heart. In "idh" there is the meaning of causation for his being among his partisans, for the meaning of causation frequently arises with "idh," as in His words ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 39]. This is a blessing upon Noah, and it is the twelfth.

The "bi" in "﴿with a sound heart﴾" is for accompaniment, meaning that a heart whose attribute is soundness came with him, so it is interpreted to mean: when he came to his Lord with soundness of heart. The heart was mentioned first and then described as "sound" because in mentioning the heart there is the bringing to mind of the reality of that pure heart, and for this reason the indefinite "a heart" was preferred over definiteness.

"Salim" (sound) is a derived attribute (sifah mushabbahah) from soundness (salamah), which is freedom from defects and diseases. Since the heart was mentioned, it became clear that its soundness is its freedom from what hearts are afflicted with of their maladies, so it is not permissible that it means bodily diseases, because they did not mean by "heart" anything other than the seat of perception and character. Therefore it is determined that the intended meaning is the possessor of the heart in relation to himself, with such things as the following of desire, self-admiration and conceit, and in relation to people, with such things as arrogance, malice, envy, showing off, and contempt.

He used the word "coming" for his dealing with it in himself by what pleases his Lord, in the manner of a figurative image of one who comes to someone bringing to him what he requested, such as weapons, gifts, or kindnesses. God had commanded him to purify his soul and he complied, so his condition resembled that of one who was called and then came. This is like His words ﴿Respond to the caller of God﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31].

His words ﴿with a sound heart﴾ comprise comprehensive elements of the perfection of the soul, and these are the source of praiseworthy deeds. In the hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."

It has been related about Abraham that he said, ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. So the pillar of the religion of Abraham was that which branches from His words ﴿with a sound heart﴾, and that is the sum of noble character. For this reason He described Abraham with His words, ﴿Indeed Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, and penitent﴾ [Hud: 75], so he was free from every blameworthy trait and every false belief.

[Page 138]

Then, noble character is capable of increase, so Abraham's share of it was a complete share, perhaps more complete than Noah's share, based on the view that Abraham is the best of the messengers after Muhammad (ﷺ). God reserved the ultimate perfection of it for His messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason he said, "I was only sent to perfect noble character." For the same reason the religion of Abraham was described as al-hanifiyyah (the upright monotheistic faith), and Islam was described as that plus more, in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was sent with the easy upright faith (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah)."

The linking of his being among the partisans of Noah with this time, which is added to that state, is a kinayah (metonymy) for describing Noah with soundness of heart. Also, from His words ﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾ there results the affirmation of attributes similar to those of Noah for Abraham, and from His words ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ there results the affirmation of an attribute similar to Abraham's attribute for Noah, by way of kinayah in both affirmations. However, that was affirmed for Abraham explicitly, while it is affirmed for Noah by necessary implication, so it is weaker in him than in Abraham.

"﴿When he said to his father﴾" is a substitute for "﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾" as a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition), for his saying this arose from his heart being filled with monotheism and with zeal for God against the polytheists, so it was like something that his sound heart encompassed, and so it issued from him.

"﴿What is it that you worship?﴾" is a rhetorical interrogative of denial against their worshipping what they worship. For this reason he followed it with another rhetorical interrogative of denial, which is "﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾". What required the use of the demonstrative after "ma" (what), which is interrogative, is that it takes on the sense of the relative pronoun referred to, and so it required that what they worship be present before Abraham. Thus the interrogation was turned by this to a meaning other than its literal one, which is the meaning of denial. This differs from His words ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 70] in Surat al-Shu'ara', for that is an interrogation about their objects of worship. For this reason they answered it, ﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 71]. He intended by the interrogation there to prepare the way for debate, so he framed it in the form of an interrogation in order to hear their answer and then move on to refuting it, as is evident from the ordering of his argument there. So that is a narration of Abraham's words at the beginning of his call to his people, whereas what is here is a narration of some of his statements when repeating and reinforcing the call.

The sentence ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the sentence "What is it that you worship?" by which he clarified the target of the denial in his words "What is it that you worship?" and elucidated it, meaning: how is it that you desire gods that are a falsehood?

The desiring of a thing is seeking it and resolving to attain it, and the proper use of this verb is that it should be transitive to meanings. Ibn al-Dumayna said:

"You desire my killing, and you have indeed triumphed in that."

When it is transitive to essences, it is in the sense of something connected to those essences, like the saying of 'Amr ibn Shas al-Asadi:

"She desired 'Irar with humiliation, and whoever desires 'Irar with humiliation, by my life, has done wrong."

Therefore the transitivity of the verb "you desire" to "gods" is in the sense of: you desire them by worship or by deifying them, so the meaning of "gods" was a sign of the aspect of desiring them.

"Gods" is in the accusative as the object, and he placed the object before the verb for emphasis on it, and because in it there is an indication of the direction in which the meaning of the verb goes beyond to the object.

"Falsehood" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of "you desire," meaning: deceiving. "Falsehood" means lying. It is also permissible that it be a state from "gods," meaning: gods that are lied about, that is, the claim of their divinity is a lie.

Describing with the verbal noun is valid whether considering the meaning of the agent or the meaning of the patient.

The circumstantial state was placed before its referent for the sake of emphasis, to hasten the expression of their lying and their error.

His words "other than God" mean: in contrast to God and apart from Him. This is valid whether one considers his people as idol-worshippers who did not acknowledge any god other than their idols, or considers them polytheists alongside God who worshipped other gods, like the polytheists of the Arabs, because some remnants of the hanifiyyah remained among the Arabs, so they did not forget describing God with divinity. The people of Abraham, who were the Chaldeans, worshipped the stars, similar to what the Greeks and the Copts were upon.

The commentary continues the argument from the rhetorical question of denial, with another question: ﴿So what is your assumption about the Lord of the worlds?﴾ This is a question used to express denunciation and to make them stop and recognise their error, and by "assumption" (zann) is meant the mistaken belief.

It is called zann (assumption) because it does not correspond to reality, and it was not called 'ilm (knowledge) because 'ilm is applied only to belief that corresponds to reality. For this reason they defined it as: "a quality that produces a discrimination that does not admit the opposite," and the possibility of the opposite is not negated except when the belief agrees with reality.

The application of zann to mistaken judgement and compound ignorance is frequent, as in His saying ﴿They follow nothing but assumption, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116] in Surat al-An'am, and His saying ﴿Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28].

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech."

The meaning is: your belief concerning the Lord of the worlds is a reprehensible ignorance.

When the verb zann is followed by the preposition bi- (ba'), it generally conveys an assumption that is not truthful, as He said: ﴿And you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10], and He said: ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you﴾ [Fussilat: 23]. From this comes the use of zanin (suspected one) for the accused, for its origin is "zanin bihi" (suspected of it), so the bi- was dropped and the adjective was connected directly. That is because when it is followed by bi-, the object is most often omitted, and the bi- is for metaphorical attachment, i.e., he assumed an assumption attached to Allah, meaning he claimed its connection to Allah; and this is only suitable for what is not fitting for Allah.

The indication of this was already mentioned at His saying ﴿And you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10] in Surat al-Ahzab.

The meaning is: "What is your evil assumption about Allah?" Since zann is one of the actions of the heart, its transitivity to the name of the essence without following the name with a qualifier is specific to the estimation of a suitable qualifier. The complement has been omitted here for the purpose of broadening the scope of the omitted element, by estimating it in every suitable possibility, to multiply the meanings. So it is permissible to take as the omitted element the attributes of the essence of the Lord of the worlds. It is also permissible to take from it the quiddity and reality. The consideration of the attribute is in two ways:

The first: the meaning derived from the word "Rabb" (Lord), which is lordship (ruboobiyyah), which is bringing a thing to its perfection gradually and gently, for the created being needs sustenance and provision, and that requires that the one who provides be thanked, so one does not turn away from worshipping his Lord. The estimate then is: "What is your assumption that He has partners, when He alone deserves gratitude, expressed in worship, because it is He who sustained you with His bounty?"

The second: that the meaning of ownership (malikiyyah) be considered, which is one of the two meanings of Rabb, and it implies the meaning of dominion and power over the owned. The estimate then is: "What is your assumption of what He will do to you in punishment for your disbelief, He being your Owner and the Owner of the worlds?"

As for the permissibility of considering the reality and quiddity of the Lord of the worlds, the estimate in it is: "What is your assumption regarding the quiddity of lordship? For you are ignorant of the attributes it requires, and at the forefront of them is oneness (wahdaniyyah)."

[p. 130]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 37, verses 75–87 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Noah had certainly called Us, and We are the best to respond.﴾ ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great calamity.﴾ ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors.﴾ ﴿And We left for him a good mention among the later generations.﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds.﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others.﴾

He followed the reminder and the consolation from the side of considering the traces of what befell the nations to whom the messengers were sent, and what He reported of their end in the Hereafter, with a reminder and consolation from the side of the report about the messengers whom their peoples denied and harmed, and how God gave victory to them, so that His Messenger (ﷺ) would be further steadied and the polytheists would be silenced with a decisive refutation.

In this surah He mentioned the stories of the messengers with their peoples, because in each story there is a distinctive feature that resembles the situation of the Messenger (ﷺ) with his people and his most perfect condition in his call. Thus in all the stories there is a lesson, an example, and a warning, as will be detailed when each story comes. What unites them all is the opposition to polytheism (shirk) and the opposition to its adherents.

[p. 131]

These six messengers were chosen: Noah is the first model, and Abraham is the messenger of the upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyya), which is the seed of the good tree, the tree of Islam. Moses is chosen because his law resembles the Islamic law in its detail and in its combining of religion and authority. These three messengers are the roots. Then He mentioned three messengers who branched off from them, and three who followed the same religion as the messengers before them. As for Lot, he follows the religion of Abraham; as for Elijah (Ilyas) and Jonah (Yunus), they follow the religion of Moses.

He began with the story of Noah with his people, for he was the first messenger God sent to the people, and he is the first model and the most excellent exemplar.

The beginning of the story with the mention of Noah's calling upon his Lord is an admonition to the polytheists, so that they would beware of the Messenger's (ﷺ) supplication to his Lord for victory against them, just as Noah supplicated against his people. This calling is what is related in His saying ﴿He said: My Lord, help me, for they have denied me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 26] in the Surah of al-Mu'minun, and in His saying ﴿Noah said: My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him only in loss﴾ [Nuh: 21] and the verses of the Surah of Nuh.

The fa' (ف) in His saying ﴿so how excellent are the responders﴾ is a consequence of "nadana" (called), meaning: He called Us, so We responded to him. The consequent was omitted because the phrase ﴿فَلَنِعْمَ المُجِيبُونَ﴾ indicates it, since it implicitly contains the meaning "so We responded to him," as the response of one of whom it is said: "How excellent is the Responder" (ni'ma al-mujib).

The object of praise is omitted, meaning: ﴿فَلَنِعْمَ المُجِيبُونَ﴾ "we are indeed the excellent responders." The first-person plural pronoun of association is used for magnification, as is well known.

The emphasis of the statement and the emphasis of what is derived from it by the oath particle (lam al-qasam) serves to affirm both matters, as a warning to the polytheists, since they were treated as one who denies that Noah called upon God and was answered.

Al-tanjiya (rescue) is causing someone to be saved (najin). Al-najat (salvation) is deliverance from a harm that has befallen. It is used here for safety from that harm before it occurs, because when his safety was attained at the time the harm encompassed his people, his safety from it, even though he was near it, was treated as deliverance from it after falling into it, by considering the approach of an act's occurrence as its occurrence. This is a frequent application of the word najat, such that it is correct to say: salvation is deliverance from a harm that has befallen or is expected.

By "his family" is meant his household, except those among them against whom the word had been decreed, and likewise the believers among his people. God said: ﴿We said: Load into it two of every kind, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth, and those who believe — and none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud: 40]. So the restriction to "his family" here is because of the small number of those who believed in him from outside them; or "family" is meant as the family of his religion, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 68].

His saying ﴿And We saved him and his family﴾ implies that the answer to Noah's supplication was by destroying his people.

Al-karb is intense grief and distress. Describing it as ﴿al-'azim﴾ (the great) indicates that it is great in its kind, so it is distress upon distress. What is meant by it is the Flood, which is a great calamity for those who fell into it. So Noah's rescue from it is his safety from falling into it, as you know, because it is a terror in appearance and a fear in its outcome, and falling into it is certain destruction. The fear does not cease to be with him until the water overwhelms him, and then he continues to suffer pains from shortness of breath, the trembling of cold, fear, and the certainty of destruction, until he drowns in the water.

God's rescuing him is a favor upon him, the rescuing of his family is another favor, the destruction of his oppressors is a greater favor, and making the population of the earth come from his descendants is a lasting favor, because they supplicate for him and his good deeds are mentioned among them, and God shows mercy to him on that account. Other favors will come that reach twelve.

The separating pronoun in His saying ﴿they are the survivors﴾ serves restriction, meaning: no one among mankind remained except those whom God saved with Noah in the Ark from his descendants, and then whoever descended from them. Thus none of the sons of Adam remained except the descendants of Noah, so all the nations are descended from the sons of Noah's three sons.

The apparent meaning of this is that those who believed with Noah, other than his sons, had no offspring. Ibn 'Abbas said: When Noah came out of the Ark, all who were with him died, men and women, except his son and his wives. By this, the contradiction between this verse and His saying in Surah Hud ﴿We said: Load into it two of every kind, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth, and those who believe — and none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud: 40] is resolved. This applies on the basis that the Flood covered the whole earth and eradicated all mankind except those whom Noah carried in the Ark, and its story has been related in Surah Hud.

The generality of the Flood is what the apparent meanings of the Book and the Sunnah require. As for those who said that the Flood did not cover the whole earth, they only denied it because of the brevity of the period in which the books of the Israelites delimit it, and it is not necessary to rely on those books in determining the age of the earth and its events. That is not among the decisive matters, and the restriction would be relative, meaning: no one remained from his people to whom he was sent. It may also be said: We grant that the Flood did not cover the entire earth, but it covered mankind, because they were confined to the lands that the Flood struck. Even if the evidence for the generality of the Flood is not definitive, the arguments of those who denied it are not sound, so the apparent meanings of the reports are not abandoned on their account.

God added to the list of Noah's honors, peace be upon him, His saying ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾, and this is a fifth favor.

Al-tark (leaving) in its real sense is leaving something behind and abandoning it. Here it is intended to mean continuance, in the sense of figurative metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal) or metaphor (al-isti'ara), because the nature of blessings in this world is that they are a passing enjoyment, after which they cease, whether they last long or short. So their cessation is as if it were a reclaiming by the Giver, as is stated in the hadith: "To God belongs what He took, and to Him belongs what He gave." So God honored Noah by letting His blessings upon him remain among nations after him.

The apparent meaning of "al-akhirin" (the later ones) is that it remains among all nations until the end of the world. The indication of the metaphor is the connection of "'alayhi" (upon him) with "taraknā" (We left), because it suits continuance; one says: "abqā 'alā kadhā," meaning he preserved it so that it would remain and not vanish. On this reading, "taraknā" has an object. Some of them assumed for it an object indicated by the context, meaning: We left a praise upon him. So this continuance may be understood as making him live a thousand years, which is the greatest extension of life that can be given to a living being beyond what is customary.

It may also mean the continuance of the good remembrance of him among nations, as Abraham said ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84]. Noah was thus remembered with praiseworthy qualities, so that it was said: No nation of the nations of the earth is ignorant of Noah, his virtue, and his glorification, even if the names by which they call him differ according to the differences of their languages. In the Book of Genesis, chapter nine, it is said: "Noah was a righteous man, perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God."

His mention appeared before Islam in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"You found trust had not betrayed it; thus was Noah, who did not betray."

His mention to the Children of Israel in the context of emulating him is in His saying ﴿Offspring of those whom We carried with Noah; indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra': 3].

[p. 133]

Ibn Khaldun mentioned that some claim Noah is Afridun, king of the land of Persia, and others claim Noah is Ushahnak, king of the Persians who came after Kayumarth by two hundred years. This agrees with the claim that Noah came after Adam by two hundred years, Adam being Kayumarth, according to the books of the Israelites. However, it is said that Kayumarth is Adam, as already mentioned in Surah al-Baqara.

The complement of "'alayhi" in His saying ﴿And We left upon him﴾ — none of the commentators, as far as I have seen, has hovered around it. The correct view is that "'alayhi" is connected to the verb "taraknā" by implying in this verb the meaning of "an'amnā" (We bestowed favor). Thus the apparent construction would require this verb to be followed by "li" (for), but since it was implicitly given the meaning of "an'amnā," its root conveyed the meaning of preserving for him, that is, giving him some of the stored-up virtues, which is like leaving someone a precious possession for one whom he leaves it to and who succeeds him in it. By attaching the preposition "'alā" (upon) to it, it conveys that this leaving is of the kind of bestowal and favor. This is the nature of implicit meaning (al-tadmin): that the implied verb conveys the meaning of two words, and it is one of the most elegant forms of concision (al-ijaz).

Then, since the object of "taraknā" is omitted, and the verb "an'amnā," which was implied in "taraknā," requires a complement denoting the object, that also is omitted together with its governing element. The original was: "and We left for him a praise, and bestowed favor upon him." So in His saying "taraknā 'alayhi" five words are omitted, which is a wondrous concision.

For this reason, most of the earlier commentators supplied "taraknā" with "a good praise upon him."

The sentence ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ is a performative statement (insha') of God's praise of Noah and a greeting to him, and its implied meaning is the consequence of a greeting, which is approval and drawing near. This is a sixth favor. The tanwin of "salam" is for magnification, and for this reason the beginning with an indefinite noun is common, since it is like a described noun.

By "the worlds" is meant the nations and the generations. It is a metonymy (kinaya) for the perpetuity of peace upon him, like His saying ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 15] concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, and His saying ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], ﴿Peace be upon Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat: 109].

"Among the worlds" (fi al-'alamin) is a circumstantial phrase (hal), so it is a fixed adverbial of place (zarf mustaqirr), or it is a second predicate (khabar thani) of "salam."

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari held that His saying ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ is in the position of the object of "taraknā," meaning: We left upon him this statement, namely ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾, which is among the speech whose quotation is intended, as you say: "I read [the surah]: 'A surah We sent down and made obligatory' [al-Nur: 1]", meaning: We made people greet him throughout all the generations, so they mention him only by saying "peace be upon him." They said the same about its parallels in these consecutive verses.

The description of Noah's peace in this surah as being "among the worlds" is added, unlike the peace upon others in the story of Abraham, Moses, Aaron, and Elijah, to indicate that the praise of Noah extended through all the nations, because they all trace their lineage to him and mention him with honest remembrance, as we have stated just before.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes of God's honoring of Noah. The particle "inna" conveys the causal explanation for God's recompensing Noah with the favors He enumerated, because he was a doer of good, meaning one who is characterized by goodness, which is pure faith, as explained in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Goodness (ihsan) is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." And what clearer proof of his goodness is there than his perseverance in calling to monotheism and piety, and the harm he endured from his people throughout the long period of his calling.

The meaning is: We indeed recompense those who do good in the same way. In this there is a commendation of Noah (peace be upon him): his reward was the model and the exemplar for the reward of the doers of good, according to the levels of their goodness and the varying degrees of their closeness to Noah's goodness and his strength in conveying the call. He was the first to be harmed for God's sake, so he established the pattern of reward for whoever is harmed for God's sake, and his own reward was of this same form. Thus it may be that he has a share (kifl) in every reward that anyone receives for patience when harmed for God's sake. Accordingly, the attribute of goodness (ihsan) is affirmed for Noah, and this is the seventh blessing. And it is affirmed for him that he is an exemplar for the doers of good in their reward for their goodness, and this is the eighth blessing.

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our servants, the believers﴾ is a causal justification for his deserving the recompense described by the words ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾. Therefore the effect of this cause differs from the effect of the preceding cause.

The description ﴿Indeed he is among Our servants﴾ conveys that he is among those who merited this description. You have learned more than once that the word "servant" ('abd), when it is attributed to the pronoun of Majesty, implies nearness and elevation of rank. He restricted the description of the servants to "the believers" to honour the matter of faith, so that those who believe may increase in faith and the polytheists may abandon polytheism. This is the ninth blessing.

Along with it, "among Our servants" is inserted to honour him through that attribution, in the same manner as what has preceded a little earlier in His words, ﴿except the sincere servants of God; for those there is a known provision﴾ [al-Saffat: 40]. This is the tenth blessing, and in it is an alert to the great worth of faith.

In this story there is a lesson for the polytheists through what befell the people of Noah, a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), and making Noah a model for him. It also contains an intimation that God will support him as He supported Noah against his people and will save him from their harm, and a commendation of the believers.

The "then" (thumma) in His words ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ indicates sequence and a delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because some of what was mentioned before it in the discourse actually occurred after the content of its clause in reality, as is evident. The meaning of the delay in rank here is that the drowning of those who denied him, along with his salvation and the salvation of his family, is greater in rank in supporting him, in showing his high standing with God the Exalted, and in showing the great power and gentleness of God the Exalted.

The meaning of "the others" (al-akharin) is those other than him and his family, that is, the rest of his people. In referring to them as "the others" there is a kind of contempt. And among what is in the hadith is that a man came to him and said, "Indeed the other (al-akhar) has committed fornication," meaning himself, according to the narration of al-akhar with the hamza extended, which is one of two narrations in the hadith.

The mention of Noah and his story has preceded at His words ﴿Indeed God chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 33] in Al 'Imran, and in al-A'raf, and in Surat Hud, and the mention of his ark in the beginning of Surat al-'Ankabut.

* * *

"﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾ ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ ﴿when he said to his father and his people, 'What is it that you worship?'﴾ ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾ ﴿Then what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾" This transitions to narrating the stance of Abraham (peace be upon him) toward his people in calling them to monotheism, what he encountered from them, and how God supported him and saved him from them. This transition came to it by describing him as among the partisans of Noah, so that with this single expression it conveys the confirmation of praise for Noah and the beginning of praise for Abraham, and the perpetuation of a distinction for Noah in that Abraham, the great messenger, was among his partisans, and that is enough praise.

Likewise, he gathered the virtues of Abraham into the phrase of his being among the partisans of Noah, which implies his sharing with him in his attributes, as will come. This is like His words ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ [al-Isra': 3].

The word "shi'ah" is a name for one who supports a man and his followers and is partisan toward him, so the word shi'ah applies to the singular and the plural. It may be pluralized as shi' and ashya' when groups are intended, each group being a shi'ah of someone. This has been mentioned previously at His words ﴿And We had certainly sent before you among the sects of the former peoples﴾ [al-Hijr: 10] in Surat al-Hijr, and at His words ﴿and He made its people into sects﴾ [al-Qasas: 4] in Surat al-Qasas.

Abraham was of the descendants of Noah, and his religion agreed with the religion of Noah in its foundation, which is the rejection of polytheism.

Abraham was made among the partisans of Noah because messengers came upon the religion of Noah before Abraham, among them Hud and Salih, for they were before Abraham, since the Qur'an mentioned them more than once directly after mentioning Noah and before mentioning Lot, the contemporary of Abraham. And [this is shown] by Hud's saying to his people, "﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69]," and by Salih's saying to his people, "﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]," and by Shu'ayb's saying to his people, "﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to earn [a punishment] like what struck the people of Noah or the people of Hud or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [Hud: 89]." Thus he made the people of Lot nearer in time to his people than the people of Hud and the people of Salih. Lot was a contemporary of Abraham, so all of these were partisans of Noah, and Abraham was among that partisanship. This is the eleventh blessing.

The emphasis of the statement with "indeed" (inna) and the lam of initiation is a response to the polytheists, because they claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham. This is like His words ﴿And he was not among the polytheists﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135].

"Idh" (when) is an adverb of past time, and it is connected to the implied predicate of the prepositional phrase that occurs as the predicate of "inna" in His words ﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾, or it is connected to the word shi'ah because of what it contains of the meaning of supporting and following, meaning: he was among his partisans at the time he came to his Lord with a sound heart, just as Noah came. Therefore the time of his being among his partisans is that time, that is, because Noah came to his Lord with a sound heart. In "idh" there is the meaning of causation for his being among his partisans, for the meaning of causation frequently arises with "idh," as in His words ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 39]. This is a blessing upon Noah, and it is the twelfth.

The "bi" in "﴿with a sound heart﴾" is for accompaniment, meaning that a heart whose attribute is soundness came with him, so it is interpreted to mean: when he came to his Lord with soundness of heart. The heart was mentioned first and then described as "sound" because in mentioning the heart there is the bringing to mind of the reality of that pure heart, and for this reason the indefinite "a heart" was preferred over definiteness.

"Salim" (sound) is a derived attribute (sifah mushabbahah) from soundness (salamah), which is freedom from defects and diseases. Since the heart was mentioned, it became clear that its soundness is its freedom from what hearts are afflicted with of their maladies, so it is not permissible that it means bodily diseases, because they did not mean by "heart" anything other than the seat of perception and character. Therefore it is determined that the intended meaning is the possessor of the heart in relation to himself, with such things as the following of desire, self-admiration and conceit, and in relation to people, with such things as arrogance, malice, envy, showing off, and contempt.

He used the word "coming" for his dealing with it in himself by what pleases his Lord, in the manner of a figurative image of one who comes to someone bringing to him what he requested, such as weapons, gifts, or kindnesses. God had commanded him to purify his soul and he complied, so his condition resembled that of one who was called and then came. This is like His words ﴿Respond to the caller of God﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31].

His words ﴿with a sound heart﴾ comprise comprehensive elements of the perfection of the soul, and these are the source of praiseworthy deeds. In the hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."

It has been related about Abraham that he said, ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. So the pillar of the religion of Abraham was that which branches from His words ﴿with a sound heart﴾, and that is the sum of noble character. For this reason He described Abraham with His words, ﴿Indeed Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, and penitent﴾ [Hud: 75], so he was free from every blameworthy trait and every false belief.

[Page 138]

Then, noble character is capable of increase, so Abraham's share of it was a complete share, perhaps more complete than Noah's share, based on the view that Abraham is the best of the messengers after Muhammad (ﷺ). God reserved the ultimate perfection of it for His messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason he said, "I was only sent to perfect noble character." For the same reason the religion of Abraham was described as al-hanifiyyah (the upright monotheistic faith), and Islam was described as that plus more, in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was sent with the easy upright faith (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah)."

The linking of his being among the partisans of Noah with this time, which is added to that state, is a kinayah (metonymy) for describing Noah with soundness of heart. Also, from His words ﴿And indeed among his partisans was Abraham﴾ there results the affirmation of attributes similar to those of Noah for Abraham, and from His words ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ there results the affirmation of an attribute similar to Abraham's attribute for Noah, by way of kinayah in both affirmations. However, that was affirmed for Abraham explicitly, while it is affirmed for Noah by necessary implication, so it is weaker in him than in Abraham.

"﴿When he said to his father﴾" is a substitute for "﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾" as a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition), for his saying this arose from his heart being filled with monotheism and with zeal for God against the polytheists, so it was like something that his sound heart encompassed, and so it issued from him.

"﴿What is it that you worship?﴾" is a rhetorical interrogative of denial against their worshipping what they worship. For this reason he followed it with another rhetorical interrogative of denial, which is "﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾". What required the use of the demonstrative after "ma" (what), which is interrogative, is that it takes on the sense of the relative pronoun referred to, and so it required that what they worship be present before Abraham. Thus the interrogation was turned by this to a meaning other than its literal one, which is the meaning of denial.
