So the offering of the most beloved thing to Abraham is fitting for a sacrifice at the noblest sanctuary. The custom of offering gifts during the pilgrimage has remained among the Arabs every year, and this is nothing but a reminder of the first year in which Abraham was commanded to sacrifice his son, and that son was the one in Mecca.

The fifth argument: "A Bedouin said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O son of the two sacrificed ones,' so he understood what he meant and smiled." Among the forefathers of the Prophet (ﷺ) there is no sacrificed one other than 'Abd Allah and Isma'il.

The sixth argument: what occurs in the Book of Genesis, chapter twenty-two, that God tested Abraham and said to him: "Take your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains that I will tell you," until the end of the story. But Isaac was not Abraham's only son, for Isma'il was born before him by thirteen years. Abraham and Isma'il remained in contact, and in chapter twenty-five of Genesis, when the death of Abraham (peace be upon him) is mentioned, it says: "and Isaac and Isma'il his sons buried him." So the insertion of the name Isaac after the phrase "your son, your only one" is an addition by the scribe of the Torah.

The seventh argument: the author of the Kashshaf said: "What indicates this is that the two horns of the ram were hung in the Ka'ba in the hands of the sons of Isma'il until the House burned during the siege of Ibn al-Zubayr." End of quote. Al-Qurtubi said, quoting Ibn 'Abbas: "By the One in whose hand my soul is, at the beginning of Islam the head of the ram was indeed hanging by its two horns from the gutter of the Ka'ba, and it had dried out." I say: as to whether that head is truly the head of the ram of ransom from the time of Abraham, there is room for examination.

The eighth argument: reports have come down concerning the wisdom behind the legislation of stoning at the pillars (jamarat), from the era of the Hanifiyya (the monotheistic faith of Abraham), that Satan confronted Abraham to turn him away from proceeding with the sacrifice of his son. This is among the rites of the pilgrimage for the people of Mecca, and the Jews had no fixed custom of sacrifice of this kind.

[Page 159]

Al-Qurtubi also mentioned, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Satan appeared to Abraham at the pillars three times, and each time he stoned him with pebbles until he left from the vicinity of the last pillar. And from him (Ibn 'Abbas): the place where the sacrifice was attempted was near the pillars, and it was said: near the rock at the base of Mount Thabir in Mina.

The ninth argument: the Qur'an is explicit that when God gave Abraham the good news of Isaac, He coupled that good news with the statement that Jacob would be born to Isaac. God says: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud: 71]. This took place in the presence of Abraham. So if God had tested him by commanding him to sacrifice Isaac, the test would have been merely nominal, because he was certain that Isaac would live until Jacob was born to him, since God does not break His promise. But when He gave him the good news of Isma'il, He did not promise him that a son would be born to him from Isma'il. This was nothing but a preparation for his being tested by sacrificing him, for Abraham had been praying for the life of his son Isma'il. Indeed, in the Book of Genesis, chapter seventeen, it says: "And Abraham said to God: 'Would that Isma'il might live before You.' God said: 'Rather, Sarah will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac, and I will establish My covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.'" And it appears that this occurred after the test of sacrificing him.

The tenth argument: if the forbearing boy had been Isaac, then God's statement after this, ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 112], would be a repetition, because the expression "We gave him good news of so-and-so" predominantly carries the sense of announcing the child's existence.

The scholars of the early generations differed in identifying the one who was sacrificed. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: it is Isma'il. Among those who said this were Abu Hurayra, Abu al-Tufayl 'Amir ibn Wathila, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. Among the Successors who said it were Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, 'Alqama, al-Kalbi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Another group said: it is Isaac. This is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, 'Umar and 'Ali among the Companions, and it was said by a group of the Successors, among them 'Ata', 'Ikrima, al-Zuhri and al-Suddi.

In the Jami' al-'Utbiyya it is stated that this is the view of Malik ibn Anas.

If you say: then what is the basis for your inclining toward it and your argument for your preference that the test was with the sacrifice of Isma'il rather than Isaac, how then do you interpret what occurs in the Book of Genesis? I say: I am of the view that what is in the Book of Genesis was transmitted in scattered form, without its order, in which the times of events are not arranged with precision that determines the time between the sacrifice and the accounts of Abraham. When the transmitters conveyed the Torah after its original was lost, following the captivity of the Children of Israel in the land of Assyria in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, it recorded the matter of the one to be sacrificed among the affairs of Abraham (peace be upon him), and there was incorporated into it what the Children of Israel believed during their exile, namely their assumption that the one sacrificed was Isaac. This is supported by the statement in chapter twenty-two: "And after these things, God tested Abraham and said: 'Take your son, your only one...'" etc. So what is meant by her statement "after these things": after all the preceding matters, or after some of what preceded?

[Page 153]

﴿So when they both submitted, and he laid him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿and We called out to him: "O Ibrahim,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was a manifest trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾

"Aslama" (submitted): it means "istaslama" (surrendered), and "sallama," "istaslama," and "aslama" are used with the same meaning: to yield and submit. The complement is omitted because it is evident from the context, meaning: they both submitted to the command of God. Ibrahim's submission was his readiness to slaughter his son, and the boy's submission was his obedience to his father in what had reached him from his Lord.

"Tallahu" (he threw him down): he struck him down onto the ground. It is a verb derived from the noun "tall," which is a heap of earth, like a mound. As for his statement in the hadith about drinking, "fatallahu fi yadihi" (he tilted it in his hand), meaning the cup, that is a figurative use, by way of comparison to the intensity of the grasp, as if he had placed it firmly in his hand.

The "lam" in "lil-jabin" (upon the forehead) is in the sense of "ʿala" (upon), like His saying: ﴿They fall down upon their faces, prostrating﴾ [al-Isra: 107], and His saying: ﴿He called upon Us, lying on his side﴾ [Yunus: 12]. Its meaning is that the thing it governs is the lowest part of its object.

"Al-jabin" (the temple): it is one of the two sides of the forehead. The forehead has two temples, and al-jabin is not the forehead itself. For this reason, they faulted al-Mutanabbi for his statement:

"Leave off the adornment for one who would verify it; the blood-stained brow of the worshipper is not what it is." 

Al-Mutanabbi followed the common usage, which is an error. Ibn Qutayba pointed this out in Adab al-Katib, and Ibn al-Sayyid al-Batalyawsi in al-Iqtidab did not object to it. However, al-Hariri did not count it among the Awham al-Khawass (Errors of the Elite), so perhaps he overlooked it. Murtada, in Taj al-ʿArus, reported from his teacher the correction of using "al-jabin" for the forehead figuratively, by the relation of contiguity (ʿalaqat al-mujawara), and he cited the verse of Zuhayr:

"My protection is by the temple and the two shoulders, and I push it away with the spear whose joints are straight."

He claimed that the commentator of Zuhayr's Diwan mentioned this.

This does not validate such usage except when there is a contextual indicator (qarina), because a figurative usage that is not frequent does not deserve to be counted among the meanings of the word. Moreover, we do not accept that Zuhayr meant by al-jabin the forehead. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention this in Asas al-Balagha.

The meaning: He threw him onto the ground on his side, in such a way that his temple touched the ground because of the intensity of the contact.

God's calling out to Ibrahim was by way of revelation (wahy) through the sending of an angel. The calling is attributed to God because He is the one who commands it.

"Tasdiq al-ru'ya" (fulfilling the vision): it means realizing it in external reality, by performing the same form of the action he had seen. It is said: a "true vision" (ru'ya sadiqa) when what matches the form of what the seer saw occurs afterward in reality. God the Exalted said: ﴿God indeed fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. In the hadith of ʿAʾisha: "The first thing with which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was begun in revelation was the true vision; he never saw a vision except that it came like the break of dawn." By contrast, it is said: "the vision lied" (kadhabat al-ru'ya) when what occurred was contrary to what was seen. In the hadith: "When the time draws near, the vision of the believer will hardly lie."

So the meaning of ﴿you have fulfilled the vision﴾ is: you have done the like of the form of what you saw in sleep, that you would do it. This is a praise from God the Exalted for Ibrahim, for his promptness in carrying out the command, and he did not delay, nor did he ask God to abrogate that.

The intended meaning: he fulfilled what he saw up to the point of passing the knife over his son's neck. When Jibril called out to him not to slaughter him, that address constituted an abrogation (naskh) of the act of slaughter in the vision. That came from God and not from any shortcoming on the part of Ibrahim. So Ibrahim fulfilled the vision until God forbade him from completing its image. Thus, his fulfilling most of it was described as his having fulfilled it, and the slaughter of the ram was made an interpretation (ta'wil) of the slaughter of the son that occurred in the vision.

The clause ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ is a causal clause (taʿlil) for "and We called out to him," because God's calling to him is an elevation of his station, so that call was a reward for his good deed.

This clause may be part of God's address to Ibrahim, or it may be a parenthetical insertion between the clauses of God's address to Ibrahim. The demonstrative in "thus" (kadhalika) refers to the verbal noun derived from the verb "sadaqta" (you have fulfilled), namely "al-tasdiq" (fulfilling). It is like the return of the pronoun to the verbal noun derived from ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8]. The meaning is: Indeed, We reward the good-doers in the manner of that fulfilling; that is, in proportion to the greatness of that fulfilling, We reward the good-doers with a great reward, namely those who are perfect in goodness, and you are among them.

Because the word "reward" (jaza') includes the meaning of recompense and equivalence between the rewarded and what is rewarded, the reward is magnified by being likened to a thing indicated by a demonstrative of distance, which conveys a relative distance, namely elevation and greatness of rank in honour. The sense is: We reward the good-doers with a reward like that good deed you performed by fulfilling the vision, as a recompense proportionate to the measure of the goodness. For he gave up the dearest of things to him in obedience to his Lord, so God gave him in return from the best of the good things that are in the hand of God the Exalted. The thing compared and the thing to which it is compared are both intellectual (ma'qulan), since neither of them is observed, but both are imagined by what imagination can encompass, the familiar imagination among the good-doers, from what their belief requires regarding the promise of the Truthful, from the reward of the Mighty and Powerful. God the Exalted said: ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60].

Because the demonstrative noun conveyed the greatness of the reward, the statement was emphasized with "inna" (indeed), to remove the suspicion of exaggeration. That is, it is above what you know in greatness and what minds can estimate.

From the mention of "the good-doers" it is understood that the reward is goodness in return for goodness, so the meaning becomes: Indeed, We reward the good-doers with the great goodness that you did. This is a promise of great degrees of divine bounty. The promise of his son was also included, with goodness of a similar kind, by the connection of the reward to goodness. The son's goodness was great, in giving up his own self.

This was emphasized by the content of the clause ﴿Indeed, this was a manifest trial﴾, meaning: this charge that We imposed on you is the clear test, that is, manifest in indicating a great degree of obedience to God's command.

The word "trial" (balaʾ) is used figuratively for its necessary implication, which is testimony to the rank of one who, if tested with such a charge, his rank in obedience, patience, and strength of certainty would be known.

The clause ﴿Indeed, this was a manifest trial﴾ serves as the reason (ʿilla) for the clause ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾, in the manner previously mentioned regarding the position of the clause ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾ [al-Saffat: 81] in the story of Nuh.

The response (jawab) to ﴿So when they both submitted﴾ is omitted, indicated by His saying "and We called out to him." It was presented in the form of a conjunction, out of preference for what that conveys of the sense of the narrative, rather than making it a response; because indication of the response is achieved by conjoining part of the narrative and not the reverse. Omitting the response in such contexts is frequent in the Qur'an and is one of its styles. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, and We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive." And they came to their father at evening, weeping﴾ [Yusuf: 15].

The clause "and We ransomed him" appears to be part of the speech that God addressed to Ibrahim.

The meaning: And indeed We ransomed your son with a great sacrifice. Without this estimation, the narration of God's call to Ibrahim would not include the purpose of the call, which is annulling the command to slaughter the boy.

[Page 156]

"Al-fidā" and "al-fidāʾ" (ransom): giving something as a substitute for a right owed to the one who receives it. It is also applied to the thing by which one is ransomed, by using the verbal noun for the object (ism al-maf'ul).

The ransom is attributed to God because He is the one who permitted it. This is a rational metaphor (majaz ʿaqli), since God revealed to Ibrahim that he should slaughter the ram as a ransom for slaughtering his son, while Ibrahim was the one who ransomed, by God's permission, and Ibrahim's son was the one ransomed.

"Al-dhibh" (with a kasra on the dhal): the thing slaughtered. The pattern fi'l with a kasra on the first letter and sukun on the middle radical is frequently used in the sense of the passive participle from the root from which it is derived, like "al-hibb," "al-tihn," and "al-iṣl." (Note: these are examples such as "al-hibb" for the beloved, "al-tihn" for the ground grain, and "al-ʿidl" for the equivalent.)

Describing it as "great" ('azim) means that the status of this slaughter is elevated, because God ransomed through it the son of a Messenger, and preserved through it the one who would become a Messenger. He magnified it by the greatness of its effect. Also, because God made it subservient to Ibrahim at that time and in that place.

These verses have pointed to the story of the one who was sacrificed, but the Qur'an did not name him, for a reason: so as not to stir up dispute between Muslims and the People of the Book about identifying the sacrificed one from Ibrahim's two sons. The aim was to win over the People of the Book in order to establish the proof against them regarding their acknowledgment of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the confirmation of the Qur'an. There was no important purpose attached to specifying the sacrificed one, nor in criticizing the People of the Book for specifying him. The sign of this is that the Qur'an named Isma'il in places other than the story of the sacrifice, and named Ishaq in places, including the announcement to his mother through the speech of the angels who were sent to the people of Lut, and it mentioned the names of Isma'il and Ishaq, that both were granted to him in old age. It did not name anyone in the story of the sacrifice, intending generality, while the purpose of the story was not lost, since the purpose of the story is to honour Ibrahim. Whichever of his two sons was the sacrificed one, the trial of him through slaughter and his determination upon it was the same, and what appeared in that of the miracle is a great honour for Ibrahim's station. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a manner that is best﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 46]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them." Al-Hakim narrated in al-Mustadrak from Muʿawiya ibn Abi Sufyan that one of the Bedouins said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and the Prophet (ﷺ) smiled. He meant that he was from the descendants of Isma'il, who was the sacrificed one, and that his father, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, whose father ʿAbd al-Muttalib had vowed: If God grants him ten sons, he will sacrifice the tenth to the Kaʿba. When ʿAbd Allah was born, the tenth, ʿAbd al-Muttalib resolved to fulfil his vow. The elders of the people of al-Bitah spoke to him, asking him to substitute ten camels for him and to cast lots with arrows over him and over the camels: if the lot of the camels came out, he would slaughter them. He did so, and the lot of ʿAbd Allah came out. They said: "Appease the gods," meaning the gods that were in the Kaʿba on that day. He added ten camels and cast lots, and the lot of ʿAbd Allah came out. They kept saying: "Appease the gods," and ʿAbd al-Muttalib kept adding ten camels, repeating the drawing of lots, and the lot of ʿAbd Allah kept coming out, until he reached one hundred camels. He cast lots over him, and the lot of the camels came out. They said: "The gods are pleased." So he slaughtered them as a ransom for him.

This was a virtue for ʿAbd al-Muttalib and for his son, the father of the Prophet (ﷺ), resembling the virtue of his forefather Ibrahim. Although it took place according to the customs of the pre-Islamic era, what is derived from it is different from what surrounded it of false accidents. The time was a period of interval (fatra), in which there was no law, and nothing in the authentic Sunna contradicts this.

However, what spread among the reports of the People of the Book was that the sacrificed one was Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, based on what came in the Book of Genesis in the twenty-second chapter, and on what the Jews used to narrate to them. What they knew of the sayings of the Messenger (ﷺ) did not contradict it, nor did they ask him about it.

Reflection on this verse strengthens the presumption that the sacrificed one was Isma'il, for it is clear and strong in showing that the one commanded to be sacrificed was the forbearing boy in His saying: ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy﴾ [al-Saffat: 101], and that he is the one whom Ibrahim asked his Lord to grant him. The verse therefore related the story of the trial by the slaughter of this forbearing boy who was granted to Ibrahim. Then it followed his story with His saying: ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]. This is close to the indication of the text that Ishaq is other than the forbearing boy whose story has been discussed, because the apparent meaning of His saying "and We gave him good tidings" is a second good tidings, and the mention of the name Ishaq indicates that he is other than the forbearing boy to whom the preceding pronouns referred. This is one first proof.

The second argument: when God tested Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice his son, the apparent reading is that the test came when Abraham had no son other than him, because that is more complete as a test, as was mentioned earlier.

The third argument: God mentioned ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾ [al-Saffat: 101] right after what Abraham had said: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100]. This shows that this forbearing boy who was commanded to be sacrificed is the one promised in answer to his prayer. It has already become clear that the purpose of the prayer was that he not be childless, leaving his inheritance to the servants of his household, as is found in the Book of Genesis and was mentioned just above.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 108–111:

﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Ibrahim﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ ﴿Indeed, he is among Our believing servants﴾. The discussion of ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ is similar to the preceding discussion concerning the mention of Nuh (peace be upon him) in this surah, and its repetition here is an emphasis on what came before, to increase the honouring of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

It may be asked: why was the sentence ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ not emphasised here with (inna) (indeed), when it was emphasised with the mention of Nuh and in what preceded concerning the mention of Ibrahim? Al-Zamakhshari, in the Kashshaf, noted that since the statement ﴿Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good﴾ [al-Saffat: 105] had already preceded in this narrative, and Ibrahim was the one rewarded, it was sufficient to emphasise its counterpart instead of emphasising it again; that is, because the interest was already aroused by the first emphasis, there remained no reason to repeat it.

He limited the emphasis to the meaning of the sentence by verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi), because it is an affirmation of the care given to his reward for his good conduct.

The phrase ﴿in the worlds﴾ was not mentioned here because Ibrahim is not known to all the nations of mankind, unlike Nuh (peace be upon him), as was mentioned in his story.

Al-Zamakhshari, in the Kashshaf, noted that since the statement ﴿Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good﴾ [al-Saffat: 105] had already preceded in this narrative, and Ibrahim was the one rewarded, it was sufficient to emphasise its counterpart instead of emphasising it again; that is, because the interest was already aroused by the first emphasis, there remained no reason to repeat it.

He limited the emphasis to the meaning of the sentence by verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi), because it is an affirmation of the care given to his reward for his good conduct.

The phrase ﴿in the worlds﴾ was not mentioned here because Ibrahim is not known to all the nations of mankind, unlike Nuh (peace be upon him), as was mentioned in his story.

"Wa-bashsharnāhu bi-Isḥāq nabiyyan min aṣ-ṣāliḥīn" ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ "Wa-bārakanā ʿalayhi wa-ʿalā Isḥāq, wa-min dhurriyyatihimā muḥsinun wa-ẓālimun li-nafsihi mubīn" ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doers and those who wrong themselves openly﴾. This is another good news given to Abraham, and an honour for him, and it is other than the good news of the forbearing boy, for Isaac is other than the forbearing boy. And this good news is the one mentioned in the Qur'an in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We gave her the good news of Isaac and, after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud: 71].

The naming of the one given good news as Isaac may imply that God designated for him a name by which he would be called, and this is what is implied by what is in the seventeenth chapter of Genesis: "Sarah your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac."

It may also imply that what is meant is: We gave him good news of a son who was named Isaac. On both possibilities, this indicates that the boy given good news of in the verse before this is not the one named Isaac, and so it is established that he is the one named Ishmael.

The meaning of the good news about him is the good news of his birth to him, because good news does not relate to essences but relates to meanings.

"Nabiyyan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from Isaac. It may be a narration of the good news, in which case the circumstantial clause is a "future circumstance" (ḥāl muqaddara), because Isaac's attribute of prophethood came a long time after the time of the good news; indeed, he did not yet exist. So the meaning is: We gave him the good news of the birth of a son named Isaac, who would be, in the future, a prophet. The non-existence of the bearer of the circumstance at the time of describing him with the circumstance does not contradict his being connected to that circumstance, on the assumption of his existence, because the existence of the bearer of the circumstance is not a condition for describing him with it; rather, the condition is the concomitance of the verb's relation to him, while observing the meaning of the circumstance. Its ultimate basis is that it is a use of the active participle for the time of the future by means of context, and a future circumstance cannot be otherwise; and the length of the future time is not determined. An example of this is what preceded in His saying, ﴿And they will come to Us alone﴾ [Maryam: 80], in Surat Maryam.

Know that the meaning of the future circumstance is that its occurrence is determined, not yet present now, and what is determined is the one who speaks of it; it is a description of its bearer in the future and a restriction on its governing element, however it may be. So do not concern yourself with what he extended on this in al-Kashshaf, nor with al-Baydawi's disagreement with it, nor with what branched from that of discussions.

If it is a parenthetical insertion in the midst of the story, it is an honouring of Isaac, and the circumstance is a present (ḥāl ḥāṣila).

His saying "min aṣ-ṣāliḥīn" is a second circumstance. He mentioned it to highlight the matter of righteousness, for the prophets are counted among its people; and otherwise every prophet must be righteous. Prophethood is the greatest of the states of righteousness because of the greatness that accompanies it.

"Bāraka" means: he made him possessor of blessing (barakah), and barakah is the increase of good in its various aspects. Its explanation has already preceded at His saying, ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 96] in Surat Ali 'Imran, and at His saying, ﴿and blessings upon you﴾ [Hud: 48] in Surat Hud.

"ʿAlā" is for figurative elevation, i.e., the establishment of the blessing enveloping both of them.

When he mentioned what He gave them, he turned the speech to their descendants and said, "and among their descendants is the muḥsin," i.e., one who acts with good deeds, "and the ẓālim li-nafsihi," i.e., a polytheist, not upright, to indicate that not all of their descendants are like them; rather they differ. Among the descendants of Abraham are prophets, righteous people and believers; and among the descendants of Isaac are likewise. Among the descendants of Abraham are those who turned away from the ways of their forefather, like the polytheists of the Arabs; and among the descendants of Isaac likewise, like those of the Jews who disbelieved in the Messiah and in Muhammad, may Allah's blessings be upon them both. Its parallel is His saying, ﴿He said, "And of my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124] in Surat al-Baqarah.

In it is an alert that the wicked and the good do not have their affairs governed by lineage and ancestry: the righteous may beget a corrupt person and the corrupt a righteous one. And that corruption of descendants is not considered a disgrace to the forefathers; that the criterion of excellence is the qualities of the self and what a person acquires of righteous deeds; and as for the honour of forefathers, it is a completion of perfection and an incitement to expanding in virtuous qualities. So in this completion is the refutation of the vanity of the polytheists in claiming they are descendants of Abraham, and that it is a distinction but that entering Islam is not equivalent to it, and that they are not more deserving of the Sacred Mosque. Abu Talib said in the proposal of Khadijah to the Prophet ﷺ: "Praise be to Allah who made us from the descendants of Abraham and the seed of Ishmael, and made us men of His sanctuary and custodians of His House,"

and that was before Islam. And Allah, Exalted, said to them after Islam: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believed in Allah and the Last Day and struggled in the cause of Allah? Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 114–116:

﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon Moses and Aaron﴾ ﴿and We saved them and their people from the great distress﴾ ﴿and We helped them, so they were the victors﴾. It is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us﴾ [al-Saffat: 75], and the connection (munasabah, the thematic link between passages) is what was mentioned there.

Here He mentions what was a favour (minnah) upon Moses and Aaron, namely prophethood (nubuwwah), for it is the highest rank to which a human being can be raised. For this reason the thing bestowed is left unspecified, so that the verb is taken in its most complete sense. It is described as a favour from God upon them both because Moses did not ask for prophethood, since prophethood is not something acquired; and it was a favour upon Aaron too, because it was Moses who asked it for him, and Aaron did not ask it himself. So it is a favour upon him and a pleasing of Moses. The favour upon them both is of the kind of conveying benefits, for God sent Moses to rescue the Children of Israel from being enslaved by the Copts, as Abraham and Israel had been.

In the difference among the beginnings of the three narratives there is an indication that God takes up the cause of His friends: either by answering a supplication, or as a reward for sound intention and a sound heart, or out of mercy and favour toward His weak servants. The deliverance of Moses, Aaron and their people is another honour for them both and for their people through them, and this is the blessing of the removal of harm. Thus Moses and Aaron received both kinds of blessing: the giving of benefits and the averting of harms.

صفحة ١٦٤
The "great distress" (al-karb al-ʿazim) refers to what they endured of humiliation under the rule of the Pharaohs, and to Pharaoh's pursuit of them in their exodus when "the two hosts saw each other," and the companions of Moses said: "Indeed we are overtaken!" Then God revealed to him: strike the sea with your staff. He struck it, and it split, and the Children of Israel passed through it. Then the sea closed its waves over Pharaoh and his army. However, the "great distress" was also applied to drowning in the story of Noah mentioned earlier, and in Surat al-Anbiya' to the peoples whose lands they passed through, such as the Amalekites and the Amorites. The Children of Israel were victorious in every battle they fought at the command of Moses, and they were defeated only when they advanced to fight the Amalekites and the Canaanites in the plains of the Valley of (Shukol), because Moses had forbidden them to fight there, as is recorded in their history.

The word (hum) in His saying "so they were the victors" is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), and it conveys restriction (qasr): that is, they are the victors over others, and others did not overcome them, meaning they were never defeated even once, since a victor may be defeated in some encounters before he prevails.

﴿And We gave them the Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿And We guided them to the straight path.﴾ ﴿And We left upon them [a good remembrance] among the later generations.﴾ ﴿Peace upon Moses and Aaron.﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants.﴾

﴿al-Kitab al-mustabin﴾ "It is the Tawrah (Torah), and al-mustabin is the one of strong clarity. The sin and the ta' are for intensification (mubalaghah), as one says: istabana al-shay' (the thing became clear) when it appeared with great clarity."

The transitive use of the verb of giving (al-iytaʾ) with the pronoun referring to Moses and Aaron, although the one who was given the Torah was Moses, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87], is because Aaron was a supporter of Moses in his mission, so he had a share in the giving of the Torah, as Allah said in another verse: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron the criterion and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48]. This is the use of the verb "giving" in both its literal and metaphorical senses.

As for ﴿al-sirat al-mustaqim﴾, it means the true religion, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Fatihah. The law of the Torah, on the day Moses (peace be upon him) was given it, was the straight path. When it was abrogated (naskh) by the Qur'an, the Qur'an became the straight path forever, and the path of the Torah was rendered inoperative.

It is also permissible that by ﴿al-sirat al-mustaqim﴾ is meant the fundamentals of religion (usul al-diyanah) on which the sacred laws (shara'i', the divine legislations) do not differ, namely tawhid (the oneness of God) and the universal principles of the laws, to which His saying, exalted is He, refers: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura: 13], up to His saying: "and Moses and Jesus."

The discussion of the interpretation of ﴿And We left upon them among the later generations﴾ up to the end of the four verses is like the discussion of its counterparts when Noah is mentioned in this surah. However, the possibility that the sentence ﴿Peace upon Moses and Aaron﴾ is an object of the verb ﴿And We left upon them﴾, on the basis of quoting the wording here, is weaker than it was in what preceded, since it is not consistent that the later generations would greet Moses and Aaron together. The one who mentions Moses says "Peace upon Moses," and the one whose speech includes the mention of Aaron says "Peace upon Aaron." Only the one whose speech includes mention of both of them together joins their two names in the greeting, as when a narrator says about Jabir: "may Allah be pleased with him," and says about 'Abd Allah ibn Haram: "may Allah be pleased with him," but when he says "from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah," he says "may Allah be pleased with both of them."

In the story of Moses and Aaron there is a complete lesson (ibrah) and example for the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning his mission, the sending down of the Qur'an upon him, his guidance, the spread of his religion and his authority after his departure from the lands of the polytheists.

"And indeed, Ilyas was among the messengers. When he said to his people, 'Will you not fear God? Do you call upon Ba'l and forsake the Best of Creators? God is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old.' But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth, except the sincere servants of God. And We left for him a good remembrance among the later generations. Peace be upon the family of Yasin. Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants."

The discourse on three messengers who brought laws is followed here by the account of three prophets and what their peoples did to them. All of it serves as evidence for consoling the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) and as a series of admonitions to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

The mention of these three is introduced with the sentence "And indeed, Ilyas was among the messengers," because they are equal in the rank of calling to the religion of God, and in that they had no sacred law of their own. The emphasis of their being messengers by the particle of emphasis is for the sake of drawing attention to the report, since it may be overlooked, given that these three did not have a specific sacred law.

Ilyas is (Ilya') from among the prophets of the Children of Israel who followed the law of the Torah. He was described as a messenger because he was commanded by God, exalted is He, to convey to the kings of Israel that God was angry with them on account of the worship of idols. Applying the description of messenger to him is like applying it to the messengers sent to the people of Antioch mentioned in Surah Ya Sin.

"Idh" (when) is an adverbial complement related to "al-mursalin" (the messengers), meaning that from the time of that statement he was conveying a message from God, exalted is He, to his people.

Ilyas has already been mentioned in Surah al-An'am. By "his people" is meant the Children of Israel, and they had worshipped Ba'l, the idol of the Canaanites, because of the intermarriage of some kings of Judah with the Canaanites. Therefore Ilyas stood calling his people to renounce the worship of the idol Ba'l and to single out God for worship.

His saying "Ala" (will you not) consists of two words: the interrogative hamza, for denunciation, and the negating "la". It is a denunciation of their lack of piety. The object of "tattaqun" (you fear) is omitted, because what follows indicates it.

Ba'l is the name of the idol of the Canaanites, and it was the greatest of their idols, because the word ba'l in their language indicates the meaning of maleness, and then it indicated the meaning of lordship. So the word ba'l is applied to the male, and among them it is a symbol of the sun. Its counterpart is the word (Tanit), with two dotted letters, meaning the female. For them there was a idol called by the Phoenicians at Carthage (Tanit), and among them it is a symbol of the moon. Among the Phoenicians of the land of Phoenicia, the original homeland of the Canaanites, this idol is called (Ashtaroth). In the time of Musa, peace be upon him, the name (Molech) was also applied to Ba'l. They depicted him in the form of a human with the head of a calf, with two horns, wearing a crown, seated on a throne with his hands outstretched as one who receives something. His image was of bronze, hollow inside, and they placed it upon a base of masonry like an oven. They would kindle fire in that oven until the bronze was heated, and they would bring offerings and place them on his arms, so they would burn from the heat. Out of their ignorance they would suppose the idol had accepted them and eaten them from his hands. They used to offer to him children of their kings and the nobles of their community. The Children of Israel worshipped him more than once, following the Canaanites, the Ammonites, and the Moabites. Ba'l had four hundred and fifty attendants in the lands of Samaria, or in the city of Sarepta.

The image of Ba'l is found in the museum of antiquities in the Louvre palace in Paris, engraved on the face of stones. They depicted him in the form of a man with a helmet on his head containing two horns, and in his hand a whip. Perhaps this is his image among some of the nations that worshipped him. No image of him is found among the antiquities of Phoenician Carthage in Tunisia.

In His saying "and forsake the Best of Creators" the attribute of God is mentioned rather than His proper name, as an allusion to deriding the minds of those who worshipped Ba'l, that they abandoned the worship of the Lord who is characterized by the best and most perfect attributes, and worshipped an idol whose essence is hideous. It is as if he said: Do you call upon an idol, a repulsive thing that combines the two elements of weakness, namely created-ness and ugliness of form, and forsake the One who possesses the quality of creating and the most beautiful names?

The majority read "Ilyas" with a hamza of cutting at its beginning, considering the alif and lam part of the proper name, so they did not drop the hamza when they joined "inna" to it. Ibn 'Amir read it with a hamza of connection, dropping it in connected speech with "inna," considering the alif and lam as a letter, in order to indicate the original form. The original of the name is Yas, in observance of His saying "Peace be upon the family of Yasin."

The Arabs have many ways of pronouncing foreign names, because it is not from their language, so they vary its pronunciation in accordance with the patterns of their speech.

As for the sentence "God is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old": the majority read the name of majesty and what is conjoined to it in the nominative, so it is a subject, and the sentence is a fresh beginning, and the predicate is used to draw attention to the error of worshipping Ba'l. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read the name of majesty in the accusative as an explicative apposition to "the Best of Creators." The purpose of the explication is to add clarity, since the context is one of clarifying the basis of the religion. On both readings the speech is directed to remind them that among the foundations of their religion is that they have no lord but God, and this is the first foundation of religion. He is the Lord of their forefathers, for their forefathers did not worship other than God from the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, who is the first father, from the time their community became distinct from others. Or it is Ya'qub. God, exalted is He, said: "And Ibrahim enjoined this upon his sons, and so did Ya'qub: 'O my sons, indeed God has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims'" [al-Baqarah: 132]. The qualifier "of old" is to exclude their forefathers who lived in the time of their kings after Sulayman.

This report was mentioned to incite the abandonment of the worship of Ba'l, because human nature loves to follow the predecessors in good. Ilyas gathered those who were with him of his followers and devised a stratagem against the attendants of Ba'l, and he killed them to the last one, as a defense of the religion and as retribution for those whom Jezebel, wife of Ahab, had killed.

In Mafatih al-Ghayb: "The one titled al-Rashid the scribe said: if it had been said, 'Do you call upon Ba'l and call upon the Best of Creators,' it would give the impression that it is the best." That is, the statement of al-Rashid suggests that if the word "tad'un" had been used instead of "tadhar√un," it would have implied that it (Ba'l) is best. Al-Fakhr answered that the eloquence of the Qur'an is not for the sake of observing these rules but for the sake of the strength of its meanings and the excellence of its wording, end of quote.

This is an unconvincing answer, since there is no way to deny the fine effect of rhetorical embellishments after the requirements of eloquence have been fully met. Al-Sakkaki said: "The basis of beauty in all of that (i.e., the rhetorical embellishments mentioned) is that words should be followers of meanings, not that meanings should be followers of words; I mean, that they should not be forced." So if we grant that "tadharun" and "tad'un" are synonyms, there is no way to refute that choosing "tad'un" is more fitting.

The answer may therefore be given in the words of Sa'd Allah, the glossator of al-Baydawi, that paronomasia is among the embellishments, and it suits only speech issued in a context of contentment, not in a context of anger and dread. He means that the speech of Ilyas reported here is reported from a context of anger and dread, so verbal subtleties are not suitable to it, that is, with regard to the state of those addressed by it, because his speech is reported in Arabic in a manner suited to its source in the language of its speaker, and that is one of the subtleties of translation. This is a precise answer, though al-Khafaji contended against it with words that are unfitting; and if you reflect on it you will be certain of its soundness.

It has also been answered with something that requires denying the synonymy between the two verbs "tadharun" and "tad'un," on the grounds that the verb "yada'" is more specific: either because it indicates leaving something together with caring that it not be left, as Sa'd Allah said, or because the verb "yada'" indicates leaving something before knowledge, whereas the verb "yadhar" indicates leaving something after knowledge of it, as Sa'd Allah related from some of the imams, attributing it to al-Fakhr.

In my view, denying synonymy is the correct position, but not as Sa'd Allah said, nor as was reported from al-Fakhr. Rather, it is because the verb "yada'" is rarely used in the speech of the Arabs, and for this reason it does not occur in the Qur'an except in an irregular reading without a sound chain, unlike the verb "yadhar." There is no doubt that the reason for this is that the verb "yadhar" indicates leaving with aversion from what is left, unlike "yada'," which implies a temporary leaving. Al-Raghib's discussion of the two also points to the difference between them.

There are several other answers, but it is better to set them aside.

The meaning of "fa-kadhdhabuhu" (but they denied him) is that they did not obey him, out of flattery to their kings, who yielded to the desire of their idolatrous wives for the erection of temples to idols. When Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians and wife of Ahab, king of Israel, learned what Ilyas had done to the attendants of Ba'l in vengeance for those of Israel's righteous whom Jezebel had killed, she sent to Ilyas threatening him with death. He went out to a place called (Beersheba), then wandered through the land and asked God to take him to Himself. God commanded him to entrust prophethood after him to his companion Elisha. Then God took him to Himself, and no one knew his whereabouts.

In the book (Elijah) of the Jewish books it is said that God raised him to the heaven in a chariot drawn by horsemen, and that Elisha saw him ascending in it. For this reason some of the predecessors said: Ilyas is Idris, of whom God said: "Indeed, he was a truthful one, a prophet, and We raised him to a lofty place" [Maryam: 56]. It was also said that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud used to read "wa-inna Idris lamina al-mursalin" instead of "wa-inna Ilyas," and read "salamun 'ala Idrasin" as a dialectal form of Idris. What is in the Jewish books about his being raised does not imply that he is Idris, because the raising, if it is established, may recur, and 'Isa, peace be upon him, was also raised.

The meaning of "they will surely be brought forth" is that God will bring them forth for punishment. This was mentioned earlier in His saying: "Had it not been for the grace of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth" [al-Saffat: 57] in this surah.

Excepted from this are the sincere servants of God, who are those who followed Ilyas and helped him in killing the attendants of Ba'l. What was said about it was mentioned in His saying "except the sincere servants of God" earlier in this surah.

Likewise His saying "And We left for him a good remembrance among the later generations: Peace be upon the family of Yasin," to the end of the verse, has an earlier parallel.

As for His saying "the family of Yasin": it was said that by it is meant Ilyas alone, and he was referred to as Yasin because he was called by it. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: Perhaps the addition of alif and nun in their language has a meaning, and the mention of "family" is an intensifier, as in His saying "Cause the family of Pharaoh to enter the severest punishment" [Ghafir: 46], according to one of the two interpretations of it, and in His saying "We had already given the family of Ibrahim the Book and wisdom" [al-Nisa': 54].

It was also said that Yasin is the father of Ilyas. So the meaning is: Peace be upon Ilyas and his relatives from the family of his father.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "Il Yasin" with a hamza followed by an alif, considering them two words: "Il" and "Yasin." The rest read it with a hamza with kasra, without an alif after it, and with the lam sukun, considering it one word which is the name of Ilyas. It is written in all the mushafs in two pieces, "Il Yasin," and there is no conflict between this and the two readings, because "al" may be written separated from what follows it.

The more apparent view is that what is meant by "Āl Yāsīn" is his helpers who followed him and assisted him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The family of Muhammad is every pious person." These are the people of Mount Carmel (Jabal al-Karmil) whom Ilyas (Elijah) sought help from against the servants of Baal, so they obeyed him, came to his aid, and slaughtered the servants of Baal, as is described at length in the eighteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings. The meaning then is: "Peace be upon Ilyasin and his family," for if they attained this honor because they were his family, then he is more deserving of this honor.

So the word ba'l is applied to the male, and among them it is a symbol of the sun. Its counterpart is the word (Tanit), with two dotted letters, meaning the female. For them there was a idol called by the Phoenicians at Carthage (Tanit), and among them it is a symbol of the moon. Among the Phoenicians of the land of Phoenicia, the original homeland of the Canaanites, this idol is called (Ashtaroth). They depicted him in the form of a human with the head of a calf, with two horns, wearing a crown, seated on a throne with his hands outstretched as one who receives something. His image was of bronze, hollow inside, and they placed it upon a base of masonry like an oven. They would kindle fire in that oven until the bronze was heated, and they would bring offerings and place them on his arms, so they would burn from the heat. Out of their ignorance they would suppose the idol had accepted them and eaten them from his hands. They used to offer to him children of their kings and the nobles of their community. Ba'l had four hundred and fifty attendants in the lands of Samaria, or in the city of Sarepta.

Ibn 'Amir read it with a hamza of connection, dropping it in connected speech with "inna," considering the alif and lam as a letter, in order to indicate the original form. The original of the name is Yas, in observance of His saying "Peace be upon the family of Yasin."

The Arabs have many ways of pronouncing foreign names, because it is not from their language, so they vary its pronunciation in accordance with the patterns of their speech.

Ibn 'Amir read it with a hamza of connection, dropping it in connected speech with "inna," considering the alif and lam as a letter, in order to indicate the original form. The original of the name is Yas, in observance of His saying "Peace be upon the family of Yasin."

The Arabs have many ways of pronouncing foreign names, because it is not from their language, so they vary its pronunciation in accordance with the patterns of their speech.

As for the sentence "God is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old": the majority read the name of majesty and what is conjoined to it in the nominative, so it is a subject, and the sentence is a fresh beginning, and the predicate is used to draw attention to the error of worshipping Ba'l. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read the name of majesty in the accusative as an explicative apposition to "the Best of Creators." The purpose of the explication is to add clarity, since the context is one of clarifying the basis of the religion. On both readings the speech is directed to remind them that among the foundations of their religion is that they have no lord but God, and this is the first foundation of religion. He is the Lord of their forefathers, for their forefathers did not worship other than God from the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, who is the first father, from the time their community became distinct from others. Or it is Ya'qub. God, exalted is He, said: "And Ibrahim enjoined this upon his sons, and so did Ya'qub: 'O my sons, indeed God has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims'" [al-Baqarah: 132]. The qualifier "of old" is to exclude their forefathers who lived in the time of their kings after Sulayman.

This report was mentioned to incite the abandonment of the worship of Ba'l, because human nature loves to follow the predecessors in good. Ilyas gathered those who were with him of his followers and devised a stratagem against the attendants of Ba'l, and he killed them to the last one, as a defense of the religion and as retribution for those whom Jezebel, wife of Ahab, had killed.

In Mafatih al-Ghayb: "The one titled al-Rashid the scribe said: if it had been said, 'Do you call upon Ba'l and call upon the Best of Creators,' it would give the impression that it is the best." That is, the statement of al-Rashid suggests that if the word "tad'un" had been used instead of "tadhar√un," it would have implied that it (Ba'l) is best. Al-Fakhr answered that the eloquence of the Qur'an is not for the sake of observing these rules but for the sake of the strength of its meanings and the excellence of its wording, end of quote.

This is an unconvincing answer, since there is no way to deny the fine effect of rhetorical embellishments after the requirements of eloquence have been fully met. Al-Sakkaki said: "The basis of beauty in all of that (i.e., the rhetorical embellishments mentioned) is that words should be followers of meanings, not that meanings should be followers of words; I mean, that they should not be forced." So if we grant that "tadharun" and "tad'un" are synonyms, there is no way to refute that choosing "tad'un" is more fitting.

The answer may therefore be given in the words of Sa'd Allah, the glossator of al-Baydawi, that paronomasia is among the embellishments, and it suits only speech issued in a context of contentment, not in a context of anger and dread. He means that the speech of Ilyas reported here is reported from a context of anger and dread, so verbal subtleties are not suitable to it, that is, with regard to the state of those addressed by it, because his speech is reported in Arabic in a manner suited to its source in the language of its speaker, and that is one of the subtleties of translation. This is a precise answer, though al-Khafaji contended against it with words that are unfitting; and if you reflect on it you will be certain of its soundness.

It has also been answered with something that requires denying the synonymy between the two verbs "tadharun" and "tad'un," on the grounds that the verb "yada'" is more specific: either because it indicates leaving something together with caring that it not be left, as Sa'd Allah said, or because the verb "yada'" indicates leaving something before knowledge, whereas the verb "yadhar" indicates leaving something after knowledge of it, as Sa'd Allah related from some of the imams, attributing it to al-Fakhr.

In my view, denying synonymy is the correct position, but not as Sa'd Allah said, nor as was reported from al-Fakhr. Rather, it is because the verb "yada'" is rarely used in the speech of the Arabs, and for this reason it does not occur in the Qur'an except in an irregular reading without a sound chain, unlike the verb "yadhar." There is no doubt that the reason for this is that the verb "yadhar" indicates leaving with aversion from what is left, unlike "yada'," which implies a temporary leaving. Al-Raghib's discussion of the two also points to the difference between them.

There are several other answers, but it is better to set them aside.

The meaning of "fa-kadhdhabuhu" (but they denied him) is that they did not obey him, out of flattery to their kings, who yielded to the desire of their idolatrous wives for the erection of temples to idols. When Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians and wife of Ahab, king of Israel, learned what Ilyas had done to the attendants of Ba'l in vengeance for those of Israel's righteous whom Jezebel had killed, she sent to Ilyas threatening him with death. He went out to a place called (Beersheba), then wandered through the land and asked God to take him to Himself. God commanded him to entrust prophethood after him to his companion Elisha. Then God took him to Himself, and no one knew his whereabouts.

In the book (Elijah) of the Jewish books it is said that God raised him to the heaven in a chariot drawn by horsemen, and that Elisha saw him ascending in it. For this reason some of the predecessors said: Ilyas is Idris, of whom God said: "Indeed, he was a truthful one, a prophet, and We raised him to a lofty place" [Maryam: 56]. It was also said that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud used to read "wa-inna Idris lamina al-mursalin" instead of "wa-inna Ilyas," and read "salamun 'ala Idrasin" as a dialectal form of Idris. What is in the Jewish books about his being raised does not imply that he is Idris, because the raising, if it is established, may recur, and 'Isa, peace be upon him, was also raised.

The meaning of "they will surely be brought forth" is that God will bring them forth for punishment. This was mentioned earlier in His saying: "Had it not been for the grace of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth" [al-Saffat: 57] in this surah.

Excepted from this are the sincere servants of God, who are those who followed Ilyas and helped him in killing the attendants of Ba'l. What was said about it was mentioned in His saying "except the sincere servants of God" earlier in this surah.

Likewise His saying "And We left for him a good remembrance among the later generations: Peace be upon the family of Yasin," to the end of the verse, has an earlier parallel.

As for His saying "the family of Yasin": it was said that by it is meant Ilyas alone, and he was referred to as Yasin because he was called by it. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: Perhaps the addition of alif and nun in their language has a meaning, and the mention of "family" is an intensifier, as in His saying "Cause the family of Pharaoh to enter the severest punishment" [Ghafir: 46], according to one of the two interpretations of it, and in His saying "We had already given the family of Ibrahim the Book and wisdom" [al-Nisa': 54].

It was also said that Yasin is the father of Ilyas. So the meaning is: Peace be upon Ilyas and his relatives from the family of his father.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "Il Yasin" with a hamza followed by an alif, considering them two words: "Il" and "Yasin." The rest read it with a hamza with kasra, without an alif after it, and with the lam sukun, considering it one word which is the name of Ilyas. It is written in all the mushafs in two pieces, "Il Yasin," and there is no conflict between this and the two readings, because "al" may be written separated from what follows it.

The more apparent view is that what is meant by "Āl Yāsīn" is his helpers who followed him and assisted him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The family of Muhammad is every pious person." These are the people of Mount Carmel (Jabal al-Karmil) whom Ilyas (Elijah) sought help from against the servants of Baal, so they obeyed him, came to his aid, and slaughtered the servants of Baal, as is described at length in the eighteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings. The meaning then is: "Peace be upon Ilyasin and his family," for if they attained this honor because they were his family, then he is more deserving of this honor.

In the story of Ilyas there is an indication that the Messenger's duty is to convey the message, and it does not necessarily follow that he must witness the punishment of those who deny or their destruction, in response to the polytheists who said: ﴿When will this victory be, if you are truthful?﴾ [As-Sajdah: 28]. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised, My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people. And indeed, We are able to show you that which We promise them."﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 93–95]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whether We show you part of what We promise them or We take you in death, to Us they will return﴾ [Ghafir: 77]. And in the other verse: ﴿...and to Us they will return.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 133–136:

Page 171

﴿And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When We saved him and his family entirely,﴾ ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ This is the second of the prophets whom the comparison (al-tanzir) gathered in this verse. Lot was a messenger to the towns in which he dwelt, so he was a messenger without a sharia of his own, except that he came forbidding the people among whom he was residing from indecency (al-fahisha), and that prohibition had not been preceded in the sharia of Ibrahim.

And ﴿idh﴾ (when) is an adverbial clause (zarf) related to "the messengers." The meaning is: at the time that God saved him and destroyed his people, he was standing in the mission from God, the Exalted, speaking what God had commanded him. The time of his salvation was specifically made the adverbial frame for his being among the messengers because that time was a setting for the circumstances indicating his mission, since those circumstances resemble the circumstances of the messengers before and after him. The story of Lot has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am and in Surat al-A'raf.

And "the old woman" is Lot's wife. Her account has already been mentioned, and its parallel has already been mentioned in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 137–138:

﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ ﴿and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ The address is to the Quraysh, to whom these narratives were brought as an admonition.

Al-murur (passing by) is the traveler's passing beyond something he leaves behind in his journey. What is meant here is their passing during travel. The people of Makkah, when they journeyed for trade to al-Sham, would pass through the lands of Palestine, and so they would pass by the land of Lut on the shore of the Dead Sea, called Buhayrat Lut (the Lake of Lut). The transitive use of al-murur with the preposition (ʿalā) specifies that the pronoun in the genitive is, by implicit construction, "ʿalā arḍihim" (over their land), as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿or like the one who passed by a town﴾.

It is said: marra ʿalayhi and marra bihi. Its transitivity with the preposition (ʿalā) conveys the passing as more firmly established than its transitivity with (bi). They would pass by the dwellings of Lut at its side, because their towns had been submerged by the Dead Sea, while its traces remain beneath the water.

Al-muṣbiḥ (the one who enters the time of morning) means one who enters the period of morning. They pass by their dwellings sometimes in the morning and sometimes at night, according to the estimated pace of travel at the beginning and end of the day, because the Quraysh's journey to al-Sham occurred in the summer, and travel was in the early morning, in the evening, and by night. The bāʾ in ﴿wa-bil-layli﴾ is for time (ẓarfiyyah).

The report in the words ﴿And indeed, you pass by them﴾ is used for awakening and reflection, not for the literal sense of informing. Its emphasis by the particle of emphasis and by the lām of emphasis is an emphasis on the meaning for which it is used, like His saying ﴿And indeed it is on a road still standing﴾ [al-Hijr: 76] in Surat al-Hijr.

The subsequent clause introduced by the fāʾ is an interrogation of denial concerning their lack of insight into what those traces indicate of the wrath of God that befell them, and of the cause of that, which is the denial of the Messenger of God, Lut.

We have already indicated the reason for singling out the story of Lut together with the five narratives at the beginning of the discussion of the story of Nuh. It exceeds those narratives in that it involves witnessing the traces of his people, who denied and persisted in disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 139–144:

﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When he fled to the laden ship.﴾ ﴿Then he drew lots and was among the losers.﴾ ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿And had he not been of those who glorify Allah.﴾ ﴿He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾

Yunus is Ibn Matta, and his name in Hebrew is (Yunan ibn Amitay). He was from the people of Palestine and was one of the prophets of the Children of Israel. Allah sent him to the people of (Nineveh). Nineveh was a great city in the lands of the Assyrians, and among them were captives of the Children of Israel who were in the hands of the Assyrians, numbering about one hundred thousand, who remained after (Daniel). Yunus lived at the beginning of the eighth century BC. His mention and the mention of his people have already preceded in Surat al-An'am and Surat Yunus.

And (idh) is an adverbial clause related to "al-mursalin" (the messengers). His mission was specified by the time when he fled to the ship because that act of his occurred when Allah commanded him to go to Nineveh to convey to the Children of Israel that Allah was angry with them because they had deviated from their law.

When Allah revealed this to him, the matter weighed heavily upon him, so he left his land and headed for the port of (Jaffa) intending to go to the city of (Tarshish), which is on the Tartusi coast on the shore of the lands of al-Sham. The sea became so turbulent that the people of the ship were forced to lighten the number of its passengers, so they cast lots over whom they should throw from their ship into the sea. Yunus was among those whose lot came out for casting into the sea, and a great fish swallowed him. His story is related in Surat al-Anbiya'. Since his fleeing from the burden of the mission coincided with his being sent, he was described as being "among the messengers."

"Abaqa" (fled) has the verbal noun iba'q, with a kasra on the hamza and a light ba', and it means a slave fleeing from his master. Its verb is like daraba and sami'a.

What is meant here is that Yunus fled from the city in which he had been given the revelation, heading for another city, seeking to escape from conveying Allah's message to the people of Nineveh. Perhaps he feared their might and doubted his own patience with their anticipated harm, since they were from the Children of Israel under Assyrian protection.

Thus the verb abaqa here is a metaphorical image (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), likening his departure from the city in which his Lord had charged him with the message to the flight of a slave from his master who had assigned him a task, in distancing himself from the burden of his Lord.

"Al-fulk al-mashhun" means the ship filled with passengers. Its meaning was discussed in the story of Nuh.

"Sahama" means he cast lots. It is derived from the noun for an arrow, because they used to draw lots with arrows, which are shafts of arrows, also called al-azlam.

The connective "fasahama" (then he drew lots) indicates omitted clauses, whose estimated form is: then the sea became turbulent and the passengers feared drowning, so he drew lots. This is similar to the connective in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63]. What is mentioned in the Book of Jonah among the books of the Jews is that some of them said to others: come, let us cast lots so that we may know who is the cause of this calamity, and they cast lots and it fell upon Yunus. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih that the lot came out upon Yunus three times.

The custom of casting lots during sea voyages was practiced among the ancients when the ship became heavy due to an abundance of passengers or a large amount of cargo. In this regard is the story of the stratagem mentioned by al-Safadi in his commentary on al-Ta'iyya (al-Tughra'iyya): some companions claimed that a boat containing Muslims and disbelievers

صفحة ١٧٤
was about to sink, and they wanted to throw some of them into the sea so that the boat would be lightened, some would be saved, and the boat would survive. They said: "We will draw lots, and whoever the lot falls upon, we will throw him." The captain of the boat looked at them while they were sitting in this manner and said: "This is not a satisfactory judgment; rather, we count the group, and whoever is ninth, we will throw him." They agreed to this, and he kept counting them and throwing the ninth, then the ninth, until he threw the disbelievers and the Muslims were saved. This is the diagram of that (and he drew a circle with red marks and black marks; the red are for the Muslims, and the counting begins from them, toward the north). He said: "I mentioned it to Nur al-Din 'Ali ibn Isma'il al-Safadi, and it pleased him, and he said: 'How can I preserve this arrangement?' I said to him: 'The rule in this is to make its unpointed letters represent the disbelievers and its pointed letters represent the Muslims,' and it is this verse:

Allah decides with every ease, and provides for the guest wherever they may be.
End. Casting lots was a method among the methods of judgment when the truth was unclear or when a number was equal in entitlement to something. It was mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran at His saying, ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would be entrusted with Maryam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 44], and it is a persuasive method by which humans resorted to resolve disputes, claiming that it indicates the will of Allah, the Exalted, among religious nations, or the will of idols among nations that worship idols, in distinguishing the rightful party in a dispute.

Perhaps it was among the inventions of priests and custodians of idols. When it spread among humans, the laws approved it because it cut off disputes and fighting. But when the true laws approved it, they were moderate in its use, such that it is not resorted to except when there is equality in right and absence of a deciding factor that influences the type of matter in dispute; thus it is among the remnants of superstitions. The Islamic law has restricted its application to the least that it requires, such as designating one of equal shares to one of the sharers when they dispute over one of them. Ibn Rushd said in al-Muqaddimat: "Casting lots was only made to console the hearts of the sharers, and its origin is established in the Book of Allah in His saying regarding the story of Yunus, ﴿Then he drew lots and was among the losers﴾."

In my view: there is no evidence in the verse for the legitimacy of casting lots in distinguishing between equals, because it does not narrate a valid law that existed before Islam, since the religion of the people of the ship who conducted the lottery upon Yunus is not known. Moreover, the matter upon which the lottery was conducted is agreed upon by the Muslims to be one in which lottery does not apply.

صفحة ١٧٥
Hence, even if it were established that this was a law for those before us, it has been abrogated by the consensus of the scholars of our community.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Casting lots to throw a human being into the sea is not permissible, so how about a Muslim? It is not permissible to kill or throw into fire or sea someone who is disobedient; rather, the prescribed punishments and discretionary penalties apply to him according to the measure of his offense. Some people thought that when the sea became turbulent upon a people and they were compelled to lighten the ship, lots should be drawn among them so that some would be cast out for lightening; this is corrupt. The ship is not lightened by throwing away some men; rather, that applies to goods, and they should be patient with the decree of Allah.

In the law of those before us, casting lots was permissible in everything in general. In our law, casting lots came specifically in three situations:

The first: "When the Prophet ﷺ intended a journey, he cast lots among his wives, and whichever one's lot came out, he took her with him."

The second: "It was reported to the Prophet ﷺ that a man freed six slaves during his terminal illness, having no property other than them, so he cast lots between two of them (which equaled one-third) and freed four."

The third: "Two men disputed before him concerning inheritances that had become obscure, and he said: 'Go and seek the truth, and draw lots, and let each of you absolve the other.'"

Our scholars differed about casting lots among wives when going on a military expedition, on two views: the correct of them is that lots are cast, and this is the view of most jurists of the major cities, because it is not possible to take all of them, and choosing one of them is favoritism, so nothing remains but lots.

Al-Qarafi said in al-Furuq (240): Whenever the benefit or right is specified in one direction, lots are not permissible, because in lots there is the loss of right; but whenever rights or benefits are equal, this is the place of lots to dispel grudges. Thus it is legislated among caliphs when they are equal in fitness for governance, among imams, among muezzins when they are equal, precedence to the first row in crowding, washing the dead when relatives crowd and are equal, among custodians (female caretakers), among wives in travel, in division, among litigants before judges, in the freeing of slaves when someone bequeathed their freedom during illness and did not burden them with the third. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hanbal. Abu Hanifa said: lots are not permissible [between them]; one third of each is freed and they are made to work to pay their value, and he agreed regarding the value of land. He said: "The truth in my view is that it applies in every difficult matter." End.

I say: In the Sahih, from Umm al-'Ala al-Ansariyya, that when the Ansar cast lots for the housing of the Muhajirun, the lot fell to 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, the hadith [follows].

Al-Jassas said: Some ignorant people argued with this verse for the obligation of lots among slaves a sick man frees. This is an oversight on his part, because Yunus was cast into the sea by lot, and that is not permissible according to any of the jurists, just as lots are not permissible in killing the one upon whom it falls or in taking his property.
