Al-Idhaḥ: making a person slippery, i.e., unsteady, unable to keep both feet firm; here it is a metaphor for loss and being defeated.

Al-Iltiqam: swallowing. The fish that swallowed him: a great fish that swallows things without biting with its teeth; it is said that it is the fish called "balyn" in European languages.

Al-Mulim: an active participle of alama, when one does something for which people blame him, since he made them blamers, so he blamed them upon himself.

His drowning was in the sea called the Sea of Rome, which we call the White Mediterranean Sea, and it was not in the River Tigris as some commentators erred in saying.

صفحة ١٧٧
He was among those who glorify (Allah) by his saying: ﴿There is no deity except You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87], as in Surat al-Anbiya'. So Allah saved him because of his glorification and repentance, and the fish cast him out from its belly onto dry land after he had remained in the belly of the fish for three nights. It was said: a day and a night, and it was said: a few hours.

The meaning of His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is perpetuity, in that Allah would cause the fish to die when it swallowed him and keep both of them at the bottom of the sea; or that the fish would be caught upon a rock in the sea or the like, so it would not float upon the water until Yunus is resurrected on the Day of Resurrection from the bottom of the sea.

﴿So We cast him onto the open shore while he was ill﴾ ﴿and caused a gourd plant to grow over him﴾. The fa' here is *fasīḥa* (the "explanatory fa'"), because it reveals an implied statement indicated by His words, "Had he not been one of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly." The implied meaning is: he glorified his Lord in the belly of the fish, saying, "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers." Allah answered him and saved him, as in Surah al-Anbiya'. The meaning is: the fish spewed him out and vomited him, and the waves carried him to the shore.

*Al-nabdh* means throwing away. His being cast out is attributed to Allah, because it was Allah who subjected the fish to expel him from its belly onto a shore with no trees on it.

*Al-'arā'* is the open land where there are no trees and nothing covering it.

Yunus had come out of the fish's belly ill, because the fish's intestines harmed his skin through their movement around him. He had removed his clothes when it was intended to throw him into the sea, so that he could be light for swimming. Perhaps Allah afflicted the fish with something like a faint, so that the movement of its digestion was suspended to some extent, and it remained like one numbed, so that its intestines would not harm Yunus's flesh.

Allah caused a gourd plant to grow for him, to shade him and cover him. *Al-yaqtīn* is the pumpkin (*al-dubbā'*); it has abundant leaves, and its branches climb up over elevated things. Apparently the branches of the gourd plant climbed over the body of Yunus, covering and shading him. The gourd was chosen for him so that he could feed on its produce, and his body could recover, as a kindness from his Lord toward him after He had brought upon him a calamity for his correction. It is the way of the Lord with His servants that He follows hardship with ease.

This was an event the like of which was not known to have happened to other messengers. Because of it the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not fitting for anyone to say, 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta,'" meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself, since it is not plausible that he meant anyone else, as no one but the prophets would think to say this.

The meaning is the negation of superiority in the description of prophethood; that is, no one should suppose that Yunus's act strips him of prophethood.

This is like his (ﷺ) saying: "Do not prefer one prophet over another," meaning in the essence of prophethood, not in its degrees, for Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others; among them are those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in degrees﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253], and He said: "﴿And We certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra': 55]."

Know that the purpose of mentioning Yunus here is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the burden of the message he bears, and that this burden had weighed upon the messengers before him. Thus the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) is made manifest in his patience with it, his not complaining, and his informing all people that he is commanded by Allah, the Exalted, to persist in calling to the religion. The polytheists used to blame him for his insistence upon them and for calling them at various times and in various circumstances, saying: "Do not come to our gatherings; whoever comes to you from among us, listen to him," as 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. So the narration of the story of Yunus has an effect of admonition, warning against falling into what he fell into of the anger of his Lord. Do you not see the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was suppressing his grief﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] ﴿Had it not been that a blessing from his Lord had reached him, he would have been cast onto the open shore while he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Qalam: 49].

And let people know that when Allah chooses someone for the message, He does not grant him leave to slacken in it, nor does He abrogate His command to him in that, because Allah knows best where He places His messages.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 147–148:

﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.﴾ ﴿So they believed, and We let them enjoy for a time.﴾ The apparent order of mention, with the sending mentioned after the rescue from the whale, indicates that it is a repetition of his sending.

This is what is implied by what is in the Book of Jonah among the books of the Jews, since it occurs in chapter three: "Then the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying: Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee."

The people sent to are the Jews residing in Nineveh while under the captivity of the Assyrians, as was mentioned earlier. The apparent meaning is that when a messenger is sent to a people mixed with others, his message encompasses all of that mixture, because singling out a part for the call would amount to affirming the disbelief of the rest. For this reason, when God sent Moses (peace be upon him) to deliver the Children of Israel, he called Pharaoh and his people to abandon the worship of idols. Accordingly, it is possible that those estimated at a hundred thousand are the Jews, and that those joined by His saying "or more" are the rest of the inhabitants of Nineveh. It is mentioned in the Book of Jonah that when Jonah's call reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, removed his robe, put on sackcloth, and commanded the people of his city to repent and believe, etc. It is not mentioned that Jonah called anyone other than the people of Nineveh from the lands of Assyria, despite their vastness.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the words of God, the Exalted, ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾, and he said: 'Twenty thousand.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith."

Thus the particle (aw, "or") in His saying "or more" carries the meaning of (bal, "rather") according to the view of the Kufans, and the preference of al-Farra', Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, Ibn Jinni and Ibn Burhan. They cited the verse of Jarir:

"What do you think of a family you have wearied of? I could not count their number except by calculation.
They were eighty, or they increased by eight, were it not for your hope, you would have killed my children."

The Basrans do not permit this except under two conditions: that it be preceded by a negation or a prohibition, and that the governing verb be repeated. Some of them interpreted this verse as meaning that (aw) is for giving choice, the sense being: when the observer sees them, he may choose between saying: they are a hundred thousand, or saying: they are more.

What supports this is that the clause introduced by (aw) is not a single word but a complete statement, which makes it fitting for the particle to be one of retraction (idrab).

The fa' in "So they believed" indicates a customary sequence, because when Jonah was sent to them and called them, they refused at first, so he informed them of a threat of their destruction after forty days; then they feared and believed, as His saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿Why was there not a city that believed and its faith benefited it, except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time.﴾ [Yunus: 98].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 149:

﴿So ask them: "For your Lord are the daughters, and for them the sons?"﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of what preceded: the rebuke of the polytheists, the nullification of their claims, and the striking of parables for them through their counterparts among the nations. Following this, God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to nullify what the polytheists attributed to God of offspring.

The pronoun of absence in His words "fastaftihim" (so ask them) refers to an unmentioned antecedent known from the context, like its previous counterpart in His words ﴿So ask them: "Are they stronger in creation, or those whom We created?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 11]. The intended meaning is mockery of them through the form of a question, since they say that God has begotten children, while they divide in an unjust division (qisma diza), for they assigned to God the daughters while they themselves desire sons and dislike females, so they assigned to God what they dislike.

In this statement they have come with three kinds of disbelief:

First: they affirmed corporeality (tajsim) for God, because begetting is among the attributes of bodies.

Second: preferring themselves with the best and assigning to God the least. God the Exalted said: ﴿When one of them is given good news of what he has attributed to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 17]

Third: they ascribed the attribute of femininity to the angels brought near (al-mala'ika al-muqarrabin), while they themselves are shamed by the fathers of females. For this reason God the Exalted repeated these types of their disbelief in His Book more than once.

Page 181

The clause ﴿For your Lord are the daughters﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the clause "fastaftihim" (so ask them). The pronoun in "li-rabbika" (for your Lord) is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is a report of the question in meaning (hikaya li-l-istifta' bi-l-ma'na), because when he asks them, he would say: "For your Lord are the daughters?" and similarly the pronoun in "wa-lahum" (and for them) is reported in meaning, because he would only say to them: "And for you are the sons." This manner of transposition occurs in reporting speech and what is similar to it, that which carries the sense of speech, such as questioning (al-istifta').

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 150:

﴿Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?﴾ "Am" (أمْ) here is munqati'ah (disjunctive, "am" in the sense of) bi-ma'na "bal" (rather, "but"), and it never loses the meaning of interrogation (al-istifham). So the speech after it is understood with an implied interrogative hamzah (hamzat al-istifham), meaning: "Rather, did We create the angels female?"

The pronoun in "khalaqna" (We created) is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (al-ghaybah) to the first person (al-takallum). It is as if, when He addresses them in the form of a question, He says to them: "Or did He create the angels..." as has preceded. The interrogation is both a denial (inkari) and an expression of wonder (ta'jibi) at their audacity and their saying without knowledge.

The clause "wa-hum shahidun" (while they were witnesses) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) and serves as a restriction on the denial. That is, they were present when We created the angels, and so they witnessed the femaleness of the angels; for this could only be established for beings like them through direct witnessing, since they have no means of knowing it except by witnessing. As for the possibility that this knowledge came through a decisive report (al-khabar al-qati'), that is what He will negate with His words: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [as-Saffat: 156]. This is because the femaleness of the angels is not impossible, but it is a claim without evidence.

The pronoun in "wa-hum shahidun" is reported in meaning in the questioning. The original form is "wa-antum shahidun" (and you were witnesses), as has preceded just above.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 151–152:

﴿Surely it is from their own falsehood that they say﴾ ﴿"God has begotten." And indeed they are liars.﴾ This is an escalation in denouncing their ignorance: that they say what is impossible, let alone saying it without any proof. For this reason He called it "falsehood" (ifk). The sentence is an interjection (mu'taridah) placed between the sentences of the questioning (istifta').

Page 182

And "ala" (alā) is a particle of alerting, for the purpose of emphasizing the report. Al-ifk means lying, i.e., their saying this is part of their falsehoods.
For this reason He followed it with the conjunctive clause "and indeed they are liars," emphasized with "inna" (indeed) and the lam (the emphatic lam), meaning: lying is their habit in this matter and in other than it of their nonsense. Therefore the sentence is not a reinforcement of His words "from their falsehood," how could it be, since it is conjoined (ma'tufah) to it?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 153–157:

﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ ﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ This is a return to the *istifta'* (questioning, inquiry). For this reason it is not joined by a conjunction, because between it and what precedes it there is complete connection (*kamal al-ittisal*). The meaning is: "And say to them: 'Has He chosen daughters?'"

The majority of reciters read *Asṭafā* with an open *hamzat al-qat'* (the hamza that is always pronounced), which is the interrogative hamza. The connecting hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*) in the verb is elided because of continuity of speech. Abu Ja'far read it with a *hamzat al-wasl*, on the understanding that the interrogative hamza is elided.

The speech is a progressive escalation in ignorance-exposure (*irtiqa' fi al-tajhil*). That is: even if we grant that Allah has taken a son, then why did He choose daughters over sons? That is, He chose for Himself daughters rather than sons, while sons are more excellent in your estimation?

The clause ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ is an inclusive substitute (*badal ishtimal*) for the clause ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾, because denying that He chose daughters entails the absence of proof for their judgment. So ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ replaces the denial of their claim that Allah chose daughters for Himself.

Their words "ma lakum" (*ma*) is an interrogative of essence (*istifham 'an dhat*), and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), while "lakum" is the predicate (*khabar*).

The meaning is: "What has happened to you?" This is vague, and for this reason the expression "ma laka" and similar ones in interrogation must be followed by a circumstantial clause (*jumlat hal*) that clarifies the action being asked about, such as ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not speak?﴾ [al-Saffat: 92] and ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph?﴾ [Yusuf: 11]. Here it is clarified by what is contained in the interrogative clause ﴿How do you judge?﴾. "Kayfa" is an interrogative noun about the state (*hal*), and it stands in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the pronoun in "tahkumun." It is placed first in order to preserve the front position of the interrogative.

The clause "tahkumun" is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the pronoun in "lakum" in the verse "ma lakum." Thus two interrogations arise: one concerning the thing that happened to them, so that they made this judgment; and second, concerning the state they were in when this false judgment was reported. This is an abridgment by omission (*ijaz hadhf*), since the implied sense is: "What is the matter with you that you judge this judgment? How do you judge it?" The object of "tahkumun" is omitted because the two interrogations indicate that what they judged is objectionable and deserves wonder. Thus both interrogations are denunciation and expression of astonishment.

On this he based the denunciatory interrogation about their not remembering, that is, the use of their *dhikr* (with a *dhamma* on the *dhal*, meaning intellect). That is: their failure to understand what issues from their judgment is to be rejected.

﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ is a transitional change of direction (*idrab intiqali*). So "am" here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*), in the sense of "bal" (rather), which conveys both the nullifying change of direction (*idrab ibtali*) and the transitional change of direction.

*Sultan* means proof. *Mubin* means that which clarifies the truth. The interrogation required by "am" after it is also denunciatory. The meaning is: "You have no clear authority for what you said, namely that the angels are daughters of Allah."

Because it is denied that they have any proof for what they say, they are addressed with the command to bring a Book supporting it, if they are truthful about what they claim. If they do not bring a book supporting it, then they are not truthful.

The command in "fa'tu" is a command of incapacitation (*amr ta'jiz*), like His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23].

The attribution of "kitab" to them is in the sense of the passive object: a book sent to you. Their debate, with these varied sentences, is arranged according to the rule of disputation (*qanun al-munazara*). He began with what resembles an inquiry about two claims: the claim that the angels are daughters of Allah, and the claim that the angels are females, with His saying: ﴿So ask them: "Has your Lord daughters while they have sons, or did We create the angels as females?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 149].

[Page 184]

Then, since their explanation of this was known from their repeated statements, they were treated as one who answers, [saying that] the angels are daughters of Allah and that the angels are females. What was intended by their inquiry was the form of inquiry, to press them and to move from the position of questioning to the position of demanding proof for their claim. This transition begins from His saying ﴿while they were witnesses﴾ [al-Saffat: 150], which is the active participle of *shahida*, meaning to be present and to see. Then comes His saying ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ ﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ He presented them with a choice between having relied on the proof of direct observation, or on some other proof. Here the latter is required, because the report must be one whose truth is certain, and there is no way to that except from Allah, the Exalted, since no other way exists to establish such a claim. Thus the proof of observation is ruled out necessarily, and the proof of reason and reflection is also ruled out, since no rational proof indicates that the angels are females or that they are males.

When it became clear that rational proof is not what is being posited here, the discussion with them was restricted to the proof of revelation (*dalil al-sam'*), which is the true report, because the sources of knowledge for created beings are limited to these three proofs. Sense perception was indicated by ﴿while they were witnesses﴾, and the proofs of reason and revelation by ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾. Then He based on this ﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful﴾, which is the proof of revelation. By this derivation He removed the possibility of the proof of reason, since its absence is certain, there being no path to it. The proof of revelation is restricted to being from Allah, as you know, since no one knows what is in the unseen of Allah except Him.

Then they were addressed with the command of incapacitation, to bring a book, that is, any book that came to them from Allah. He specified this for them because they believed it impossible for a messenger to come from Allah, and impossible for Allah to speak to any of His creation. This is called *mu'arada* (counter-supposition). It was inserted in the middle of the argument against them, and not placed together with the report of their claim, so that the final point of the disputation with them would be the proof that sweeps away everything they had built: His saying ﴿Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ This is among the excellent weaves that combine the style of disputation, the style of admonition, and the style of instruction.

The majority read *tadhakkarun* with a shadda on the *dhal*, on the basis that its original form is *tatadhakkarun*, and one of the two *ta*'s was assimilated (*idgham*) into the *dal* after being changed into a *dhal*, because their points of articulation are close. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim, and Khalaf, read it with a light *dhal*, on the basis that one of the two *ta*'s was deleted for ease of pronunciation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 153–157:

﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ ﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ This is a return to the *istifta'* (questioning, inquiry). For this reason it is not joined by a conjunction, because between it and what precedes it there is complete connection (*kamal al-ittisal*). The meaning is: "And say to them: 'Has He chosen daughters?'"

The majority of reciters read *Asṭafā* with an open *hamzat al-qat'* (the hamza that is always pronounced), which is the interrogative hamza. The connecting hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*) in the verb is elided because of continuity of speech. Abu Ja'far read it with a *hamzat al-wasl*, on the understanding that the interrogative hamza is elided.

The speech is a progressive escalation in ignorance-exposure (*irtiqa' fi al-tajhil*). That is: even if we grant that Allah has taken a son, then why did He choose daughters over sons? That is, He chose for Himself daughters rather than sons, while sons are more excellent in your estimation?

The clause ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ is an inclusive substitute (*badal ishtimal*) for the clause ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾, because denying that He chose daughters entails the absence of proof for their judgment. So ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ replaces the denial of their claim that Allah chose daughters for Himself.

Their words "ma lakum" (*ma*) is an interrogative of essence (*istifham 'an dhat*), and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), while "lakum" is the predicate (*khabar*).

The meaning is: "What has happened to you?" This is vague, and for this reason the expression "ma laka" and similar ones in interrogation must be followed by a circumstantial clause (*jumlat hal*) that clarifies the action being asked about, such as ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not speak?﴾ [al-Saffat: 92] and ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph?﴾ [Yusuf: 11]. Here it is clarified by what is contained in the interrogative clause ﴿How do you judge?﴾. "Kayfa" is an interrogative noun about the state (*hal*), and it stands in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the pronoun in "tahkumun." It is placed first in order to preserve the front position of the interrogative.

The clause "tahkumun" is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the pronoun in "lakum" in the verse "ma lakum." Thus two interrogations arise: one concerning the thing that happened to them, so that they made this judgment; and second, concerning the state they were in when this false judgment was reported. This is an abridgment by omission (*ijaz hadhf*), since the implied sense is: "What is the matter with you that you judge this judgment? How do you judge it?" The object of "tahkumun" is omitted because the two interrogations indicate that what they judged is objectionable and deserves wonder. Thus both interrogations are denunciation and expression of astonishment.

On this he based the denunciatory interrogation about their not remembering, that is, the use of their *dhikr* (with a *dhamma* on the *dhal*, meaning intellect). That is: their failure to understand what issues from their judgment is to be rejected.

﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ is a transitional change of direction (*idrab intiqali*). So "am" here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*), in the sense of "bal" (rather), which conveys both the nullifying change of direction (*idrab ibtali*) and the transitional change of direction.

*Sultan* means proof. *Mubin* means that which clarifies the truth. The interrogation required by "am" after it is also denunciatory. The meaning is: "You have no clear authority for what you said, namely that the angels are daughters of Allah."

Because it is denied that they have any proof for what they say, they are addressed with the command to bring a Book supporting it, if they are truthful about what they claim. If they do not bring a book supporting it, then they are not truthful.

The command in "fa'tu" is a command of incapacitation (*amr ta'jiz*), like His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23].

The attribution of "kitab" to them is in the sense of the passive object: a book sent to you. Their debate, with these varied sentences, is arranged according to the rule of disputation (*qanun al-munazara*). He began with what resembles an inquiry about two claims: the claim that the angels are daughters of Allah, and the claim that the angels are females, with His saying: ﴿So ask them: "Has your Lord daughters while they have sons, or did We create the angels as females?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 149].

[Page 184]

Then, since their explanation of this was known from their repeated statements, they were treated as one who answers, [saying that] the angels are daughters of Allah and that the angels are females. What was intended by their inquiry was the form of inquiry, to press them and to move from the position of questioning to the position of demanding proof for their claim. This transition begins from His saying ﴿while they were witnesses﴾ [al-Saffat: 150], which is the active participle of *shahida*, meaning to be present and to see. Then comes His saying ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ ﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ He presented them with a choice between having relied on the proof of direct observation, or on some other proof. Here the latter is required, because the report must be one whose truth is certain, and there is no way to that except from Allah, the Exalted, since no other way exists to establish such a claim. Thus the proof of observation is ruled out necessarily, and the proof of reason and reflection is also ruled out, since no rational proof indicates that the angels are females or that they are males.

When it became clear that rational proof is not what is being posited here, the discussion with them was restricted to the proof of revelation (*dalil al-sam'*), which is the true report, because the sources of knowledge for created beings are limited to these three proofs. Sense perception was indicated by ﴿while they were witnesses﴾, and the proofs of reason and revelation by ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾. Then He based on this ﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful﴾, which is the proof of revelation. By this derivation He removed the possibility of the proof of reason, since its absence is certain, there being no path to it. The proof of revelation is restricted to being from Allah, as you know, since no one knows what is in the unseen of Allah except Him.

Then they were addressed with the command of incapacitation, to bring a book, that is, any book that came to them from Allah. He specified this for them because they believed it impossible for a messenger to come from Allah, and impossible for Allah to speak to any of His creation. Thus the proof that was posited on the side of revelation was restricted to being a report from Allah that a book would be sent down to them from heaven, because they accepted that possibility, as in their saying: ﴿And we will not believe in your ascension until you send down to us a book we can read.﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. But they would not be able to bring a book.

The mention of the word "kitabikum" is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, because the expected form would be "fa'tu bihi" (bring it), that is, the clear authority, for it cannot mean anything but a book from Allah.

The attribution of "kitab" to their pronoun is from the attribution of what has the sense of a verbal noun to what has the sense of the object, by way of ellipsis and conveyance (*al-hadhf wa al-iṣal*). The implied sense is: "a book to you," because the root of writing does not transitively govern the addressee by itself, but through the preposition "ila" (to).

Therefore, their silencing has clearly been made evident through this debate conducted according to rational rules. For this reason they became like those who admit that they have no proof for what they claimed. So the questioner moved from the position of objection in the debate to turning it into an argument drawn as an inference from their silencing. That is His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own falsehood that they say, "Allah has begotten," and indeed they are liars.﴾ [al-Saffat: 151], which comes as a parenthetical interjection (*mu'taridan*) between the presentation of the proof and its alternatives.

As for His saying ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾, it is in the position of a concession (*taslim*) within the debate, as you know from what was said about it. This is called *mu'arada* (counter-supposition). It was inserted in the middle of the argument against them, and not placed together with the report of their claim, so that the final point of the disputation with them would be the proof that sweeps away everything they had built: His saying ﴿Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾ This is among the excellent weaves that combine the style of disputation, the style of admonition, and the style of instruction.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim, and Khalaf, read it with a light *dhal*, on the basis that one of the two *ta*'s was deleted for ease of pronunciation.

[Page 186]

﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a lineage﴾. This is coordinated with the clause "they say" (*layaqulun*), meaning that they embellished their statement, "God has begotten [a son]." So they made between God and the jinn a lineage through that begetting. That is, they explained how that begetting came about, by making it a lineage between God Most High and the jinn.

The *jinnah* is a group of the jinn. The feminine form of the word follows the meaning of "group," as in the feminine of *rajlah*, a band of men. This is because the polytheists claimed that the angels were daughters of God, from among the nobles of the jinn, that is, from a group of jinn women who were among the jinn's nobility. This was mentioned in His words: ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:184) in Surat al-A'raf.

*Nasab* (lineage) is kinship, whether vertical (ancestral) or horizontal (by alliance), that is, from the sides. The statement involves an elided noun, meaning "those who have a lineage with God," and this is the lineage of prophethood, since they claimed the angels were daughters of God Most High. That is, they made for God a lineage with the jinn and for the jinn a lineage with God.

His words ﴿between Him and the jinn﴾ may be a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) modifying "lineage," meaning "existing between Him and the jinn." That is, His lineage, namely His offspring, glorified be He, arises from between Him and the jinn. It may also be connected to "they made," meaning "they made, in the joining between Him and the jinn, a lineage for Him." That is, they made from that a lineage that is born to Him. So His words ﴿between Him and the jinn a lineage﴾ are like your saying, "Between so-and-so and so-and-so are sons," meaning he has sons from her and she has sons from him. This meaning is what those who interpreted it as "they made the jinn in-laws of God Most High" intended. Their explanation of *nasab* as *musaharah* (affinity by marriage) is an interpretation of meaning, not a claim that *nasab* is used for *musaharah*, as many have supposed. This usage is not found in the lexicographical dictionaries, so do not be deceived by it.

Because they did not penetrate the meaning of the verse, some have held that the "jinnah" means the angels, that is, they made between God and the angels the relation of fatherhood and sonship. This is a corrupt interpretation, because it would make His words ﴿and they made between Him and the jinnah a lineage﴾ a repetition of what came earlier, His words ﴿Surely they say out of their own lie, "God has begotten"﴾ (As-Saffat 37:151), and His words ﴿Did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ (As-Saffat 37:150).

As for those who held that the "jinnah" means the origin of the jinn, which is Satan, and that the meaning of the verse is that they made God a relative of Satan by the relation of brotherhood, exalted is God above that. Moreover, this points to the claim of the Dualists among the Magians, who affirm the existence of a god of good, who is God, and a god of evil, who is Satan. They are among the sects of the Magians of Persia, and they named the god of good "Yazdan" and the god of evil "Ahriman." They said: the god of good existed alone, then a thought of evil occurred to him in his soul, and from it arose the god of evil, who is "Ahriman." This is what al-Ma'arri criticized them for in his saying:

Some people said, their claim is false, so be mindful of God and do not make such claims.
Yazdan thought in heedlessness, and from his thinking Ahriman was fashioned.

This religion was known among some Arabs in the pre-Islamic period, from the Arabs of Iraq who bordered the land of Persia and were subject to its rule. It was not known among the people of Mecca, to whom these verses were addressed. Moreover, the term *jinnah*, when used without qualification, does not include the devils, since Satan was one of the jinn, but a particular class among them was distinguished by that name.

The clause ﴿And the jinnah certainly know that they will surely be brought forth﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the clause ﴿and they made between Him and the jinnah a lineage﴾ and the clause ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾ (As-Saffat 37:159). The phrase "and they made between Him" and so on is a circumstantial clause, and the *waw* is a *waw* of circumstance. The pronoun in "they" (*innahum*) refers either to the polytheists or to the jinnah, and both meanings are intended, since the two groups are interchangeable. *Al-muhdarun* means those brought forth to be present. The intended meaning is "brought forth for punishment," by the context of rebuke, since rebuke is followed by threat. The usual sense of the verb *ihdar* (bringing forth) is the bringing of evil, as He Most High said: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth﴾ (As-Saffat 37:57). Therefore, the object of *muhdarun* is omitted. But bringing someone forth for honor is described by the term "coming."

The meaning is that the jinn know the polytheists' lie in that matter, a gross lie for which they will be requited with being brought forth for punishment. So "brought forth" is made a metonymy (*kinayah*) for their lie, because if they had been truthful, they would not have been punished for that claim.

The apparent sense is that this knowledge was present for the jinn in the past, and perhaps it came to them from the time they were able to eavesdrop (*istiraq al-sam'*, stealing hearing from the heavens).

It may also be a use of the past tense in place of the future, to affirm that it will certainly occur, like His words ﴿The command of God has come﴾ (An-Nahl 16:1), meaning "the jinnah will know that on the Day of Resurrection." The intended point is that they will be certain of it and will not be able to repel the punishment from themselves. They used to worship the jinn, believing they had standing with God through the in-law relation they had with Him.

Glory be to Allah above what they describe. The utterance of their false claims and their threat against Him is followed, by way of an interjection placed between the exception and the excepted, by an expression of Allah's transcendence above what they attributed to Him. It is thus a declaration from Allah Himself of His own exaltation, an instruction to the believers to follow Allah's example in this glorification, and an expression of wonder at the monstrousness of what they attributed to Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 160:

﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) placed between the phrase "Glory be to Allah above what they describe" and the clause "Indeed, you and what you worship," and the exception is disjunctive (istithna' munqati', an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it). It has been said that it arises from His saying "Indeed they will be brought forward (for punishment)," and the meaning is: but the sincere servants of Allah will not be brought forward. It has been said that it arises from His saying "above what they describe," meaning: but the sincere servants of Allah do not describe Him with that. It has also been said that it refers back to the pronoun in "and they made," meaning: but the sincere servants of Allah do not make that (attribution). This is part of the meaning of the second view, so the sincere servants here refer to the believers.

My own view is that it is a disjunctive exception that arises from His saying "﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat: 159]," and it is connected to it, because "what they describe" indicates that they attribute to Allah that the angels are His daughters, as His saying "﴿Has your Lord then chosen daughters for Himself?﴾ [al-Saffat: 149]" indicates.

The meaning is: but the angels are the sincere servants of Allah. Thus, by "﴿the sincere servants of Allah﴾" is meant the angels. This verse is in the sense of His saying: "﴿They say: The Most Merciful has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 161–163:

﴿So indeed you, and what you worship,﴾ ﴿you cannot lead astray concerning Him,﴾ ﴿except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire.﴾ Their statement about the angels and the jinn was followed by this because their statement led them to worship the jinn and to worship the idols which Satan had embellished for them and which the soothsayers, the servants of the jinn, had incited them to worship,

Page 189

so this was followed by a discouraging of the polytheists from bringing temptation upon the believers in their faith, through what they attempt with them of returning to polytheism. Or it is a fa' of eloquent expression (fa' fasiha), and the implied meaning is: if you know that the sincere servants of God are exempt from the likes of your statement, then indeed you do not lead astray except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire.

This statement may be included within the scope of the questioning in His saying ﴿So ask them: Has your Lord got daughters?﴾ [al-Saffat: 149], and so on. It may also be a consequence of His saying ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158], and so on.

The waw in His saying "and what you worship" is either the waw of conjunction or the waw of accompaniment (wa al-ma'iyya), and what follows it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), and the predicate is ﴿you cannot lead astray concerning Him﴾.

The pronoun "you" (antum) is an address to the polytheists, like the pronoun in "indeed you" (innakum).

The meaning is: you, accompanied by the jinn whom you worship, do not lead anyone astray. The reason for mentioning the object of accompaniment is that they used to deceive people into believing that the jinn benefit and harm, and that the idols are likewise, and they used to frighten people with their might and retribution, as the wife of Tufayl ibn 'Amr al-Dawsi said when he embraced Islam and invited her to Islam: "Do you not fear for the children from Dhu al-Shara?" He said: "No." So she embraced Islam. They also used to claim that whoever reviles the idols would be struck by leprosy or elephantiasis.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Dimam ibn Tha'laba, envoy of the Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, came to his people from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said in his statement: "Wretched are al-Lat and al-'Uzza." They said: "O Dimam, beware of elephantiasis, beware of madness."

It is not correct for the waw to be a conjunction, because idols cannot be attributed with leading astray.

In the Kashshaf it is permitted that His saying "and what you worship" be an object of accompaniment occupying the place of the predicate of (inna), and the meaning is: indeed you, along with what you worship, that is, indeed you are companions of your gods, never ceasing to worship them, and this is like the saying: "Every man with his estate," meaning along with his estate, that is, attached to it.

"What you worship" applies to the jinn, based on His exalted saying ﴿And they have made partners for God: the jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 100], because the jinn are the ones from whom the temptation of people into polytheism proceeds, not the idols, since that cannot be conceived of them,

Page 190

He, exalted, said: ﴿And on the Day We gather them together, and what they worshipped besides God, He will say: Did you lead these servants of Mine astray?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], and so on.

The pronoun in "upon Him" (alayhi) may refer to the Name of Majesty in His saying ﴿They say: God has begotten offspring﴾ [al-Saffat: 151], or to His saying "except the servants of God." It may also refer to "what you worship," taking into account the singular form of the relative pronoun, which is (ma).

The object of "you cannot lead astray" is omitted to intend generality. The implied meaning is: you cannot lead astray anyone, and the criterion for this is the validity of the exception in His saying ﴿except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire﴾, so the exception is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh), and the excepted element is the object of "you cannot lead astray."

The preposition (ʿalā) is connected to "you cannot lead astray" either by implying the meaning of "corrupting" (mufsidin), if the pronoun attached to it refers to the Name of Majesty, as one says: "the slave corrupted against his master," and "so-and-so turned the woman against her husband," and (ʿalā) here is for figurative elevation, because the implication of "corrupting" in it carries the meaning of dominance.

Or by implying the meaning of "bearing" and "being answerable for" (hamilin wa mas'ulin), and (ʿalā) then means the preposition of causation, like His saying ﴿and that you may glorify God for having guided you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. There would then be an implied noun between (ʿalā) and its object, the implied phrase being: "upon the worship of what you worship." The meaning is: you and the devils, no one will follow you in your religion except one who exposes himself to become destined to burn in Hellfire. This is in the sense of His saying ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided. And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 42].

In the Mushaf, "ṣāli al-jaḥīm" is written without a yā' after the lām, in consideration of the state of connected recitation, since the yā' is not pronounced; so the scribe of the Mushaf wrote it in accordance with the state of pronunciation. For this reason, one should not pause upon "ṣāli."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verses 161–163:

﴿So indeed you, and what you worship,﴾ ﴿you cannot lead astray concerning Him,﴾ ﴿except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire.﴾ Their statement about the angels and the jinn was followed by this because their statement led them to worship the jinn and to worship the idols which Satan had embellished for them and which the soothsayers, the servants of the jinn, had incited them to worship,

Page 189

so this was followed by a discouraging of the polytheists from bringing temptation upon the believers in their faith, through what they attempt with them of returning to polytheism. Or it is a fa' of eloquent expression (fa' fasiha), and the implied meaning is: if you know that the sincere servants of God are exempt from the likes of your statement, then indeed you do not lead astray except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire.

This statement may be included within the scope of the questioning in His saying ﴿So ask them: Has your Lord got daughters?﴾ [al-Saffat: 149], and so on. It may also be a consequence of His saying ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158], and so on.

The waw in His saying "and what you worship" is either the waw of conjunction or the waw of accompaniment (wa al-ma'iyya), and what follows it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), and the predicate is ﴿you cannot lead astray concerning Him﴾.

The pronoun "you" (antum) is an address to the polytheists, like the pronoun in "indeed you" (innakum).

The meaning is: you, accompanied by the jinn whom you worship, do not lead anyone astray. The reason for mentioning the object of accompaniment is that they used to deceive people into believing that the jinn benefit and harm, and that the idols are likewise, and they used to frighten people with their might and retribution, as the wife of Tufayl ibn 'Amr al-Dawsi said when he embraced Islam and invited her to Islam: "Do you not fear for the children from Dhu al-Shara?" He said: "No." So she embraced Islam. They also used to claim that whoever reviles the idols would be struck by leprosy or elephantiasis.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Dimam ibn Tha'laba, envoy of the Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, came to his people from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said in his statement: "Wretched are al-Lat and al-'Uzza." They said: "O Dimam, beware of elephantiasis, beware of madness."

It is not correct for the waw to be a conjunction, because idols cannot be attributed with leading astray.

In the Kashshaf it is permitted that His saying "and what you worship" be an object of accompaniment occupying the place of the predicate of (inna), and the meaning is: indeed you, along with what you worship, that is, indeed you are companions of your gods, never ceasing to worship them, and this is like the saying: "Every man with his estate," meaning along with his estate, that is, attached to it.

"What you worship" applies to the jinn, based on His exalted saying ﴿And they have made partners for God: the jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 100], because the jinn are the ones from whom the temptation of people into polytheism proceeds, not the idols, since that cannot be conceived of them,

Page 190

He, exalted, said: ﴿And on the Day We gather them together, and what they worshipped besides God, He will say: Did you lead these servants of Mine astray?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], and so on.

The pronoun in "upon Him" (alayhi) may refer to the Name of Majesty in His saying ﴿They say: God has begotten offspring﴾ [al-Saffat: 151], or to His saying "except the servants of God." It may also refer to "what you worship," taking into account the singular form of the relative pronoun, which is (ma).

The object of "you cannot lead astray" is omitted to intend generality. The implied meaning is: you cannot lead astray anyone, and the criterion for this is the validity of the exception in His saying ﴿except one who is destined to burn in Hellfire﴾, so the exception is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh), and the excepted element is the object of "you cannot lead astray."

The preposition (ʿalā) is connected to "you cannot lead astray" either by implying the meaning of "corrupting" (mufsidin), if the pronoun attached to it refers to the Name of Majesty, as one says: "the slave corrupted against his master," and "so-and-so turned the woman against her husband," and (ʿalā) here is for figurative elevation, because the implication of "corrupting" in it carries the meaning of dominance.

Or by implying the meaning of "bearing" and "being answerable for" (hamilin wa mas'ulin), and (ʿalā) then means the preposition of causation, like His saying ﴿and that you may glorify God for having guided you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. There would then be an implied noun between (ʿalā) and its object, the implied phrase being: "upon the worship of what you worship." The meaning is: you and the devils, no one will follow you in your religion except one who exposes himself to become destined to burn in Hellfire. This is in the sense of His saying ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided. And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 42].

﴿There is none among us but has a known station﴾ ﴿and indeed we are those who stand in ranks﴾ ﴿and indeed we are those who glorify [Him]﴾. It may be that this is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to His saying ﴿except the sincere servants of God﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 160], according to the first of the two interpretations, regarding the meaning of "the sincere servants of God." It would then be conjoined to the meaning of a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), since its meaning is that they are not the children of God, Exalted is He, and it is conjoined to this that they disavow that. The wāw is then a conjunctive wāw introducing an omitted speech, which is indicated by the fact that what follows the wāw cannot be anything but the speech of a speaker. The implied sense is: "And they say: ﴿There is none among us but has a known station﴾ ﴿and indeed we are those who stand in ranks﴾ ﴿and indeed we are those who glorify [Him]﴾." This interpretation is more fitting with the attributes mentioned in His saying "﴿but has a known station﴾" and His saying "those who stand in ranks... those who glorify," since it is common in the Qur'an to describe the angels with similar attributes, as was mentioned at the beginning of the sūrah, where they are described as "those who stand in ranks" (al-ṣāffāt). Their being described as glorifying is frequent, as in His saying ﴿and the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Shūrā: 5], and the mention of their stations in His saying ﴿of power, with the Lord of the Throne firmly established, obeyed there and trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwīr: 20], and His saying ﴿and he saw him in another descent, at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 13].

In many hadiths, for example the hadith of the Night Journey: "Gabriel found in every heaven an angel, and Gabriel would ask permission from him to enter that heaven, and the angel would ask him: 'Who are you? And who is with you? And has he been sent to him?' When he said, 'Yes,' the angel opened it for him."

On the authority of Muqātil, that His saying "﴿There is none among us but has a known station﴾" up to "those who glorify" was revealed when "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and Gabriel fell back, and the Prophet said to him: 'Do you part from me here?' He said: 'I cannot advance beyond my place.'" And God revealed, relating the words of the angels, "﴿There is none among us but has a known station﴾," the two verses.

It is also possible that this is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say to the polytheists, conjoined to the consequential clause in His saying "﴿So indeed you and what you worship﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 161]" to its end, so that the speech connects with His saying "﴿Ask them: 'Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?'﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 149]" up to here.

The meaning is: "You cannot tempt us into the temptation of insolence against our Lord, so that we would say what you say: the angels are the daughters of God and the jinn are the in-laws of God. Rather, there is none among us but has a known station that he does not exceed, and it is the station of being created by God and of servitude to Him."

The negated element with "mā" (not) is omitted, indicated by its being described by the phrase "among us," and the implied sense is "There is not any one of us," as in the verse of Suḥaym ibn Wathīl:

"I am the son of Jalā, and of the one who climbs the high passes; whenever I put down the turban, you will know me."

The implied sense is "the son of a man named Jalā."

The predicate is His saying "﴿but has a known station﴾," and the implied sense is: "There is none among us but is one who has a known station."

The word maqām (station) originally means the place of standing. Since standing usually happens for the sake of some work, the term maqām came to be used widely for the work a person performs, as related in Noah's saying "﴿If my station [presence] is burdensome to you﴾ [Yūnus: 71], meaning my work."

The word maʿlūm (known) means specified and fixed. The attribute "known" is applied to it because a specified and fixed thing is not confused for the one who looks at it carefully; whoever contemplates it knows it.

The meaning is: "There is not any one of us, the company of believers, but has an attribute and a work toward his Creator, which nothing can make him slip from, and no whisperings can prevail over him in it. So you cannot make us slip from the worship of our Lord." Thus maqām is the attribute of servitude to God, by the indication of this sentence coming after His saying "﴿So indeed you and what you worship, you cannot tempt [anyone] against Him﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 161–162]," meaning: you cannot tempt us, so the merit of the angels will not be confused for us, so that we would raise it to the station of sonship to God, Exalted is He; nor will we liken your belief about the jinn's dispositions to the claim that you attain for them the station of in-lawship with God, Exalted is He, and nearness to His majesty, as in His saying "﴿and they made the jinn partners with God, though He created them﴾ [al-Anʿām: 100]."

As for His saying "﴿And indeed we are those who stand in ranks, and indeed we are those who glorify [Him]﴾," the sense is: "And indeed we—the company of Muslims—are those who stand in ranks," that is, those who stand in rows for the worship of God in prayer. Their standing in prayer is described as "ranks" in imitation of the order of the angels. The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith of Muslim: "Our rows have been made like the rows of the angels." By "those who glorify" is meant those who declare God far above taking a son, or having created in-laws for Him, or a consort, in contrast to your polytheism, since your worship is "whistling and clapping," and in contrast to your disbelief, since you make for Him female companions, daughters and in-laws. The object of "those who stand in ranks... those who glorify" is omitted, indicated by His saying "﴿what you worship, you cannot tempt [anyone] against Him﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 162]," so that the sense is: those who stand in rows for His worship and glorify Him, since the discourse in all these verses concerns the affairs of God, Exalted is He.

The definiteness of the two parts of the sentence, and the separating pronoun in "lanaḥnu" (indeed we), give a emphatic restriction (qaṣr), so it is a restriction by reversal (qaṣr qalb), meaning: "in contrast to what you have ascribed to Him of sonship to God."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 170:

Page 193
﴿And indeed they used to say﴾ [al-Saffat: 167] ﴿"If only we had a reminder from the former peoples"﴾ [al-Saffat: 168] ﴿"we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah"﴾ [al-Saffat: 169] ﴿But they disbelieved in it, so they will come to know﴾. This is a transition from the mention of the disbelief of the polytheists in the plurality of gods, their denial of resurrection, and what they attributed to the Messenger ﷺ of sorcery and madness, then to what they ascribed to Allah that is not fitting for His divinity, and what lay between that of admonitions and threats against them, promises to the believers, and lessons from the fate of the earlier deniers and what the messengers of Allah encountered from their peoples.

The discourse then moved to the mention of what the polytheists disbelieved in: the denial of the Qur'an which Allah sent down as guidance for them. The intended point of this is His saying "so they disbelieved in it", that is, in the Reminder. He placed before it, in the arrangement of the speech, what records their incoherence in speech, for before Muhammad ﷺ brought them the Clear Book, they used to wish that Allah would honour them with a Book of their own as He had honoured the former peoples, and they hoped that, if that were so, they would be sincere servants of Allah. Then when what they had desired came to them, they disbelieved in it. This is the most grievous kind of disbelief, because it is disbelief in what they had clear insight into, since they used to wish for it for themselves and envy the nations to which the like of it had been sent down. Therefore their disbelief was not out of surprise, nor out of lack of capacity for reflection.

The emphasis of the statement by (in) the lightened form of (inna) from the heavy form, and by the lam of initiation which distinguishes the lightened from the negating, is for recording against them the certainty of that occurring from them, so as to close off denial to them.

The insertion of the verb "kanu" is to indicate that the predicate of "kana" is established for them in the past.

The expression with the present tense in "yaqulun" is to convey that this was repeated from them.

"Law" is conditional, and "anna" with its complement took the place of the conditional clause, which is common in speech.

"Al-dhikr": the written Book. It was called a reminder because it reminds people of what is incumbent upon them, being named by the verbal noun. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] in Surat al-Hijr.

"﴿From the former peoples﴾" is an attribute of "dhikran", and the intended meaning of "al-awwalin" is the earlier messengers, and "min" is for origin, i.e., a reminder coming from the earlier messengers, such as Musa and Isa.

Page 194
By this they mean that the earlier messengers were not sent to them, nor did they convey their Book to them; and if they had been sent to them, they would have believed in them and thus would have been sincere servants of Allah. So he mentioned in the answer to "law" what is more specific than faith, in order to convey the meaning of faith by way of implication.

In the clause ﴿we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ there is a form of restriction, because the subject is definite by pronoun and the predicate definite by annexation, meaning: "we would be the servants of Allah, not others." And since the predicate was described by "sincere", which is defined by the lam of the genus, there results a restriction of the servants of Allah who possess the attribute of sincerity to the subject; and this is an assumed (ideal) restriction, for the sake of emphasis on the establishment of the attribute of sincerity for them, to the point that they were like those who are alone in sincerity, since the sincerity of others is not counted alongside theirs. This ultimately amounts to the meaning of preferring themselves in sincerity to Allah at that time, as expressed in His saying ﴿Or you might say, "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them"﴾ [al-An'am: 157].

The "fa" in His saying "fa-kafaru bihi" is for sequence following the verb "layaqulun", i.e., their saying continued until its end was that the Book came to them and they disbelieved in it. Or it is for the sake of exposure, and the implied meaning is: "so there was a reminder with them, and they disbelieved in it." The pronoun refers to the Reminder, which is the Qur'an. Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them—and indeed it is a mighty Book﴾ [Fussilat: 41]. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿And they swore by Allah, their most solemn oaths, that if a warner came to them, they would be better guided than any of the nations. But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾ [Fatir: 42].

Thereby the threat in His saying "﴿so they will come to know﴾" has its fitting, well-placed position in the speech, and its awe lies in what it contains of indefiniteness.

"Sawfa" is a sister of "sin" in conveying the general meaning of the future.

[Page 195]

Verses 171–173 of Surah al-Saffat, the Qur'anic quotations, are: ﴿And Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they will be the ones given victory.﴾ ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers will be the victorious.﴾ This is a consolation (tasliya) for the Prophet ﷺ regarding what is implied in His saying, "but they denied him," and it is an explanation of part of the threat contained in His saying, ﴿So they will soon know﴾ [al-Saffat: 170], functioning as badal al-ba'd min al-kull (substitution of a part for the whole). However, the aspect of consolation predominates over it, so it is connected with "and" (wa), as the connection of one narrative to another narrative.

The word "kalima" (word) here means speech (kalam). It expresses speech by the term "word" to indicate that it is arranged around one meaning that signifies the intended purpose with a swift signification. It is likened to a single word in the speed of its signification and the brevity of its expression, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿No! It is merely a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The truest word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid:

"Surely everything other than God is vain."

The "word" is clarified by the clause ﴿Indeed, they will be the ones given victory﴾, meaning the speech containing the promise that God will give them victory over those who denied them and opposed them. This is good news for the Prophet ﷺ following his consolation, because he is included in the general meaning of "the messengers."

The clause ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers will be the victorious﴾ is connected as good news for the believers, for the believers are the soldiers of God, meaning His helpers, because they supported His religion and received His speech. Similarly, they are called the party of God in His saying, ﴿God has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail. Indeed, God is Powerful and Mighty"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], up to His saying, ﴿Those are the ones in whose hearts He has written faith and whom He has supported with a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22], up to His saying, ﴿Those are the party of God. Unquestionably, the party of God are the successful﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22].

His saying, "they will be the victorious," includes their dominance over their enemy in the setting of argument and the battles of war in this world, and their dominance over them in the Hereafter, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. This is the use of "the victorious" in both its literal and figurative senses.

The meaning of "the ones given victory" (al-mansurun) and "the victorious" (al-ghalibun) is in most cases and with regard to the final outcome. This does not preclude that they may rarely be defeated, after which the final outcome will be theirs. Or, what is intended is the victory and dominance promised to them as near at hand, and these were what occurred on the Day of Badr.

The meaning of "the ones given victory" (al-mansurun) and "the victorious" (al-ghalibun) is in most cases and with regard to the final outcome. This does not preclude that they may rarely be defeated, after which the final outcome will be theirs. Or, what is intended is the victory and dominance promised to them as near at hand, and these were what occurred on the Day of Badr.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 37, verses 174–175:**

﴿So turn away from them for a time﴾ ﴿and watch them, for they will see﴾. This is a consequence of the consolation contained in His words ﴿And Our word had already preceded﴾ [al-Saffat: 171].

Page 196

Al-tawalli (turning away) literally means separation, as explained earlier in the story of Ibrahim: ﴿so they turned their backs and departed﴾ [al-Saffat: 90]. Here it is used figuratively to mean not caring about what they say and abandoning the distress caused by their opposition.

Al-hin (ḥīn) means a time. It is stated here in indefinite form to suggest its shortness, meaning that it is near. The indefiniteness is for moral belittlement (tahqīr maʿnawī), which is minimization.

The meaning of ﴿and watch them﴾ is "look at them", that is, from now on. The verb abṣara (to look at) is followed by a pronoun referring to their persons, but the intended meaning is not looking at their persons, rather at their circumstances. That is, "consider their situation and you will see how He gave you victory over them." This is a warning of what befell them on the day of Badr.

The object of the seeing, whether a state (ḥāl) or an accompanying object (maf‘ūl maʿahu), is omitted, with the implied meaning: "and watch them as captives, as slain", or "and watch them and what will be decreed against them of capture and killing." This is indicated by what precedes it in His words, "they are the ones who will be helped" and "Our army will surely be the victors." The thing commanded to be seen is not their persons either. This is an instance of implication (iqtiḍāʾ, a semantic inference required for meaning).

The imperative form in ﴿and watch them﴾ is used for guidance (irshād) in the manner of the verse:

*"If the times make you admire the condition of a man,*
*leave him, and entrust his affair to the nights."*

That is, if you wish to know the true state of his affairs, wait and observe him.

The arrangement of the descent of the warning upon them is expressed by the verb of seeing to indicate that what they were threatened with is certain to happen and is near, so much so that the one promised victory is eager for its arrival. This is a metonymy (kināya) for its certainty and nearness, since intent gazing is directed only at something that is about to occur.

The clause ﴿so they will see﴾ follows ﴿and watch them﴾ as a consequence, serving to warn them of a near punishment after the Prophet ﷺ was given good news of its nearness. That sight pleases the Prophet ﷺ and grieves his enemies. In the speech there is thus an ellipsis (ikhtifāʾ), as if it were said: "Watch them and what will befall them; you will see what We have promised you, and let them see what will befall them; they will see it."

The object of ﴿they will see﴾ is omitted because it is indicated by what the implication (iqtiḍāʾ) has already shown.

Know that the consequence ﴿so they will see﴾ following ﴿and watch them﴾ prevents the meaning from being that: "Watch them when the punishment descends upon them after that time," as is not hidden.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 37, verse 176–177:

Page 197

﴿Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ ﴿But when it descends upon their courtyard, evil will be the morning of those who were warned.﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of the respite mentioned in His saying "until a time" (ḥattā ḥīn), for the warning he gave them of a punishment that would befall them implied that they would be expected to say, mockingly: "Show us the punishment you threaten us with, and hasten it for us."

Some exegetes have mentioned that they actually said this, so this was taken into account and a rhetorical question (istifhām ta'jībī) expressing wonder at their haste for it, and at its postponement, was built upon it, out of mercy toward them and to preserve them for a while.

The fa' in His saying fa-idhā nazala bi-sāḥatihim is the fa' of explanation (fā' al-faṣīḥa), meaning: if they are seeking the punishment hastily, then when it descends upon them, wretched is the time of its descent.

Attributing the descent (nuzūl) to the punishment and placing it in their courtyard is a figurative metaphor (isti'āra tamthīliyya makniyya), comparing the state of the punishment reaching them after they had been warned of it, and they did not heed it, to the state of an enemy army descending into their courtyard after a naked warner (al-nadhīr al-'uryān) had warned them of it, and they did not take their readiness until it had camped upon them.

He mentioned the morning (ṣabāḥ) because it is one of the associations of the image compared with, for it is the nature of a raid to occur in the morning. For this reason, the herald of an enemy raid would cry: "Yā ṣabāḥāh!" as a cry of lamentation and dismay.

For this reason the answer to (idhā) is His saying fa-sā'a ṣabāḥu al-mundhirīn, meaning: evil is the morning of their morning.

In describing them as "those who were warned" (al-mundhirīn) there is an allusion (tarshīḥ) to the metaphor and a double meaning (tawriya) in the wording, because those compared are warned by God of the punishment. And those whose morning is evil at the time of a raid are the defeated, so it is as if it were said: when it descends upon their courtyard, they will be vanquished.

This metaphor is capable of having its parts separated in the comparison, such that the punishment is likened to the army, its arrival upon them to the descent of the army into the courtyard of a people, the harm of the punishment that befalls them to the harm of defeat, and the time of the punishment's descent upon them to the enemy's dawn attack upon a people's encampment. Al-Zamakhsharī said in the Kashshāf: "This verse would not have been eloquent, nor would it have had the awe you feel, and its entry upon yourself and your nature would not have pleased you, except for its coming in the manner of a metaphor.

Know that in the choice of this wondrous metaphor there is a wondrous meaning, an allusion (īmā') that the punishment they were promised is what befell them on the day of Badr of killing and capture, by way of double meaning (tawriya)."

And turn away from them for a time. And watch, for they will soon see.

This is an address of the Prophet (ﷺ) that concludes his earlier address, which began with the words of the Most High: ﴿So ask them: Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?﴾ [al-Saffat 37:149], and so on. It is a comprehensive summary of what that address contained: the glorification of God and His support of His messengers. This verse is a recapitulation (fadhlaka) of the themes the surah contained. It combines the glorification of God, the praise of the messengers and angels, and the praise of God for the blessing He bestowed on the Muslims, namely guidance, victory, and success in attaining everlasting bliss.

These three aims are the foundations of the perfection of souls in this world and the next. The knowledge of God, as befits Him, rescues the soul from falling into the abysses of ignorance, which lead to error and a wretched condition. This is achieved only by declaring Him far above whatever is unbefitting to Him. Thus His words ﴿Glory be to your Lord﴾ and so on point to His transcendence. The description "Lord of Might" points to His characterization by attributes of perfection, for might comprises the essential attributes (al-sifat al-nafsiyya) and the attributes of meaning (sifat al-ma'ani), as well as the attributes that are meaningful in a non-literal sense (al-ma'nawiyya). This is because lordship (rububiyya) is the perfection of independence from anything else. Since souls, though they differ in degrees of perfection, are never free of deficiency or perplexity, they need guides who convey them to the degrees of perfection by God's guidance. This happens through the messengers to people, and through the angels who convey the message to the messengers.

The ultimate end of this is attaining perfection in this world and success in receiving everlasting bliss in the Hereafter. This is a blessing that obliges people to praise God for it, because praise requires that the one praised possess virtues and bestow bounties. The greatest of these is the blessing of guidance through the messengers, for they are the ones who convey God's guidance to creation.

Here "Lord" (rabb) means "master" (malik). The meaning of God being the Master of might is that He alone possesses true might, which is a might not tainted by need. The attachment of "Lord" to "might" carries the sense of the particle of exclusivity (lam al-ikhtisas), as in the expression "sahib sidq" (a person of truthfulness), said of one who is singled out for truthfulness and is deeply rooted in it. The transition from the preceding verses to the glorification and the salutation marks the conclusion of the surah in the manner of an excellent closing (bara'at al-khatm), even though these words are among the comprehensive expressions (jawami' al-kalim).

The definite article in "might" is, like the one in "praise," the article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). It therefore entails that He alone possesses it, because whatever is established for others of that genus is as nothing (ka-l-'adam), as was mentioned earlier in the commentary on Surat al-Fatiha.

The indefinite form of "peace" (salam) is for magnification.

[Page 200]

The description "the messengers" includes the prophets and the angels, for the angels are also messengers in carrying out God's command.

Al-Qurtubi related in his tafsir, with his chain of narration (isnad), from Yahya ibn Yahya al-Tamimi al-Naysaburi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say, not once or twice, at the end of his prayer or when he was about to leave: '﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾ ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾ ﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾.'"

Among what is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Whoever wishes to receive the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let him say at the end of his sitting, when he wishes to rise: '﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾,' up to the end of the surah." In some of its chains it is reported that he traced it back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but this is not authentic.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat Sad. It is called in the mushafs (copies of the Qur'an), in the books of tafsir (exegesis), and in the books of Sunnah (the prophetic tradition) and transmitted reports from the early generations (al-salaf), "Surat Sad," as the name of the letter sad is pronounced, naming it after its first word, which is sad (pronounced with sad, then alif, then dal, with a sukun of pause), as is the practice with the disjointed letters (huruf al-tahajji) when spelled out, that they be pronounced in pause, that is, with the final consonant quiescent. As for the verse of al-Ma'arri, mentioning Sulayman (peace be upon him):

"He is the one to whom humans and jinn were subjected, by what was truly attested by Sad."

the final vowel is a kasra of the rhyme-letter that is quiescent, changed to a kasra (because kasra is the basic vowel for avoiding quiescence), as in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount."

In al-Itqan, quoting from the book Jamal al-Qurra' by al-Sakhawi, it is said that Surat Sad is also called Surat Dawud (the Surah of David), but he did not mention the chain for this.

Its name is written in the mushafs in the form of the letter sad, like the rest of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs, following what is written in the mushaf.

It is Meccan by the consensus of all. It is mentioned in al-Itqan that al-Ja'bari related an opinion that it is Medinan, and al-Suyuti said: "This contradicts the consensus that other scholars have reported that it is Meccan." And from al-Dani, in his book al-'Adad, there is an opinion that it is Medinan, but he said: "It is not sound."

It is the thirty-eighth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Qamar ("The Hour has drawn near") and before Surat al-A'raf.

[Page 202]

Its verses are counted as eighty-six according to the people of the Hijaz, Syria, and Basra. Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil al-Basri counted them as eighty-five. According to the people of Kufa, they are counted as eighty-eight. Al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:

"Abu Talib fell ill, and Quraysh came to him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came to him as well. There was a man's gathering with Abu Talib, so Abu Jahl stood up to prevent the Prophet (ﷺ) from sitting down. They complained about him to Abu Talib, who said: 'O son of my brother, what do you want from your people?' He said: 'I want from them one word, by which the Arabs will submit to them and the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya (poll tax).' He said: 'One word!' He said: 'O uncle, say: there is no god but God.' They said: 'A single god? We have not heard of this in the last religion. This is nothing but fabrication.' So the Qur'an was revealed concerning them: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad 38:1], up to His words ﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion. This is nothing but fabrication﴾ [Sad 38:7]." He said: "This is a good (hasan) hadith."

This is a clear text that it was revealed toward the end of Abu Talib's life, and that this illness was his final illness, as in Ibn 'Atiyya. Therefore this surah was revealed in the third year before the Hijra.
