Its aims: its root is what you have learned from the hadith of al-Tirmidhi concerning its occasion of revelation, and what is connected to it: the rebuke of the polytheists for their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ) and their arrogance in refusing to accept what he was sent with; the threat to them with the same fate that befell the nations that denied before them; and the fact that they denied him only because he brought the oneness of God, and because he was singled out for prophethood over them.

Consolation of the Messenger (ﷺ) for their denial, and that he should take as a model the messengers before him, David, Job, and others, and what they were rewarded for their patience. Also the digression of praise upon David, Solomon, and Job, and the mention of other prophets follows, for a reason that we will mention.

The affirmation of resurrection for the wisdom of recompensing those who act according to their deeds, whether good or evil.

The recompense of the believing God-fearing, and its opposite: the recompense of the tyrants and of those who led them astray, and who made Islam and the Muslims appear ugly to them.

The description of their condition on the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 203]

The mention of the first act of misguidance that occurred and the root of every error, which is the misguidance of Satan in the story of the prostration before Adam. Its opening has come suitable to all of its aims, for it begins with an oath by the Qur'an, which the polytheists denied. The sworn matter follows, that those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition. Everything mentioned in it about the condition of the deniers is caused by their self-exaltation and opposition, and the condition of the believers is caused by the opposite of that. In addition, the opening with an oath carries an incitement toward what follows. Thus its opening fully possesses the qualities of an excellent beginning.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat Sad. It is called in the mushafs (copies of the Qur'an), in the books of tafsir (exegesis), and in the books of Sunnah (the prophetic tradition) and transmitted reports from the early generations (al-salaf), "Surat Sad," as the name of the letter sad is pronounced, naming it after its first word, which is sad (pronounced with sad, then alif, then dal, with a sukun of pause), as is the practice with the disjointed letters (huruf al-tahajji) when spelled out, that they be pronounced in pause, that is, with the final consonant quiescent. As for the verse of al-Ma'arri, mentioning Sulayman (peace be upon him):

"He is the one to whom humans and jinn were subjected, by what was truly attested by Sad."

the final vowel is a kasra of the rhyme-letter that is quiescent, changed to a kasra (because kasra is the basic vowel for avoiding quiescence), as in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount."

In al-Itqan, quoting from the book Jamal al-Qurra' by al-Sakhawi, it is said that Surat Sad is also called Surat Dawud (the Surah of David), but he did not mention the chain for this.

Its name is written in the mushafs in the form of the letter sad, like the rest of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs, following what is written in the mushaf.

It is Meccan by the consensus of all. It is mentioned in al-Itqan that al-Ja'bari related an opinion that it is Medinan, and al-Suyuti said: "This contradicts the consensus that other scholars have reported that it is Meccan." And from al-Dani, in his book al-'Adad, there is an opinion that it is Medinan, but he said: "It is not sound."

It is the thirty-eighth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Qamar ("The Hour has drawn near") and before Surat al-A'raf.

[Page 202]

Its verses are counted as eighty-six according to the people of the Hijaz, Syria, and Basra. Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil al-Basri counted them as eighty-five. According to the people of Kufa, they are counted as eighty-eight. Al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:

"Abu Talib fell ill, and Quraysh came to him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came to him as well. There was a man's gathering with Abu Talib, so Abu Jahl stood up to prevent the Prophet (ﷺ) from sitting down. They complained about him to Abu Talib, who said: 'O son of my brother, what do you want from your people?' He said: 'I want from them one word, by which the Arabs will submit to them and the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya (poll tax).' He said: 'One word!' He said: 'O uncle, say: there is no god but God.' They said: 'A single god? We have not heard of this in the last religion. This is nothing but fabrication.' So the Qur'an was revealed concerning them: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad 38:1], up to His words ﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion. This is nothing but fabrication﴾ [Sad 38:7]." He said: "This is a good (hasan) hadith."

This is a clear text that it was revealed toward the end of Abu Talib's life, and that this illness was his final illness, as in Ibn 'Atiyya. Therefore this surah was revealed in the third year before the Hijra.

* * *

Its aims: its root is what you have learned from the hadith of al-Tirmidhi concerning its occasion of revelation, and what is connected to it: the rebuke of the polytheists for their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ) and their arrogance in refusing to accept what he was sent with; the threat to them with the same fate that befell the nations that denied before them; and the fact that they denied him only because he brought the oneness of God, and because he was singled out for prophethood over them.

Consolation of the Messenger (ﷺ) for their denial, and that he should take as a model the messengers before him, David, Job, and others, and what they were rewarded for their patience. Also the digression of praise upon David, Solomon, and Job, and the mention of other prophets follows, for a reason that we will mention.

The affirmation of resurrection for the wisdom of recompensing those who act according to their deeds, whether good or evil.

The recompense of the believing God-fearing, and its opposite: the recompense of the tyrants and of those who led them astray, and who made Islam and the Muslims appear ugly to them.

The description of their condition on the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 203]

The mention of the first act of misguidance that occurred and the root of every error, which is the misguidance of Satan in the story of the prostration before Adam. Its opening has come suitable to all of its aims, for it begins with an oath by the Qur'an, which the polytheists denied. The sworn matter follows, that those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition. Everything mentioned in it about the condition of the deniers is caused by their self-exaltation and opposition, and the condition of the believers is caused by the opposite of that. In addition, the opening with an oath carries an incitement toward what follows. Thus its opening fully possesses the qualities of an excellent beginning.

* * *

Sad. The discussion of this letter is like the discussion of its counterparts among the disjointed letters that occur at the beginnings of some surahs, with no difference in that they are intended for spelling out, as a challenge to the eloquent Arabs to produce the like of this Qur'an, and as a rebuke for them since they were unable to do so. The scholars of verse counting (ahl al-'add) agree that "Sad" is not an independent verse, but rather is at the beginning of a verse extending to His words "full of reminder." It was not counted as a verse because it is a single letter, just as "Qaf" and "Nun" were not counted as verses.

[Page 199]

This is an address of the Prophet (ﷺ) that concludes his earlier address, which began with the words of the Most High: ﴿So ask them: Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?﴾ [al-Saffat 37:149], and so on. It is a comprehensive summary of what that address contained: the glorification of God and His support of His messengers. This verse is a recapitulation (fadhlaka) of the themes the surah contained. It combines the glorification of God, the praise of the messengers and angels, and the praise of God for the blessing He bestowed on the Muslims, namely guidance, victory, and success in attaining everlasting bliss.

These three aims are the foundations of the perfection of souls in this world and the next. The knowledge of God, as befits Him, rescues the soul from falling into the abysses of ignorance, which lead to error and a wretched condition. This is achieved only by declaring Him far above whatever is unbefitting to Him. Thus His words ﴿Glory be to your Lord﴾ and so on point to His transcendence. The description "Lord of Might" points to His characterization by attributes of perfection, for might comprises the essential attributes (al-sifat al-nafsiyya) and the attributes of meaning (sifat al-ma'ani), as well as the attributes that are meaningful in a non-literal sense (al-ma'nawiyya). This is because lordship (rububiyya) is the perfection of independence from anything else. Since souls, though they differ in degrees of perfection, are never free of deficiency or perplexity, they need guides who convey them to the degrees of perfection by God's guidance. This happens through the messengers to people, and through the angels who convey the message to the messengers.

The ultimate end of this is attaining perfection in this world and success in receiving everlasting bliss in the Hereafter. This is a blessing that obliges people to praise God for it, because praise requires that the one praised possess virtues and bestow bounties. The greatest of these is the blessing of guidance through the messengers, for they are the ones who convey God's guidance to creation.

Here "Lord" (rabb) means "master" (malik). The meaning of God being the Master of might is that He alone possesses true might, which is a might not tainted by need. The attachment of "Lord" to "might" carries the sense of the particle of exclusivity (lam al-ikhtisas), as in the expression "sahib sidq" (a person of truthfulness), said of one who is singled out for truthfulness and is deeply rooted in it. The transition from the preceding verses to the glorification and the salutation marks the conclusion of the surah in the manner of an excellent closing (bara'at al-khatm), even though these words are among the comprehensive expressions (jawami' al-kalim).

The definite article in "might" is, like the one in "praise," the article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). It therefore entails that He alone possesses it, because whatever is established for others of that genus is as nothing (ka-l-'adam), as was mentioned earlier in the commentary on Surat al-Fatiha.

The indefinite form of "peace" (salam) is for magnification.

[Page 200]

The description "the messengers" includes the prophets and the angels, for the angels are also messengers in carrying out God's command.

Al-Qurtubi related in his tafsir, with his chain of narration (isnad), from Yahya ibn Yahya al-Tamimi al-Naysaburi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say, not once or twice, at the end of his prayer or when he was about to leave: '﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾ ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾ ﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾.'"

Among what is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Whoever wishes to receive the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let him say at the end of his sitting, when he wishes to rise: '﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾,' up to the end of the surah." In some of its chains it is reported that he traced it back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but this is not authentic.
